title: Settlement Calls for Apology, Restorative Measures in Federalsburg Voting Rights Case
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Settlement calls for apology, restorative measures in Federalsburg voting rights case

 April 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 921
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — Plaintiffs in a historic lawsuit against Federalsburg this week reached a $260,000 settlement that includes an apology to the town's Black residents and other requirements memorializing the case.At a table in the newly opened Harlem's Kitchen restaurant in Federalsburg, two Black residents of the town, Roberta Butler and Jeff Stevenson Jr., sat down Friday to discuss shifts in their hometown.
Much of the change in Federalsburg is visible. On Sept. 26, the town elected its first two Black council members, a result of the lawsuit leading to the town's settlement with the Caroline County branch of the NAACP, the Caucus of African American Leaders and Federalsburg residents regarding its discriminatory election system.
"It's a work in progress," Butler said. "But I think we will get there."
The settlement is seen by many as not only a step forward for Federalsburg, but for the nation.
The conversation between the two Federalsburg residents echoed those happening throughout the town. Butler said Federalsburg's historically Black community is happy about the settlement.
For Butler, who was a plaintiff in the lawsuit, it's about the future generations. She said her grandchildren are "very excited" and added that if you talked with her granddaughter, her granddaughter would say "'My mom mom is doing this for me."
"I'm proud of all my grandkids," Butler said. "I'm doing it for them."
Stevenson, who was not named in the lawsuit but who ran for mayor in the September election, said a lot of the town's Black residents just want to see change.
"We just hope that they take us (seriously)," he said.
The April 1 settlement includes a sweeping array of measures aimed at providing reconciliation after Federalsburg's previous at-large election system was determined to have prevented Black residents from electing their chosen representatives.
The town's Black population has grown steadily over the years, with Black residents now accounting for about 43% of the roughly 2,800-resident population.
But until last September, the town had never had Black representatives on the Town Council in its 200-year history.
The settlement came just over a year after the plaintiffs filed suit in federal court in Baltimore under the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Through months of charter amendments, legislation and federal court rulings, the town's previous at-large election system was changed in June to a two-district system to ensure more representation of Federalsburg's Black residents. District 1 has a 64% Black population and District 2 is predominantly white.
Two Black women were elected to the Town Council during Federalsburg's Sept. 26 election — Darlene Pitt Hammond and Brandy James.
The settlement calls for a total of $260,000 in legal fees to be paid by the town to the American Civil Liberties Union of Maryland Foundation. Within 30 days of the agreement, $50,000 to be paid to the ACLU, then $35,000 every October between 2025 and 2030.
Under the settlement, the town will be required to:
Deliver an official signed and written apology addressed to those who brought the lawsuit. This apology will be framed and posed permanently in Federalsburg's town hall.
Affix a plaque "marking the town's voting rights victory brought about through the contributions of the Plaintiffs in this case" to the town hall building.
Create a photo display in conjunction with the historical society and the plaintiffs featuring Black community contributions to the town, which will be displayed at town hall.
Rename Gerardi Boulevard to Brooklyn Avenue.
Erect a historical marker in the town's Black community of Brooklyn celebrating the contributions of the neighborhood's residents and their ancestors.
Proclaim Sept. 26 as Voting Rights Day in recognition of Black voters' historic win on that date in 2023.
Create a town committee to focus on community engagement in future elections and matters related to the promotion, engagement and enhancement of the town's diverse community. At least one elected town official and two community members from each election district will serve on the committee.
Establish an annual multicultural celebration for the town.
"The Town of Federalsburg formally acknowledges responsibility and expresses its deep regret for actions and inactions contributing to racial discrimination and exclusion of Black residents, including its use of an election system that prevented any Black person from holding a position on the Town Council over 200 years," reads the town's written apology. "As officials of the Town, we accept moral accountability for the harms these actions inflicted upon Black residents, their families, and ancestors before them."
Carl Snowden, convener of the Caucus of African American Leaders, said that in his more than 30 years of involvement in voting rights cases, he has never before seen a municipality willing to admit its wrongs and apologize for it.
He said this "historic landmark decision" is bigger than Federalsburg.
"What Federalsburg has done is become a model to what can happen throughout Maryland and the rest of the nation," he said.
Snowden said he will use Federalsburg as a model in other cases the caucus takes on.
Willie Woods, president of the Caroline County branch of the NAACP called the settlement rewarding.
She said they are focusing on what has been accomplished and plan to build on that success moving forward.
"Build on the foundation that's been put in place," Woods said.
An event to celebrate the settlement is in the works.
"There's a degree of optimism when you have achieved something you worked hard for and you wondered if it would come to pass," Woods said. "And to see that that has happened — Yes, that's going to be a major celebration."
Since the settlement, Butler has been thinking about her parents, grandparents and other Black Federalsburg residents that are no longer alive.
"I just wish my ancestors could have seen this," she said.

title: Ex-Officers Sue Ridgely, Sheriff Over Disbanding Force
author: Konner Metz
content:
Ex-officers sue Ridgely, sheriff over disbanding force

 September 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Push 
 
 568
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Former Ridgely police officers have filed a lawsuit against the town and Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker, claiming the defendants "orchestrated a coup" to disband the now-defunct Ridgely Police Department.The lawsuit was filed Aug. 13 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland by seven former officers, including former Police Chief Jeff Eckrich, and a civilian employee. Named as defendants are Baker, Chief Deputy Rodney Helmer, current and former town officials and a former Ridgely officer, as well as the State of Maryland and the Town of Ridgely.
The lawsuit includes 13 counts, claiming the defendants violated due process and the 14th Amendment, committed civil conspiracy and committed defamation.
One count claims the Ridgely Town Commissioners at the time — John Hurley, John Buckle and Anthony Casey — wrongfully discharged the police officers. Hurley is an active commissioner; Casey resigned in June 2024 and Buckle lost a reelection bid in April.
Baker declined to comment on the lawsuit when reached Tuesday evening, citing legal advice. Patrick Thomas, an attorney for the Town of Ridgely, wrote in an email that he can't "comment on pending litigation involving" clients.
Eckrich and former police department employees ask for the town to pay economic damages for lost wages and benefits, among other items. Plaintiffs are also seeking the court to demand the town reinstate its department and employees.
In March 2024, Ridgely commissioners suspended Eckrich and the entire department with pay pending an investigation by the state prosecutor. At the time, the town didn't indicate reasons for the investigation.
At a closed session meeting in April, the town laid off the dismissed officers and support staff, a move that took effect July 1, 2024.
Later that July, the Maryland Office of the State Prosecutor released a report in which it investigated Eckrich for "suspected" perjury and misconduct in office. The report found "no sufficient evidence" of the alleged criminal activity, closing its investigation into Eckrich.
Other officers were not investigated in that state prosecutor's report.
In September 2024, Ridgely commissioners stuck by their plans not to reinstate the police department despite heavy criticism from residents at town meetings.
By that time, the town had already sold police vehicles and equipment to nearby agencies, including the Caroline County Sheriff's Office. Those transactions were made in the days leading up to and following July 1, 2024, the effective date the officers were laid off.
The lawsuit alleges that the investigation by the Office of the State Prosecutor was based on allegations made by former Ridgely police officer James Joles, also named as a defendant. Joles, according to the lawsuit, blamed Eckrich for his threatened termination from the Ridgely force in January 2024 that led Joles to resign from the department.
The lawsuit claims Joles met with Baker, the sheriff, "and the two devised a plan that would eliminate the RPD and allow Sheriff's Office to assume responsibility for law enforcement in the Town of Ridgely."
The town has been under contract with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office for police coverage since. Currently, three county officers are dedicated to Ridgely patrol.
This May, the town opted to continue its memorandum of understanding with the Sheriff's Office, agreeing to pay $493,000 for policing services, according to the town's fiscal year 2026 budget.
This story has been updated to clarify the plaintiffs and defendant listed in the lawsuit. As of Sept. 2, this story has been updated to correct John Buckle's title as a former Ridgely commissioner.

title: CPS Staff Under Investigation in Caroline County
author: Lily Tierney
content:
CPS staff under investigation in Caroline County

 August 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Caroline 
 
 746
 Words 

 Read News Document

 An investigation into the work of Caroline County Child Protective Services is long overdue, county Sheriff Donnie Baker said.The internal investigation into CPS staff was prompted by an incident on July 13, where a social worker never arrived to a home where child abuse and neglect was reported, according to Baker.
He said the agency has been "lacking in their responses," including showing up over an hour after being called or not responding to calls of abuse or neglect until law enforcement has already handled the situation.
"There are some issues that the local Caroline County Department of Social Services needs to work out, and we have been working with them for quite some time to work out," Baker said.
The state Department of Human Services is conducting the internal investigation. Maryland State Police are investigating the report of abuse and neglect.
Baker and Caroline County State's Attorney Sloane Franklin met with the secretary of Human Services about a year ago to address long CPS response times.
"We were promised a lot of changes, and unfortunately, those changes have not come to fruition," Baker said.
The Caroline County Department of Social Services, which oversees CPS, did not respond to requests for comment.
Ben Shnider, director of communications for the state Department of Human Services, which oversees the Caroline County department, wrote in an email to the Star Democrat, "The safety and well-being of Maryland's children is our highest priority, and local departments of social services respond to every report of alleged child abuse or neglect."
According to Department of Human Services policy, the Caroline County Child Protective Services response times fall within the guidelines for responding to reports for the examples that Baker cited.
The policy calls for:
Answering calls of physical or sexual abuse within 24 hours.Answering calls for reports of neglect within five calendar days.Answering calls for cases of substance-exposed newborns within 48 hours.
But Baker and Franklin said this policy leaves law enforcement to act as a middle man, but addressing the problem is complicated.
The Caroline County Department of Social Services is a state-run agency over which the county has no control, making it difficult for local agencies and officials to affect change, Franklin said.
"I have no power to enforce changes, I can only make recommendations," Franklin said.
Baker and Franklin said there have been unfulfilled promises of solutions since the problems began during the pandemic but were vague as to what those problems and promises were, saying they wanted to preserve their working relationships with CPS.
Both said they want a better working relationship with Child Protective Services. State law mandates law enforcement agencies working with CPS.
After-hours reports of child neglect or abuse can be handled in a few different ways. In cases involving high or even moderate risks, a Child Protective Services case worker should be automatically dispatched, but if they cannot respond, law enforcement, generally the sheriff's office, will be sent.
Because of the mandated joint investigations, Baker said law enforcement officers have been picking up the slack when the case workers do not arrive, leading to increased frustration by the officers on the scene.
Part of the problem may be vacancies in the state Department of Human Services, where there is a 7% vacancy rate, although Baker said he thinks the root cause stems from procedural and cultural issues that start with upper management.
"I would say that everything starts from upper management and works its way down as far as a cultural issue," he said. "And I think that there are some procedural issues within the agency itself."
Baker spent a majority of his career working in child abuse investigations and said they are near and dear to his heart.
"I know how hard that is, so it's very disheartening to me when we do not have good partners," Baker said.
Shnider, the Department of Human Services communications director, said his agency "is committed to holding ourselves accountable." His email statement said the department will address any systemic issues that are identified through the investigation.
"Any failure to respond to a report of abuse or neglect in a timely manner is unacceptable," Shnider said. "When mistakes are made, we hold ourselves accountable and take action to ensure we do better moving forward."
In the meantime, Baker and Franklin hope the investigation will bring systemic change that will enhance their partnerships and the safety of the children in Caroline County.
"I hope that some accountability and changes will come to better protect the kids," Franklin said.
This report has been updated to clarify that MSP and DHS are conducting separate investigations.

title: Police Accountability Legislation Worked on by Caroline County Commissioners
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Police accountability legislation worked on by Caroline County Commissioners

 May 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 470
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Tuesday, the Caroline County Commissioners conducted the second reading and public hearing for a legislative bill making changes to legislation defining the county's Police Accountability Board, Administrative Charging Committee and trial boards.The changes come after law enforcement agencies voiced confusion about how far the powers of these boards and committees extend.
"I will tell you in practice that (law enforcement agencies) have to work with the ACC. This has to be a partnership. This should not be a combative relationship," Executive Director of Police Training and Standards Commission Wayne Silver said.
The committees and boards were formed as a result of the Maryland Police Accountability Act of 2021, which aimed to create a system for evaluating and investigation complaints against law enforcement agencies.
The county implemented the accountability board, charging committee and trial boards when required by the state. But the exact duties and appearances of these boards are still being fine-tuned through the county's legislative processes.
Silver talked with the county commissioners about the trends seen in other counties and about how these counties implemented the boards and committees.
One of the questions presented by the commissioners asked about the subpoena power of the charging committee. Silver gave insight on how subpoena power should be implemented.
"To my knowledge, Caroline County is the only county to ever subpoena an officer," Silver said. "The ACC does not have subpoena authority... Our position on this, ladies and gentlemen, is that it is the law enforcement agency that would issue the subpoena if it was necessary."
In December, law enforcement officials from multiple counties gathered at a Caroline County Commissioners meeting, bringing concerns about an incident involving a Caroline County sheriff's deputy and its implications for police accountability practices throughout the state.
The deputy, who was not named, was investigated by the administrative charging committee about a harassment complaint. Committee members invited the deputy to meet with the committee regarding the complaint, a move considered by some sheriff's departments to be "not proper protocol" or an "overreach."
After a 40-minute conversation with Silver on Tuesday, the commissioners opened the public comment period for the legislative bill.
While no one spoke during the public comment period, the county received multiple letters from the Police Accountability Board and Administrative Charging Committee and a letter from Denton Chief of Police George Bacorn on behalf of other chiefs in Caroline County.
After discussion, some of the important changes made within the legislative bill establishing the roles and powers of the boards include:
Clarifying definitions and language and correcting grammar errors.Adjusting requirements of board members, including removing the three-year residency requirement and allowing members to attend meetings virtually. The commissioners will also appoint an alternate member of the Police Accountability Board.Removing subpoena language from the legislation. The ACC recommended paragraph removal on subpoena responsibilities, but commissioners decided to the remove "subpoenas" sentence from the paragraph.

title: Gasser Plans to Take Federalsburg Police in the Right Direction
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Gasser plans to take Federalsburg police in the right direction

 January 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 539
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — Joseph Gasser has taken his new role of chief of police in stride, setting goals to help further the Federalsburg Police Department amid turnover and a third-party investigation.On Wednesday, Gasser was publicly named chief of police in a Facebook post made by the town government. Gasser has been interim chief of police since October, when an unspecified incident caused the town to have a third party investigate the department.
Gasser comes into this position with a military background, and he has been serving the Town of Federalsburg for almost 30 years. He believes his strong background and experience will help him serve as chief.
"The jobs that I have had throughout both my military and my police career have pointed me in this direction," Gasser said. "As not somebody simply to have a standard to take over, but someone that has the ability and the knowledge to build from."
On Oct. 14 the Town of Federalsburg made a facebook post about an unspecified incident causing the town to have a third party investigate the department.
"The Town of Federalsburg received a complaint about an incident involving the Federalsburg Police Department that occurred on October 9, 2024. We are engaging an independent third party to investigate this incident," the post said.
When asked whether turnover in the Federalsburg Police Department was related to the October incident, Mayor Kim Abner referred the Star Democrat to the Facebook post.
Gasser confirmed the October incident was a consideration in his appointment. "But that's as far as I'll go with it," he said.
In the post announcing Gasser promotion, the town stated former Chief Michael McDermott, who had served in law enforcement for more than 40 years, resigned effective Jan. 5.
"The Mayor and Council, on behalf of the Town of Federalsburg, extend our appreciation to Chief McDermott for his years of service to the Town and wish him all the best in his future endeavors," the town said in the Facebook post.
In McDermott's years as chief, the department saw a significant reduction in crime rates, the post said. Gasser wants to continue McDermott's work.
"We've had a good several years here with the former chief, and I want to expound upon that and make it even better for the future," Gasser said.
Some of Gasser's goals and plans will be executed within three years, the new chief said. He plans to shape the department better for the future.
"We have several new officers with less than a year in the field," Gasser stated. "They are the future of this department. My primary goal is to prepare this department three years down the line, five years down the line, for those individuals to take over this department and to run it effectively and in service of the community."
In addition to continuing the work that has been done, Gasser plans for some reorganization as well.
"There's certainly some internal reorganization to the department that needs to be done," Gasser said. "That's going to be a transitional point, both with me coming in as Chief, even though I've been here forever. It's also going to be a task to better serve the officers themselves, like some officers have things they like to do more than others, I want to get them headed in that direction."

title: Commissioners Approve Extended MOU with Sheriff's Office for Ridgely Policing
author: Tom McCall
content:
Commissioners approve extended MOU with sheriff's office for Ridgely policing

 May 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Life 
 
 655
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Building on a temporary agreement forged in the weeks following the March suspension of Ridgely's entire police force, the Town of Ridgely and the Caroline County Sheriff's Office have agreed to a more permanent plan for ensuring law enforcement coverage in the town.At their May 6 meeting, the Ridgely commissioners approved a memorandum of understanding for fiscal year 2025 that will ensure the sheriff's office provides law enforcement services to Ridgely in the absence of the Ridgely Police Department.
This is a longer term arrangement than originally conceived.
On March 13, the commissioners of Ridgely suspended the entire Ridgely police department with pay, effective immediately, pending an investigation by the Office of the Maryland State Prosecutor. No reason for the investigation has been indicated publicly.
"To guarantee uninterrupted public safety services, the Commissioners initiated a temporary agreement with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office," said Ridgely in a press release. "Now, building upon this temporary arrangement, Ridgely and the Caroline County Sheriff's Office have established a long-term partnership through an updated Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). This MOU will provide the Town of Ridgely with complete law enforcement coverage, by the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, for the fiscal year 2025, with the option to renew service annually. This agreement includes a provision for maintaining 480 hours of coverage per month."
According to the first amendment to agreement for law enforcement services, a document between the town of Ridgely, the Caroline County Commissioners and Caroline County Sheriff Donald L. Baker, the estimated annual cost of this service is $474,971.44.
According to two versions of the town's proposed FY2025 budget, one with the town's police department and the other with the sheriff's office providing policing, posted to the town website Tuesday, the MOU with the sheriff's office cheaper the cost of maintaining a town police force.
"This partnership underscores our shared commitment to safety and community well-being," Baker said in the press release. "By working closely with the Ridgely community, we aim to build trust and ensure seamless law enforcement services to all residents. The updated MOU will take effect July 1, 2024, with the current MOU remaining in effect until then."
This matter was also addressed during the May 7 Caroline County Commissioners meeting.
"At this point in time, I plan on signing it if the County Commissioners sign it, and the (Ridgely) commissioners signed it last night," Baker said about the agreement at that meeting. "Frank Bartz was there. There was a lot of heated discussion, but that is to be expected. I look forward to the continued efforts by the county, the town and the sheriff's office. So I think that only good things are on the horizon."
Many Ridgely residents, like Lakia Harris-Pierce, who went to the meeting, are concerned about what they feel is a lack of transparency. Harris-Pierce said she is still wondering who gave the orders to suspend the police force in the first place.
Commissioner Larry Porter said, "I know there has been a lot of social media discussion about this, but basically this is going to provide 120 hours per week."
Then he asked the sheriff, "Just for clarification, how much coverage was the Ridgely Police Department providing when they were there?"
Baker said originally they were supposed to cover the town 140 hours a week. Vacancies and sickness kept them from reaching that number. The sheriff's office will cover the town as much as the police department had under the new agreement.
"Just so everybody knows, the sheriff's department is constitutionally obligated to handle and provide law enforcement services in Caroline County," Baker said. "Even if we back up the towns of Federalsburg, Greensboro or Denton, who have their own police departments… we are obligated to go in there… I do that in cooperation with the commissioners and your staff."
Baker said he takes the responsibility seriously and that he wants to give the citizens of Ridgely some peace of mind.
The county commissioners' motion unanimously passed to approve the MOU.

title: Ridgely Suspends Entire Police Department
author: Staff Report
content:
Ridgely suspends entire police department

 March 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Crime 
 
 251
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Commissioners of Ridgely suspended the entire Ridgely Police Department with pay, effective immediately, pending an investigation by the Office of the Maryland State Prosecutor, according to a Wednesday release from the town.The commissioners are developing a temporary agreement with the Caroline County Sheriff's Department to guarantee uninterrupted public safety services for the Ridgely residents, the release said.
According to the Ridgely Police Department website, six officers are employed by the department.
The Commissioners of Ridgely met in closed session Monday evening to discuss matters of personnel and "to consult with staff, consultants, or other individuals about pending or potential litigation," according to an agenda for the meeting posted to the town's website.
Sheriff Donnie Baker said the Caroline County Sheriff's Department is ready to continue to provide services to the town of Ridgely.
"We cover the town when their police is off the clock," Baker said. "We provide them with back up. We're familiar with the citizens."
A statement from the Sheriff's Office read, "Given the recent events involving the Ridgely Police Department, the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, in collaboration with the Caroline County Commissioners and the Commissioners of the Town of Ridgely, are committed to providing continuous police services to the town's citizens, ensuring their safety remains a top priority. Together with the Maryland State Police, the Sheriff's Office will guarantee seamless and uninterrupted police coverage within the town limits of Ridgely."
Residents are asked to continue to dial 410-479-2515 for non-emergencies and 911 for emergencies.
This report will be updated as information becomes available.

title: Greensboro Candidate: William C. Schaffner
author: Staff Writer
content: WILLIAM C. SCHAFFNER Age: 77 Family: Widower, granddaughter and son live with me. I have one daughter that lives independently in Greensboro and another that lives in Milford, Delaware. I have 6 grandchildren, 2 great grandchildren and am proud of all of them. Education: Graduated from Rostraver High School in Belle Vernon, Pennsylvania, and received Master's in Science degree in health care administration from Wilmington University. Occupation: Retired from Holy Cross Hospital in Silver Spring, Maryland, where I was director of patient accounting and director of payor contracting Political Experience: No previous political experience. 1. Why are you running for Greensboro Town Council? I want to bring unity, integrity and honesty to our town government and to my town. One area that I believe has been under utilized is that of oversight of the affairs of the town, from the town manager to each department and project the town involves itself with. 2. What issues will you prioritize if elected? I am keeping an open mind on what needs to be prioritized, but I do believe our eroding roads and infrastructure need special attention. 3. Transparency with the residents has been questioned by Greensboro residents. How would you plan to be transparent with the residents? Transparency is a word often used, but, in my opinion, not well understood. I do believe that our citizens need to be kept informed as much as possible on the affairs of the town but do have an understanding that that transparency cannot always be delivered in the time that our residents would like. While I do want the citizens to be informed, it is important that they are informed with correct, reliable information. Being transparent does not always mean doing what everyone wants to be done, but making sure our citizens do understand why actions are taken in the way that they are. 4. Multiple solar projects have been proposed for Caroline County. What rules should Greensboro have in place for these projects? I am not at this time knowledgeable enough to know for sure what or how the various solar projects can be affected by the town's actions, but I do believe we need to maintain as much as possible the valuable farmland we have in Caroline County. To what extent the town can affect the solar projects will require study, listening and understanding of that process in our state, county and towns to better make any decision(s) on the solar projects, if any meaningful decisions can even be made at the town level.

title: GREENSBORO CANDIDATE: Paula Turner
author: Staff Writer
content:
GREENSBORO CANDIDATE: Paula Turner

 October 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Caroline

 FEDERALSBURG — As Federalsburg continues to work through multiple town issues, it will have to navigate the coming months without a town treasurer.Treasurer Jamie Washington informed the town she was leaving her position earlier this month. Federalsburg officials said the town is working through a transition plan to make sure the coming weeks go smoothly.
In addition to other responsibilities, Washington handled the town's billing responsibilities and oversaw town finances.
The town is working to eliminate $5 million of debt.
In a text message to the Star Democrat on Tuesday, Mayor Kim Abner outlined the town's plan to make sure Washington's transition is smooth and won't hurt the town.
"Mayor and Council have an interim treasurer in place to ensure business continues to move forward and staff and bills are paid. We have reached out to the county to assist with more complicated permits as we do not have in-house experience at the moment. Mayor and Council are committed to continuity of government and we appreciate residents patience as we work to get the right staff in place at Town Hall," the text message said.
Federalsburg has faced frequent turnover of town staff throughout 2025, starting with the resignation of Police Chief Michael McDermott on Jan. 5.
Washington was the third person to serve in the treasurer role since the beginning of the year.
Former Treasurer Debbie Lawler was laid off in February, then Mercedes Moyer served as interim town manager and treasurer before Washington took over during the summer.
With Washington set to leave the town, Federalsburg will be looking for its fourth town treasurer of 2025.

title: Federalsburg Council Member Confronts Colleagues Over Emails Calling Her 'Rogue'
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Federalsburg council member confronts colleagues over emails calling her 'rogue'

 October 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 816
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — A Federalsburg council member expressed frustration with her colleagues Monday night, claiming they failed to defend her when she was accused of taking action without council approval.Council member Brandy James alleged former contractual town manager Ken Decker called James a "rogue council member" in emails exchanged with town council members.
James said that in the emails, Decker accused her of taking actions without the full council's approval.
"I've never been a rogue, as I was termed in the emails, council member," James said during Monday's Town Council meeting.
"Anything that I have done I have done with everyone's up here OK. I have a whole stack of emails where I was called these names, and you all just stood by and not said a thing, but I'm a big girl, but I have all of this that shows anything that I have ever done, it has shown that you all have said, 'OK,'" James said.
According to James, the email exchange claims James acted alone in hiring a cleaning crew to clean town hall after the building was closed for mold remediation. James said the decision to bring in a cleaning crew was approved by the Town Council.
"You all OK'd all this," she said. "Now all of this that's being alleged in here is making me a rogue council member, but none of you spoke up. So, to me it sounds like you're going along with it."
While Decker said he could not remember the emails James referenced, he said any issues he had with the town were normal professional issues, not personal ones.
Decker elected not to renew his contract with the town after he served 30 days in the contractual town manager role in September.
"I don't think there's a lot to be accomplished by trying to go in and get into the details about interactions I had with individual members of the council," Decker told the Star Democrat on Tuesday morning.
Decker said he thought he worked well with the town but didn't think he could help the town do what needed to be done.
"If councilwoman James is unhappy about something I wrote, I'm not hard to find," Decker said.
Council member Ian Ferguson told the Star Democrat on Tuesday morning that Decker sent the emails James referenced. Ferguson said he did not say anything in James' defense because Decker is allowed his opinion.
"Now, I can see the point that she's making of 'Hey, you know, you don't got my back, and I feel this is wrong,' and that's fair. She has a valid point to that," he said. "But at the end of the day, I looked at it more like we have larger things to worry about than somebody throwing names and shade or whatever you want to call it at people. … My focus was getting the MOU passed, and the wastewater treatment plant up to snuff and getting rates set for that."
James' comments were raised after a discussion about the town's water billing schedule. The town discussed raising water and sewer rates in meetings throughout September, a recommendation made by Decker to increase revenues and tackle the town's $5 million debt.
During public comment at the meeting Monday, a resident raised a question about whether the town was considering switching from quarterly to monthly billing for water and sewer. Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said there was discussion by the town but there was not a motion made to change its billing schedule.
James said that she had made this motion at a prior meeting and that it was passed by the council. According to the town minutes for the council's July meeting, a motion was made by James to change water bills from quarterly to monthly and was seconded by Mayor Kimberly Abner and passed 5-0.
Ryan clarified to the Star Democrat that the motion could have been to further a conversation, but the motion to switch to monthly could not be passed without an ordnance with approved legislation.
James said that in previous meetings and closed sessions, there were conversations about potentially moving the town water billing to a monthly schedule to ensure more consistent revenue to the town.
James said when a county official visited the town of Federalsburg, the official said, "Town of Federalsburg, you have three to four months out of the year where you had zero income coming in, and that's where one of your shortfalls are."
"Three to four months, and that's one of the reasons why we couldn't make payroll," James said.
"...Y'all forgot that, and that was where the discussion with staff came in of how can we make sure income is still coming in during those three or four months that we have no income. That was where the inception of monthly billing payment, but how conveniently everybody forgot."
The council introduced an ordinance Monday to raise water and sewer bills by 20% and will hold a public hearing at its Nov. 3 meeting.

title: Caroline County Commissioners, State Legislators Discuss Priorities for General Assembly
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County Commissioners, state legislators discuss priorities for General Assembly

 September 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 463
 Words

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners hosted multiple state legislators at the Health and Public Service Building for their annual meeting with the county on Tuesday.The meeting gave the commissioners a chance to make requests for the upcoming General Assembly, which will begin in January.
All towns within Caroline County were allowed to add to the list of requests. The town of Denton was the lone town to make a request this year.
Here are the requests made by Caroline County:
Local Legislative Requests
The county made a request that the state allow the county to designate a newspaper of record. A paper of record is the paper in a county that is designated by a government or entity to publish official notices, laws and public information.
Bond Bills
Denton is requesting a bond upgrade for the town's wastewater treatment facility. According to the county's request, the facility's "sludge drying system is nearing the end of its usable life and requires replacement. A Preliminary Engineering Study identified the best upgrade alternative, with an estimated cost exceeding $8 million."
The town applied for grants for three years but only received loan options with partial forgiveness. The request said state funding is critical.
Sharp Road Park Expansion
Denton is also requesting a bond for a playground at Sharp Road Park. According to the request, the "total project costs are estimated at more than $1 million. While the town has secured some funding from the Department of Natural Resources and submitted additional applications, further support is needed."
Items of Concern
Restore full funding for the Rural Maryland Prosperity Investment Fund. The Mid-Shore Regional Council and the Rural Maryland Council are requesting the state restore full funding for the Rural Maryland Prosperity Investment Fund to its intended level of $9 million in fiscal year 2027. The fund aims to help raise the overall standard of living in rural areas to a level that meets or exceeds statewide benchmark averages by 2030.State highway request to build Gay Street/Shore Highway intersection with coordinated traffic light. Denton has supported the construction of Commerce Drive, a roadway connecting Gay Street to Legion Road at the Walmart intersection. The Maryland Department of Transportation previously approved a signalized intersection at Gay Street and Route 404. While private partnerships to build the road have stalled, the town remains committed to advancing the project and requests county support.Renewal of highway user revenue. Denton and the county request the restoring of the highway user revenue. The request states how important the highway user revenue is for residents of Caroline County. "Without these funds, roadway conditions deteriorate, creating safety concerns and vehicle damage for residents and visitors. Restoring local Highway User Revenues would provide the Town with the resources necessary to address road maintenance needs in a timely and responsible manner," The county said in the request.

title: Caroline County Commissioners Advance Solar Ordinance with Amendments
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County Commissioners advance solar ordinance with amendments

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners have had multiple discussions about the future of solar energy in the county. Another discussion was on the agenda for the commissioners' meeting Tuesday.They discussed a solar energy ordinance designed to help bring the county's solar laws in compliance with state laws passed by Maryland General Assembly.
The ordinance would allow the county to put certain requirements for solar electric energy generating facilities in place.
Commissioner Larry Porter has had multiple safety questions about battery energy storage systems, which he feels were never answered by the state.
"I don't want to use the word lie, but I will because we've been lied to about this from day one," Porter said. "From the time this was brought up, we have been told by various agencies, various departments, that there were going to be safety provisions that were going to be introduced in this. There isn't anything in the Senate Bill 931. There was nothing in that bill, contrary to what I was told on record in that hearing that addresses self-contained fire suppression in these systems."
"Now, I was told down it when we were at MACO, I stopped and talked at one of the booths for the Maryland State Fireman's Association, and I was told it at that time, and that was August, that there had been some changes to the bill, but the guy didn't know what they were. So, until somebody can tell me that these things are going to be safe and they're not going to propose a hazard to our firefighters and first responders, I'm not going to agree to include them in this bill," Porter said.
Commissioners president Travis Breeding said he agrees with concerns for safety, but he said the county cannot completely remove battery energy storage systems from the law because it is against state law. Breeding suggested adding some safety precautions for the local fire departments in case of solar battery emergency.
While battery solar was the commissioners' main concern Tuesday, four amendments were suggested by the commissioners to take the legislative bill into second reading and public hearing.
The amendments were:

title: Chickens Find Community Support in Ridgely
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Chickens find community support in Ridgely

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 381

 RIDGELY — On Monday, Ridgely commissioners and residents discussed potentially allowing chickens within town limits.Listed in Chapter 64-4 of the town's code, the breeding, feeding, pasturing and penning of chickens and multiple other animals is currently prohibited within the town. But after some discussion from town residents, rules regarding chickens could change.
According to town staff, the conversation has been ongoing through the past couple of months, but it gained traction after residents began preparing petitions and presentations on chickens.
Mason Sparks, a resident of the town, gave a presentation to the town on chickens at the commissioners' August meeting. At Monday's meeting, Sparks said that he knocked on 471 doors and received 178 responses from residents, 87.6% of whom were in favor of allowing chickens.
Resident Andrew Meyer also spoke on Monday in favor of chickens being allowed within the town limits.
"I just want to start by saying that I strongly support allowing chickens in town," Meyer said. "There's towns and cities all over the country that currently allow chickens. Today, more and more people want to know where the food's coming from, and raising backyard chickens for eggs is one way that people can ensure that they have healthy raised source of food."
Meyer addressed some concerns he said he has heard about chickens.
"As far as noise, hens are no louder than barking dogs or children playing. As far smells, a small backyard coop that's kept clean would have minimal smell. It's no more disturbing than any other farm smells that town is currently surrounded by. I think the benefits outweigh any small disturbance that would cause to any neighbors around the town."
After hearing from residents, the commissioners voiced their opinions.
"It seems like the residents are definitely in favor," Commissioners Chad Leister said. "I know that I personally reached out to all our neighboring town councils and spoke to them, mainly just to see, some I guess bad feedback they would have for the chickens, and, as you know, there wasn't really a whole lot of it. So, I think I'm willing to be okay with it."
The commissioners made a motion to work on the legal wording of the town code to draft an ordinance to allow chickens within the town. The ordinance is expected to be presented at the next meeting.

title: Caroline Commissioners Consider Committee to Review Their Pay
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline commissioners consider committee to review their pay

 September 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 410
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At their meeting Tuesday, the Caroline County Commissioners discussed appointing a committee to review their compensation rate.According to a draft bill presented at the meeting, the committee would be created to review the commissioners' current compensation rate and make recommendations for a new rate based on state and local laws.
A potential pay raise for the commissioners, which would take in effect in the next commissioners term, was suggested by county staff, County Attorney Stewart Barroll said.
"Staff have brought to the commissioners' attention that it has been since 2009 that their compensation has been reviewed," he said. "The cost of living has greatly increased and so has the time it takes to be a good commissioner. So we've brought it to the commissioners' attention because it's long overdue."
The commissioners' annual pay is $15,000, and the commissioners president makes $16,000. This figure is similar to some surrounding counties. According to the Talbot County charter, county council members make $14,400 per year.
Compensation is much higher in other Maryland counties. The Montgomery County Council president makes $171,912, while other council members make $156,284.
Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter had some questions about the draft bill and how the committee would properly calculate the hours the commissioners work.
"I think the question that I would have would be, I'm not sure that committee would be able to really understand or have information on the hours," Porter said. "I mean we all serve differently.
"For example, the president of the commissioners is asked to do things that the other members are not. In other words, the president represents the commissioners… there's hours in here that we don't, I don't know if this committee would even recognize or understand."
Barroll made a suggestion that Kim Raeder of the Office of Law help make the appointments to the committee. Barroll said committee members could interview the commissioners to make a proper evaluation.
The commissioners will not have a say in whether their compensation is raised or not. The appointed committee will make a recommendation after its investigation into the work of the commissioners.
The committee would have to report back by Dec. 15, and the commissioners would have 60 days to act on the recommendation.
The commissioners voted to introduce the draft bill that would create the committee and move the legislation to a first reading at their next meeting. If the bill is passed, Barroll and Commissioners President Travis Breeding said the committee is likely to be formed in early November.

 FEDERALSBURG — The Federalsburg Town Council hosted a special meeting Wednesday to consult with Ken Decker, a one time was the Caroline County administrator, about becoming Federalsburg's town manager on a contractual basis.The contract would be on a month-to-month basis to help the town address issues while seeking a candidate to permanently fill the position vacated by Sally Slook, who stepped back as town manager due to a family emergency.
"I think the first order of business is to kind of dig in and see what's really going on in terms of the town's finances and sort of their operational challenge," Decker said Thursday.
"The second is to start helping them get ready to hire a permanent town manager because at the moment, what I'm just doing is proposing to provide some contractual managerial administrative services to kind of help them get organized."
Decker has worked as a city manager or county administrator for just over 20 years in Delaware, Pennsylvania and Maryland. He served as the Caroline County administrator from 2011 to 2018.
During the meeting, town officials said current County Administrator Kathleen Freeman had recommended Decker for the role. However, Freeman told the Star Democrat on Thursday that she did not recommend Decker.
Decker and Freeman had a general conversation, in which Federalsburg came up, Freeman said. Decker approached Federalsburg about offering help.
The town councilmembers and Decker spoke about multiple issues at Wednesday meeting.
Federalsburg is in the process of paying off more than $5 million of debt, most of which comes from the town's wastewater treatment facility.
The facility was built to support a housing development in the town that was never constructed, making it outsized to the town's needs.
Mayor Kim Abner said the facility is built to handle 750,000 gallons per day, more than double the current usage.
The town has many issues with taking care of the facility due to improper usage and rates for town residents not being enough to cover the cost of the facility.
"The wastewater and water plant need a thorough look through," Decker said. "I mean, we've talked about the rate study, and even though that there's been a recommendation for that rate study out there, there's been no movement on it. No pun intended, but water and sewer is where you're leaking the most money right now."
While the town didn't make a motion to officially bring Decker on has a contracted town manager, they moved to go into closed session to discuss what a contract would look like for Decker.

title: Trash Dumpsters Removed from Multiple Apartments in Greensboro Due to Undercharges
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline 
 
 395

 GREENSBORO — At the Greensboro Town Council meeting, Town Manager Cindy Yost revealed that multiple audits have been conducted on different parts of the town's finances.Within the audits, multiple overcharges and undercharges were discovered.
Yost reported on audits of phone accounts showing the town paying for multiple inactive phone lines. The audit led to about $18,000-$20,000 in savings for the town.
Yost also reported School House, Maple Village, Rolling Meadows and Greensboro Heights apartments were underbilled for trash services for a 23-month period, amounting to more than $18,000 in under paid fees.
The underbilling was due to an error with the flat rate on trash bills. The bill was divided by dumpster size. The town was not charging enough for the dumpsters including when dumpsters were full and over the trash line, resulting in an extra $100 charged by Republic.
The undercharges were deemed by council members to not be the apartment complexes' fault, so they decided to pay up to $24,000 in fees. The town notified the apartment complexes that trash service will end on Sept. 2, and Republic has been notified.
In addition to the issues with the dumpsters, the town discovered that the apartment complexes were being billed a flat rate for water and sewer services, which has been corrected for the next billing cycle.
Yost stated the cost could go up or down depending on residents' usage.
While the town is disappointed this has happened, they are thankful that Yost came in and discovered savings for the town and multiple undercharges.
"This all started looking at a phone bill," Mayor David Spencer said. "We're trying to be as transparent with the citizens as we can be to let you know where we are and where we're going and where we're headed to.
"There's been a lot of mistakes and as the mayor I have to own that. We can't go backward, we have to move forward. I think that we're doing a good job at doing that, and we owe it all to Cindy. She has uncovered a lot of money, a lot of savings for the community. In the end, I think it will turn out well. It's going to hurt for a little while hearing some of the things that have happened. It's going to hurt for some of you that haven't been billed properly, but we need to make it fair to everybody in the community."

title: Potential Bill on Public Nuisances Workshopped at Caroline County Meeting
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Potential bill on public nuisances workshopped at Caroline County meeting

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners workshopped a potential legislative bill addressing public nuisances at their Tuesday meeting.The commissioners discussed a proposed amendment to the definitions section of chapter 137 of the county's code and a new section addressing public nuisances and their abatement in Caroline County.
As defined in the current legislation, a public nuisance affects an entire area or the public at large, unlike a private nuisance, which affects a single property.
Public nuisance properties can be properties that can cause harm to public health and safety or properties that have been abandoned or unkept. The main priorities for the commissioners with the potential bill are burning trash, temporary use of recreational vehicles and abandoned homes and properties.
The proposed ordinance provides framework for identifying the nuisances, which would include notifying landowners and tenants and providing due process hearings in case of disagreement.
"The county does have the power, as does the health department, the health officer and the secretary of the department of health, all have these powers under the state statutes to abate nuisance," County Attorney Stewart Barroll said.
"It doesn't give you a great deal of direction how you're supposed to do it, but you have the power," he said. "So the purpose of ordinances at county level is to give some framework to how public nuisance is identified by the director of planning and codes."
Inspections would be conducted by the county code enforcement office, and coordination with the health department would depend on the nature of the complaint.
Concerns were raised about the feasibility of incorporating appeal hearings into the regular County Commissioners schedule, given the potential for lengthy hearings, but county officials said most of the appeals would not reach the commissioners.
County officials and the county health department agreed to work on the commissioners' concerns within the proposed legislation.

title: Federalsburg Officials Address Town's Mounting Issues at Public Forum
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Federalsburg officials address town's mounting issues at public forum

 July 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 719
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — The Federalsburg Town Council hosted hundreds of residents for a public forum at Federalsburg Elementary School Monday evening.Town officials wanted to set the record straight about town rumors, addressing issues like misappropriation of town funds, employee resignations, $5 million of debt, wastewater treatment issues and police department cost.
A 50-minute explanation by the council members explained the root of these issues and the options and plans to solve them.
Debt and staff accountability
Council members revealed the town's $5 million of debt dates back to 1995.
"We did not get into a over $5 million debt overnight, but here we are and we're trying to clean it up piece by piece," council member Brandy James said. "When I came on council, the math just didn't add up. So, looking into things, some of this debt goes back to 1995.
"The town has had a very historic past of one not paying bills on time, two robbing Peter to pay Paul, and three in order to get anything done instead of doing the right thing and figuring out how to better utilize the funds that were coming in, they would just take out loans or they would take out grants. Some grants were grants that the town wasn't even qualified for, but that's what they would do."
James said the town must pay back grants to grant providers because the grant providers have discovered that the town wasn't eligible to receive the grants. She said the town has lost grants because of not having audits done since fiscal year 2023.
Federalsburg officials plan to establish a plan to pay off debt within 12 months using money from the town's general fund. The town has frozen spending and committed to a hiring freeze, except for a part-time code enforcement officer.
After the hiring freeze, James said that the town will shift its employment focus to hiring staff who are qualified for their positions, no longer hiring employees based off relationships.
Wastewater and water issues
Council member Darlene Hammond led the discussion on the fire department water usage. She said the town will not charge the fire department for water used to fight fires, but the fire house will be metered for non-emergency uses, which it previously has not been.
The town will install meters on hydrants to help track and detect leaks and start billing churches and other town serving companies for water and sewer usage.
Town officials acknowledged past issues with inconsistent billing and old meters. They plan to take steps to clear billing statements and update account balances. They will explore tools for online payments and text alerts when bills are due.
The town's wastewater treatment plant was also discussed at the meeting. The facility was built to support a housing development in the town that was never constructed, making it outsized to the town's needs.
Mayor Kim Abner said the facility is built to handle 750,000 gallons a day, more than double the current usage of 350,000 gallons per day.
The town has many issues with taking care of the facility due to cost and improper usage.
"It costs a lot of money to fix the water main. It costs a lot of money to maintain the wastewater treatment plant," Abner said. "There are state mandates that we have to deal with. We also need a new sludge press because the sludge press presses the water out, and if you don't press all the water out, you're paying more at the landfill. So, the wastewater treatment plant's a lot. It's a big investment. It's a lot of money, but we have to do it for safe drinking water and safe toilets."
Police Department
Council member Ian Ferguson talked about the cost of the town's police department.
If the town were to sign a memorandum of understanding with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to provide policing services, it would save the town between $300,000 and $500,000, he said.
The town currently pays $1.146 million for the Federalsburg Police Department.
Sheriff Donald Baker told residents that he would hire Federalsburg's police officers if it were to assume policing duties for the town.

The town plans to continue to have quarterly public meetings to keep the town informed on all issues and improvements.

title: Federalsburg Sets Town Hall Meeting to Answer Questions
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Federalsburg sets town hall meeting to answer questions

 July 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline 
 
 1054
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Federalsburg — Misappropriation of funds, resignations and now $5 million of debt have riddled the town of Federalsburg in the last year.Now town officials want to set the record straight.
The Federalsburg Town Council will be holding what town officials are calling a "state of Federalsburg address" Monday at 6 p.m. at the Federalsburg Elementary School gym.
"I'm encouraging the public to come out because what we have planned is full transparency, full answers to questions," council member Brandy James said. "We do have an agenda where we're going to go down and we're going to lay out the length of whatever it is."
At this meeting, officials said issues like the town's high employee turnover rate and budget concerns would come up. When the Star Democrat reached out to Federalsburg town officials, they all refused to answer questions about these issues prior to the meeting.
The forum, they said, would make things more clear.
Federalsburg council members confirmed to the Star Democrat on Monday the town is $5 million in debt, accumulated over multiple years from loans.
On top of the debt, the town of Federalsburg passed an unbalanced budget at its June 17 meeting. The budget shows planned expenditures at $5,382,649.28 while the anticipated revenues sit at $4,931,594.74, leaving a shortfall of $451,054.54.
Multiple water pump problems and insufficient revenues with the wastewater treatment facility were cited as a big reason the town could not present a balanced budget.
On top of the debt and unbalanced budget, the town has experienced employment turnover with multiple town positions. This has caused lack of consistent work and confusion for the town.
Now the town of Federalsburg town hall building has been closed for mold remediation.
"We're addressing everything, everything from town hall, wastewater, treatment plant, maintenance, police, anything that is Federalsburg is the purpose of that meeting," James said.
Debt
$5 million worth of debt towers over Federalsburg. Council members plan to be fully transparent about how the debt was accumulated and how the town plans to go about paying off the debt.
"It's no hiding, and we are going to go into full detail about where the debt came from, how the debt was accumulated, who's responsible for the debt, all of that stuff will be addressed there," James said.
Councilman Ian Furgeson thinks solving all of the issues with the debt will help the town solve other issues the town faces.
"The debt is probably the biggest thing," Furgeson said. "Because if you don't have the means of getting that debt taken care of, you're going to have issues with how do you go forward with the police. How do you go forward with the wastewater treatment plant? The debt is one of the bigger things."
Police Department
The Federalsburg Police Department will be a topic of discussion next week. At the July 7 town meeting, Federalsburg Mayor Kim Abner announced Police Chief Joseph Gasser resigned from his position on June 25.
Mayor Kim Abner said that the Caroline County Sheriff's Office would take over leadership of the Federalsburg Police Department to give the mayor and council time to figure out police department leadership.
The sheriff's office and the town of Federalsburg are in the early stages of conversations about the sheriff's office taking over police coverage for Federalsburg. Sheriff Donnie Baker believes all options are on the table for the Federalsburg Police Department, including an memorandum of understanding with the sheriff's office that could disband the police department.
Gasser was appointed as interim police chief in October 2024 and announced as the police chief in January.
On Oct. 14, the Town of Federalsburg posted on Facebook about an unspecified incident requiring the town to have a third-party investigate the department.
"The Town of Federalsburg received a complaint about an incident involving the Federalsburg Police Department that occurred on October 9, 2024. We are engaging an independent third party to investigate this incident," the post said.
Gasser confirmed the October incident was a consideration in his appointment.
"But that's as far as I'll go with it," he said.
Worker turnover
In the last year, Federalsburg has experienced high turnover. The town has been through two police chiefs, a town treasurer, a town manager and a new council member.
Former Police Chief Michael McDermott started with an official announcement of resignation in January. Following McDermott, former Town Manager Kristy Marshall, resigned in February and according to the town, former Town Treasurer Debbie Lawler was laid off in February.
Also announced in February, former council member Torbert Williamson II resigned because he moved out of town.
"The town has lacked structure on many levels, including employment," James said. "That's not any secret to anyone who's ever worked there. There's not been that stable structure there for employees. So we have reformatted the way we're doing things.
While town issues have continued to grow throughout the year, according to town council members, consistent town employees have helped shape where the town can improve on issues. Implementing new training programs and policies will help the town, council members say.
"We are creating new policies and procedures and structures to make sure staff feel supported and to make sure they're getting the adequate training that they need by making sure the employee handbook is there to be a guide for not just the town but for town employees as well," James said.
Wastewater facility
According to conversations during previous meetings, Federalsburg's wastewater treatment facility has been a drain of money.
"From what I can gather and understand is that the wastewater treatment plant should pay for itself," council member Furgeson said. "Our water bills should pay for it, and it's not going to make a profit, but it certainly should not lose money. What we're finding is that we are spending more money on it than we are bringing in."
According to discussions at the June 17 meeting, raising the water rates still would not cover the almost $500,000 shortfall in the budget. The wastewater treatment plant is operating with a significant deficit.
Furgeson said the age of the facility leads to issues.
"Part of it is the age, there's certain things that need to get fixed and that's what we got to figure out, where we can shore that up," Furgeson said.
The agenda for the public forum includes a welcome with a meeting rules reminder. Next the town plans to discuss a finance update, wastewater treatment plant update, public works update, police department update and last a public comment and questions portion.

title: Greensboro Historical Society Building Decision to be Made June 5
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Greensboro Historical Society building decision to be made June 5

 May 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 471
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — At the Greensboro Town Council Meeting Thursday, the council decided that on June 5, they will make a decision on whether or not the historical society would keep its space.Town officials began discussing potentially moving the Greensboro Historical Society out of the Weaver Building in March. The move would free up space for other organizations and town agencies, but it would leave the historical society without a permanent home.
Though no decision was made Thursday, Councilman Joe Noon made it clear he feels the council and the town should make a decision very soon because the town needs the building.
"Mayor, council, this was already discussed," Noon said. "We said that we were going to ask them to leave at one meeting, then we come back, then we say, 'we don't know if we want them to leave or not.' We need our building back.
"Let's stop playing with the historic society, please. You already know that we all need the building back. Let's just come up with the date."
The council members elected to hold a public hearing at the June 5 meeting, then make a decision on the historical society after the public hearing.
Councilwoman Christina Robinson and Councilman Pete Brelia said they had met with Greensboro Historical Society President Charles Dean and discussed multiple relocation options for the historical society.
While Dean couldn't make it in person to Thursday's meeting, he told the Star Democrat that the he had a "pleasant exchange" with the council members.
"We had a pleasant exchange of ideas when we did meet," Dean said. "It was not adversarial at all, nor did I think it would be, so I just look forward to the June 5 hearing and hope that the public would turn out to support the Greensboro Historical Society."
Robinson and Brelia made points on different locations, but no location has been solidified and no final decision was made. The council members say they plan to continue to work towards a solution that would be best for both parties.
"We all value the historical society," Robinson said. "We are trying to keep it within the town limits. No final decision has been made, but we're all aware that something needs to be done, and we are working to try and work out a solution that works out for everybody."
Dean assures residents that the Greensboro Historical Society will not be dissolved and will work to find a location if moved.
"If they vote to remove us from the Weaver building, they're not dissolving the historical society," Dean said. "The Greensboro Historical Society will continue to exist. We will find a place for the collection even if the museum has to go dormant for some time, things will be in storage and eventually we'll find a better place and we will to continue to celebrate Greensboro's history at that point."

title: Program Open Space Bill is 'a Success,' County Says
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Program Open Space bill is 'a success,' county says

 May 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 383
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Bruce Bereano and Steve Wise, Caroline County's lobbyists, presented their 2025 legislative session wrap-up at the Caroline County Commissioners meeting Tuesday.Bereano and Wise spoke about House Bill 717, a bill that was passed this session regarding Program Open Space, a state program that allocates funding from transfer tax collections.
"This was a success," Wise said. "We were able to get all counties in the state to use that capital money for operating, upgrades and improvements."
House Bill 717 originally started as a departmental bill, spearheaded by the Department of Natural Resources. Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding testified on a panel to support the bill with Secretary of the Department of Natural Resources Josh Kurtz.
Breeding originally sent a request to Maryland Association of Counties and the counties' lobbyist to have Program Open Space changed to allow the counties to use acquisition funds for park improvements, he said.
The association then suggested "instead of making the bill a standalone bill let's see if Secretary Kurtz is willing to include it in their department bill," Breeding said. Kurtz agreed and then included it in DNR's bill.
The bill states, "altering and repealing certain provisions of law regarding the use of Program Open Space local funding"
"We got it put in, and it made its way through the legislature and passed. It hasn't been signed yet," Breeding said. "What it's going to do, it'll allow Caroline County to use 25% of the money it gets in Program Open Space and additional 25 towards building park infrastructure. Whereas before, roughly 25% of the money allocated to the county from the state had to be used to purchase property."
According to Breeding, projects like the Sharp Road Park project and the North County Park project could see improvements from this bill.
"It does make more money available for us to do the improvements at Sharp Road Park and North County Park and various other parks around the county," Breeding said. "So, it does give us more state funds to work with to make improvements."
The county's lobbyists credit Kurtz for help with getting the Program Open Space into the bill.
"Really very thankful to the secretary for being so flexible, and open-minded and accepting, and throughout all of it, he was very insistent on having that as a part of the bill," Bereano said.

title: Federalsburg Council Member: Misuse of Town Funds Brought to State Prosecutor
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Federalsburg council member: misuse of town funds brought to state prosecutor

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 429

 FEDERALSBURG — The Town of Federalsburg announced on Facebook Tuesday morning it had investigated allegations of misappropriation of town funds.The investigation was conducted by the mayor and the council. They learned of town funds being used to purchase personal items, financial errors costing the town to spend money, personnel policies that were not followed, inappropriate purchases and employees engaging in inappropriate discussions in the workplace, the post said.
"The Town was reimbursed for the personal and inappropriate purchases and the interim town manager is working to rectify and improve personnel and financial management of the town," the town said.
While the internal investigation was completed, District 1 Councilwoman Brandy James said she reported the investigation findings to the Office of the Maryland State Prosecutor, where she said the investigation is ongoing.
"It was only me who went to the office of the state prosecutor and said, 'Hey, this is what's going on in the town and has been historically happening,' So, they got involved, and they started to investigate like toward the end of February into March. It's to my knowledge they're still investigating," James said.
James said the fiscal year budget of 2024 brought attention to some of these issues.
"So a lot of what's going on is historical misuse of funds, it's historical stuff," James said. "Since I have gotten there, it has always been a rush to pass the budget. There was things in the budget that just did not add up. There was line items to pay somebody to cut grass for a crazy amount of money."
According to James, toward the end of November 2024 she received a complaint from a individual about misuse of funds in the town office and the alleged individual wanted the complainant fired.
James said she immediately reached out to town leadership and suggested they call a meeting to discuss the allegations further.
"Everybody on the dias said, 'Oh, we have holiday plans, we have this.' I was put off again. So we never got around to addressing the allegations until we had a meeting in January," she said.
Through closed session meetings that followed, the town ultimately decided to let go a member of the town staff, James said.
"While we feel it is important that our citizens are aware of the issues the Town faces, we have decided to not release the specific complaints received at this time to avoid the risk of liability for releasing confidential personnel information," the Town said in the Facebook statement.
The Star Democrat repeatedly tried to reach out to Mayor Kim Abner Tuesday, but she could not be reached for comment.
