title: Caroline County Enacts Cannabis and Permit Emergency Bills
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County enacts cannabis and permit emergency bills

 April 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 305
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners held the third reading for emergency legislative bills on cannabis facilities and permit denials. Both emergency bills were enacted.The emergency cannabis bill was proposed to allow Caroline County to get on track with regulations and requirements of from the state.
Adjustments were required to county legislation as a result of House Bill 805, a 2024 state bill establishing zoning requirements for cannabis businesses that are more restrictive than some that existed prior to the legalization of recreational cannabis in the state.
The state regulation mandates cannabis dispensaries cannot be located within 500 feet of schools, child care center programs, recreation centers, libraries, public parks or churches.
The county commissioners discussed potentially increasing the distance mandates further than 500 feet.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter brought attention to the distance because of the close proximity to schools in the county.
All dispensaries are required to be in the C2 district of the county, which leaves two schools in close proximity of the district.
"The only two areas we found was in Denton close to Lockerman Middle School. It is outside that 500 feet setback requirement," Caroline County Director of Planning and Codes Crystal Dadds said. "Then over by Denton Elementary school, but still outside the 500 feet setback requirement."
In response, the commissioners decided to keep the 500 foot mandate.
Permit Denials
The second emergency bill passed at the meeting added a new section to county legislation that will allow the Department of Planning and Codes to deny applications for new work if an applicant is not within code or zoning compliance on that same property.
If a resident comes into fix a violation, the county will permit to allow the resolution of the violation.
If an applicant has multiple properties, they can apply for permits on one property and not be denied because of a violation on another property.

title: Emergency Bills Introduced in Caroline County for Wastewater Definitions, Term Limits
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Emergency bills introduced in Caroline County for wastewater definitions, term limits

 March 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 420
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Emergency bills on wastewater treatment facilities and eliminating term limits for members of the Board of Zoning Appeals were discussed at the Caroline County Commissioners meeting Tuesday.Emergency bill #2025-04, discussing wastewater treatment, would add a definition of what exactly a wastewater treatment facility must be, a facility that must be for treatment, storage and disposal of wastes.
The current definition suggest that a facility can be for treatment, storage or disposal of wastes.
"Currently the way the definition is written it's an 'or' instead of an 'and', so that meant you could do any of the three items without all three," said Crystal Dadds, county director of planning and codes. "That was one of the concerns, that you could do storage only without treating it, without disposing of it or store it and dispose of it without any treatment of it. So that's what we wanted to clean up to say that the intention of the wastewater treatment facility is for all three components."
Commissioners President Travis Breeding offered situations for the smaller rural areas in the county. He suggested the definition should stay the same instead of adding "and."
"I feel like it should probably stay 'or' because the treatment component," Breeding said. "If you were just going to dispose of waste and you just want to dispose and apply as an accessory use, that would still be permitted."
The county commissioners will continue to work to figure out exactly what the verbiage of the emergency bill will state.
Emergency bill #2025-03 discussed eliminating term limits for members of the Board of Zoning Appeals and potentially eliminating term limits on the planning commission.
The bill is being proposed because the Board of Zoning Appeals believes by the time they gain knowledge of all county zoning rules they have termed out.
"If we have citizens who are willing to continue to serve, then we'd like them to have that opportunity to do that," Dadds said.
While the proposed emergency bill is exclusively for the Board of Zoning Appeals, Dadds also had discussion with the Planning Commission about receiving the same elimination of term limits.
The commissioners discussed potentially proposing in another emergency bill in the near future.
"We've got two members who've done a good job that want to re-up and do it again," Breeding said. "It's hard to find people to appoint to these boards. I think the knowledge that they both have is very important to the county, I think this is the right move."
The commissioners will discuss both emergency bills at their April 8 meeting.

title: Greensboro Meeting Frenzy Caused by Potential Movement of Town Agencies
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro meeting frenzy caused by potential movement of town agencies

 March 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 597
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — The potential shuffling of town agencies' offices sent Greensboro residents and officials into a frenzy at town hall meeting.Town officials discussed potentially moving the Greensboro Historical Society out of the Weaver Building to allow the food pantry Aaron's Place to occupy a bigger location. The officials also discussed potentially moving the Greensboro Police Department into another space inside the town building.
Discussions, led by Mayor David Spencer and then Town Manager Tammy Kelledes, took a turn when Commissioner Joe Noon voiced his frustration about how residents treat town representatives and the confusion taking root with town officials.
"I've have never been on a more dysfunctional, I don't know what's going on here," Noon said. "But I can promise you we are going to get this straight. I can promise you I will back this council. I will back every person up here on this council, and I will back my employees on this."
"... The disrespect that comes from the citizen since the way you talk to our staff is terrible, and it makes me upset. We do this because we love our town. We don't do this because we have to do this. We work full-time jobs. How are we ever going to come together we don't work as one?"
Spencer reiterated to the public that the town is not trying to kick the Greensboro Historical Society out of its home, but he said all options are on the table to help accommodate the town's needs for space.
"I know that it's going to be difficult for us not to utilize the historical society. That's terrible," Spencer said. "I'm a lifelong resident of Greensboro. I want to do everything, I want to do whatever I can to help, but we need that space."
There was confusion among the town officials and Community Programs Coordinator Amanda Weaver on whether the town had already decided to put the food pantry in the Weaver Building or just had discussed moving them into the building.
Spencer was out of town during this discussion at the town's Feb. 22 working session, so he declined to comment on whether a decision was made or not.
During the public comment period, Weaver wanted to make it clear to residents and officials that she did not come up with the idea of moving the historical society. She said it was brought to her by the commissioners.
"I would like the record to show that commissioners brought this idea to me," she said.
Spencer hit his gavel to let Weaver know she was out of order, but Weaver rebutted, "That's OK. I'm going to leave now, but the commissioners brought this to me, I didn't ask to take over the historical society."
Charles Dean, president of the Greensboro Historical Society, and other members of the historical society offered a presentation during the public comment period of the meeting stating why the society should stay in its building.
"You can imagine my shock and dismay after I heard from the February meeting that the displacement of the historical society was being considered," Dean said.
Dean and town officials discussed how they could move the historical society artifacts without damaging them. Town officials are willing to help with that move if the price doesn't exceed a $5,000 threshold.
Dean assured moving and safely storing the historical society artifacts would cost more than $5,000.
During the public comment period, residents offered many different solutions to historical society and food pantry dilemma. All were listened to by town officials.
Town officials suggested that the historical society and some town officials would meet to discuss what would be the best course of action.

title: Emergency Cannabis Bill Discussed at Caroline Commissioners Meeting
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Emergency cannabis bill discussed at Caroline commissioners meeting

 March 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 522
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners held the first reading of an emergency cannabis legislative bill and the introduction of permit zoning on property legislative bill at Tuesday's meeting.The emergency cannabis bill is proposed to allow Caroline County to get on track with regulations and requirements of from the state.
The adjustments are being made as a result of House Bill 805, a 2024 bill that established zoning requirements for cannabis businesses that are more restrictive than some that existed prior to the legalization of recreational cannabis in the state.
The state regulation mandates that cannabis dispensaries cannot be located within 500 feet of schools, child care center, programs, recreation centers, libraries, public parks or churches.
At last week's meeting, Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter suggested a zoning map be created to show the zoning locations for the proposed emergency cannabis bill.
While Caroline County Director of Planning and Codes Crystal Dadds is still working on the zoning map, Porter made a suggestion on increasing the distance for dispensaries from schools.
"My concern is the dispensaries, I don't think 500 feet is enough," Porter said. "I'm particularly concerned about the schools."
The 500 feet distance of schools, child care center, programs, recreation centers, libraries, public parks or churches is mandated by the state.
While dispensaries will only be allowed to be located in C1 and C2 commercial zoning districts, some schools in Caroline County are close to commercial zoning districts.
"I don't think we will ever run into a situation where a dispensary is that close to a school," County Commissioners President Travis Breeding said, "but to Commissioner Porter's point, 500 feet is not enough."
The county could be at legal liability if they decide to mandate that the buffer between cannabis businesses and schools will be bigger.
"So what will happen if you enact an ordinance with a greater distance and someone applies within the 500 feet and they are denied, it would be an appeal by the judge to rule in favor of the applicant," County Attorney Stewart Barroll said. "Or somebody can file suit against the county stating their ordinance is invalid."
The officials will discuss all avenues of the proposed bills and make some revisions before making a final decision.
The county commissioners also discussed a new section to denials of a zoning legislative bill. The new section will allow the Department of Planning and Codes to deny applications if an applicant is not within code or zoning compliance of the county on that same property.
"If you had a violation on your property, let's say you put a pool in without a permit and it's unresolved," Batts said, "now you come in and you want to seek a permit for something else, we would not grant that permit until you updated or gotten your proper permits for the other structure."
If a resident comes into fix a violation, the county will permit to allow the resolution of the violation.
Also covered in the proposed bill if an applicant has multiple properties they can apply for permits on one property and not be denied because of a violation on another property.
Both proposed bills will move on for the first and second reading.

content:

 DENTON — On Del. Jefferson Ghrist (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) list of priorities for the 2025 Maryland General Assembly is a bill aimed at making alcohol more available to rural event venues in Caroline County."Each year our County Delegation is proud to work closely with the Caroline County Government to bring their legislative requests to the General Assembly," Ghrist stated in a press release.
This year, the Caroline County Government requested HB 1335, a delegation bill to create a beer, wine and liquor license for rural special event venues.

"Right now, you could go and get a license to serve for one event," Breeding said. "The problem that these nonprofits are running into at the end of each one of those events, they have to dispose of any leftover alcohol.
"It's a very it's a tough projection to make when you organize these events, or you plan them, because you don't want to run out. So this would give them ability, these nonprofits, the ability to lock up any excess alcohol and store it until the next event that they would have."
According to Breeding, this proposed bill is important because it gives local businesses and nonprofit organizations a chance to flow in another revenue stream.
"Right now, the event venues would have to hire a alcohol catering company," Breeding said, "which would come in and cater the event essentially. We don't have anybody that I'm aware of, or we don't have many in-county businesses that provide that service, so this would be an opportunity to allow local businesses to fill that that role, give them another revenue stream to help make their business ventures viable and more profitable."

title: Greensboro Suspends Zoom Meetings After 'Vulgar' Meeting Interruption Monday
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro suspends Zoom meetings after 'vulgar' meeting interruption Monday

 February 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 322
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Town of Greensboro's special meeting stream on Monday was cut short.The Zoom meeting was a victim of a "disturbing experience," which led the town to continue the meeting without the live stream.
"We were just having a normal meeting, and next thing we know, there's an interruption with vulgar racial language and pornographic video," Town Manager Tammy Kelledes said. "It was stopped within a minute or less than that."
After the meeting, the town put out a statement via Facebook stating all future Zoom meetings for the town would be suspended.
"Last night, during the Council meeting, an individual or individuals hijacked the Zoom feed. There is an active investigation to identify the individual(s) responsible for what appeared to be an intentional transmission of obscene materials over the internet," Town of Greensboro said in a statement.
"Council will take all necessary steps to prevent such incidents from happening in the future, including the suspension of all Zoom meetings," Town of Greensboro said in a statement."
The town later clarified that Zoom meetings would be suspended while the incident is investigated by the FBI, not indefinitely.
"The suspension is like a school suspension, Kelledes said. "It's not a permanent thing. It will be evaluated as the investigation goes forward and council is able to talk and decide what they want to do."
Greensboro will still be uploading the meeting minutes for residents to check and see what was discussed, the town said.
"They can always get a copy of the of the meeting minutes. There's certainly, there are plenty of people that attend that put the content out on social media," Kelledes said.
The town of Greensboro's plan is to have another form of video up after the investigation has been conducted and they receive recommendations on what software is good to use to conduct meetings without interruption.
"We're just trying to get through the investigation and see what the FBI tells us and what they recommend," Kelledes said.

title: Caroline County Commissioners Offer Legislative Session Update
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Caroline County Commissioners offer legislative session update

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 513
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County Sheriff Donald Baker and County Commission Vice President Larry Porter agree that Senate Bill 292 would not be good for Caroline County.Concerns with the proposed state legislation were brought to the Caroline County Commissioners' Tuesday meeting by the sheriff, who detailed how the bill would impact traffic stops.
The proposed bill, which includes several measures related to traffic stops, would turn some primary enforcement offenses into secondary enforcement offenses. A primary offense is a reason for an officer to pull someone over and give a citation. A secondary offense requires a primary offense to occur first in order to be enforced.
The changes outlined in the bill could cause some evidence to be inadmissible, the sheriff's office argues.
"If it comes to find out if that a stop was in fact supposed to be a secondary violation and the officer stops them on primary violation, any evidence after the fact would be inadmissible in court," Chief Deputy Capt. Rodney 'RJ' Helmer said.
For example, some primary violations that would be moved to secondary violations include driving an unregistered vehicle; improper display of registration plates or tags; and driving, standing or parking a vehicle in dedicated bus lane.
If an officers pulls over a vehicle for one of these reasons as a primary violation, any evidence discovered thereafter will be inadmissible in court.
"So, for example, if a car was riding with their headlights off at night time to avoid detection and you stop that vehicle and its supposed to be a secondary stop and not a primary stop, and their is evidence of rape, sexual assault, or an armed robbery in the car, that evidence would not be admissible in court," Baker said.
The county plans to send in a letter opposing the proposed bill.
Other proposed billsAt Tuesday's meeting, Porter mentioned multiple other proposed bills from the Maryland General Assembly and the county's stances on them.
Proposed Senate Bill 478 would prohibit the Public Service Commission from approving a solar energy generating station unless they receive written approval from the county. The county is in favor of the bill, with Porter saying, "obviously that's a support for us."
Proposed House Bill 487 and Senate Bill 484 would ban a local legislative body from prohibiting the placement of a certain manufactured homes in certain residential zoning districts under certain circumstances. The county will oppose the bills.
"This basically means someone can come pitch a tent and live on the courthouse greens, and it will be nothing we can do about it, and if we do they can sue us," Porter said. "We had a long discussion about this last night, and we will have a big discussion about it tomorrow. This is something we should oppose."
Proposed Senate Bill 481 prohibits the Maryland Department of Health from limiting the amount of revenue the holder of an on-farm home processing license may derive from food processed under the license. This is another bill the county will oppose.
"This is for people the grow produce and sell it, Porter said. "I don't think we should be involved in limiting the revenue they make."

title: Caroline County Commissioners Offer Legislative Session Updates
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Caroline County commissioners offer legislative session updates

 January 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub | Section: News 
 
 458
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At the Caroline County Commissioners meeting Tuesday, officials discussed bills working their way through the General Assembly.Commission Vice President Larry Porter led the discussion about the legislative session. He highlighted two proposed bills that the county commissioners are concerned about.
Senate Bill 0189 prohibits counties and the state from taking preserved farm or conservation land via eminent domain and Senate Bill 0724 would mandate seatbelts on all school buses.
SCHOOL BUS SEATBELTSThis isn't the first time seatbelt requirements on school busses has been proposed in the General Assembly. Similar bills have been filed for many years and have not passed, with counties largely complaining about the cost of implementation.
This year's bill would mandate that every school bus made, brought or built after 2027 must have a seatbelt installed on every seat.
The county commissioners said they would have a conversation with Caroline County Public Schools about the bill, but they expressed concerns about the potential cost of enacting it.
"I don't think I'm interested in testifying," Larry Porter said about a request he received to oppose the legislation. "But I think we could probably reach out to the superintendent because there were some concerns from their transportation department about it."
The concerns for the County Commissioners have been the same every time this measure has been proposed — the cost of installing seat belts on every school bus, who is liable if the kids don't put seatbelts on and how the school bus drivers will enforce seatbelt wearing.
"We have the same concerns that we had before," Porter said at the Tuesday meeting.
In an interview, Commission President Travis Breeding mentioned but he believes the design of the seats on the bus helps keep students safe without seatbelts.
EMINENT DOMAINThe county is more receptive to eminent domain bill, but they want to see some revisions before it's passed.
"The eminent domain bill was prohibiting the state or county from taking land by eminent domain in areas that were preservation areas," Porter said. "In the beginning, that sounds like that's something we would absolutely support."
The county recently had a situation at Long Swamp Bridge that made the commissioners feel revisions needed to be made to the measure. The county needed more space for the construction of a new bridge at the site, and it brought some preserved land from a owner to make more space.
If the eminent domain bill was enacted it would have been way more trouble for the county to go through that process of buying the land, Breeding said. It could have caused a lane closure.
"We didn't use eminent domain, but because (of) the landowner. It was in preservation land, and he negotiated," Breeding said.
They commissioners suggest maybe revising the bill to make it easier to work out future land preservation problems.

title: Greensboro Library Lease to be Renewed and Emergency Bill Passed
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro Library lease to be renewed and Emergency Bill passed

 January 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 411
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Greensboro Library's 30-year lease is coming to an end, and the intention is to renew the lease, but the Caroline County Commissioners want some changes before signing.The lease expires on March 31 and has to be renewed within 60 days of the expiration date.
The Maryland Rural Development Corporation, which holds the lease, is between administrators. The corporation has selected a person to be administrator but has not confirmed the new hire, which is holding up the lease extension.
The commissioners' concern was with Section 2.3 of the lease, which does not direct any part of the lease payments into a fund for library maintenance. The county wants to structure a fund that will handle the library's maintenance but doesn't want to fund a property they don't own.
The library's maintenance has been a problem, according to Jonah Owens, executive director of the Caroline County Public Library. He said the HVAC system has not been working properly the past two months. Sometimes employees can come into work and see temperatures of 40-50 degrees on the thermostat.
The county commissioners want to establish a good working relationship with the library and the Maryland Rural Development Corporation. The first step, they said, is fixing the HVAC system.
"I'm no longer prepared to accept the building not being heated and cool," Caroline County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said. "I mean, that's just a standard when you lease a space. It's your responsibility to make sure everything works properly, so we need to resolve that."
To establish a good working relationship with all three parties, the plan is to renew the 30-year lease so the library can stay open and work on a new lease that allows some money to flow to a fund to upkeep the library.
The process of reworking a new lease will be derailed until the corporation appoints a new administrator.
The county commissioners made a motion to sign the lease with the intention to rework the lease at a later date.
ALCOHOL, CANNABIS TAXThe Caroline County Commissioners passed the emergency bill establishing the Caroline County Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund.
The tax sales of alcoholic beverages and cannabis will go to the fund, which will benefit low-income communities in Caroline County.
The emergency bill was proposed by the county to comply with the Maryland Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article, which allows the sales tax of these items to be used for the county's benefit. The state mandated each county create its own version of this fund.

 The Town of Greensboro conducted its Town Council meeting on Thursday via Zoom discussing many issues on the agenda, as well as some raise by members of the audience.A Greensboro resident, who did not identify herself during the meeting, suggested a YouTube channel be created for residents who can't attend the Town Council meetings, which at this time are only offered online via Zoom call. Streaming the meetings on YouTube would allow residents to watch them after the meeting has happened.
"I kind of put out an idea about having a YouTube channel that we could upload these meetings to," the resident stated, "so that the public isn't confined to coming out in person or watching a live Zoom, something that they could go back and watch after the fact as they're available to was pretty well received. They like the idea that they could go back and view after the fact, so that's just something to consider for the council."
Suggested citizen patrolAnother suggestion offered by the same town resident was a citizen security patrol to work with local law enforcement on keeping the community safe.
This suggestion came in response to the town's lack of law enforcement. Earlier this year, the town weighed whether to close its police department, which was down to only one officer.
"Another thing that I put out that was also pretty well received with a few concerns, was a community citizen security patrol," the resident said. "Putting together some volunteers that could work with the local law enforcement, with some training and background checks to be qualified to be a volunteer, to ride around, identified with maybe a magnet saying that there are community watch, maybe some signs throughout the town saying there's community watch in the area, just to kind of reduce since we're having a police staffing issue too."
New historical society presidentThe president of the Greensboro Historical Society, Vanice Myers, is stepping down as president and moving on to another position in Caroline County as Vice President of the Caroline County Branch of the NAACP.
"Effective Dec. 31, I will no longer be the president of Greensboro Historical Society. The new president of the historical society will be Chad Dean," Meyers said.
When Meyers took the position in 2023, she was the youngest and the first Black president of the historical society.

title: Caroline Commissioners Discuss Lack of State Guidance on Cannabis Reinvestment Funds
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Caroline commissioners discuss lack of state guidance on cannabis reinvestment funds

 December 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 507
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — As Caroline County works to comply with a section of Maryland's Cannabis Reform Act of 2023, concerns are being raised about a lack of direction from the state in spending money collected from cannabis sales tax.The Cannabis Reform Act created a Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund, designed to allocate 35% of the collected taxes from cannabis sales back into communities most affected by the disproportionate enforcement of previous cannabis laws.
The Caroline County Commissioners introduced an emergency bill during Tuesday's meeting that if passed, would establish a Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund at the county level, which is required by the 2023 state legislation.
However, four counties — Caroline, Garrett, Kent and Queen Anne's — do not have any communities identified by the state's Office of Social Equity as "disproportionately impacted areas."
The Reform Act defines those areas as ones that "had above 150% of the state's 10-year average for cannabis possession charges."
"So as we sit here today and we're talking about introducing this legislation, we don't know where the money can be spent in the county?" Commission Vice President Larry Porter asked during Tuesday morning's weekly meeting.
Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox said his correspondence to the Office of Social Equity seeking guidance on where the county is permitted to spend the money has gone unanswered for more than a month.
"I cannot, with an honest heart, sit here and tell you that we have any guidance," Fox said.
"In a phone call, the guidance was, 'you guys can certainly interpret it how you want and self-identity disproportionately impacted areas,'" Fox later said. "And I think my question was, 'OK, so we get to this reporting period, what's to say you're (not) going to pull the rug out from under us?'"
County Attorney Stewart Barroll said the 2024 portion sent to Caroline County was just over $367,000. The county's bill introduced Tuesday would give the county the ability to spend that money.
Porter said while he supports introducing the bill to work toward the creation of a county reinvestment fund, he's "not going to be big on self-interpreting anything when it comes to this money."
"My recommendation would be if we don't have an answer on where we can spend this money," Porter said, "we don't spend a dime until we get a specific answer."
Commission President Travis Breeding said even if the county were to spend the money on low-income communities that fall within the legislation's other guidelines, it could be breaking the state law since it technically doesn't have any "disproportionately impacted areas" as defined by the state.
"To me, the Legislature needs to go back and amend it," Breeding said.
Breeding, Porter and Commissioner Frank Bartz all voted to introduce the emergency bill. A second reading and public hearing will be held Dec. 17, with a third reading and potential vote on the bill set for Jan. 7.
"We need guidance," Porter stated earlier in the meeting. "The money is coming. It's a substantial amount of money. If there are going to be regulations or requirements on this … we need to know that."

title: Caroline County Introduces Two Pieces of Emergency Legislation
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County introduces two pieces of emergency legislation

 July 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 577
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At Tuesday's Caroline County Commissioners meeting, the commission introduced two pieces of emergency legislation.The commissioners discussed a bill to create a food processing residuals storage permit along with a bill to add reasonable accommodation procedures to county code. Both bills were not voted on and will be discussed at upcoming county meetings.
STORAGE BILL
Since late last year, the county has been under pressure from residents to crack down on the usage and storage of food processing residuals, often referred to as DAF residuals, on farms and properties.
Dissolved air flotation is a method for processing wastewater from food processing plants. The method leaves behind a sludge-like byproduct, or DAF residuals.
On the Shore, much of the material generated from DAF comes from poultry processing plants, though some comes from industrial and wastewater treatment sludge.
Both the county and industry leaders have noted there are certain "bad actors" creating odors for neighbors and residents.
The bill would create a food processing residuals storage permit under the county's Department of Planning and Codes. The proposed legislation would put a focus on the storage of the residuals, including the ban of all "open top container" storage.
Holly Porter, the executive director of the Delmarva Chicken Association and a Denton resident, expressed her disappointment with the legislation as written. She asked that the commissioners look at procedures in Wicomico and Carroll counties.
"You don't disregard your biggest economic driver in the county," she said to the commission. " … In my mind, these 25 pages do not show that farmers are the priority."
Commissioner Frank Bartz — Commissioner, Caroline County Commissioners, Larry Porter — Vice President, Caroline County Commissioners, and Travis Breeding — President, Caroline County Commissioners said he believes Carroll County legislation is too "open-ended" and will have future consequences. Porter, meanwhile, brought up concerns that continued restriction could hurt the agriculture industry.
"You potentially open up the door that five years or ten years from now," she said, "people are going to come in and complain about other odors."
"I think we're probably a ways apart on this unfortunately," Breeding said. "But we will certainly take your comments and take them into consideration."
ACCOMMODATION BILL
County Attorney Stewart Barroll presented a new bill that would add a reasonable accommodation procedure to the county law. Barroll said under the bill, the county would be required to determine whether a request for an accommodation — such as a wheelchair ramp or elevator — is granted or not.
The bill outlines that the Planning Commission would review requests for reasonable accommodation.
"This is best practice," Barroll said. "Not every local government has this. … But research reveals that it's a glaring source of a potential federal liability for you to not have a procedure in place."
Commission Vice President Larry Porter said that while the county could make every effort possible to accommodate a request, he was unsure of where the cutoff would be.
"Where does it stop?" Porter said. " … I'm just not clear where it stops here."
Barroll said "it's not one size fits all," and that requests will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. As the legislation is currently written, any appeals for requests must come from the person who submitted the accommodation request, Barroll said, and not from neighbors.
Breeding noted that the Planning Commission provided a favorable recommendation for the bill. It will also give the county a better standing if lawsuits come up, he said.
"At least we can show a federal judge, if it ever did get there," Breeding said, "that we have a procedure in place and these are the reasons why we didn't grant the accommodation."

title: Gov. Moore: 'The Shore Must Be Able to Live Up to All of Its Promise'
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Gov. Moore: 'The Shore must be able to live up to all of its promise'

 June 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 503
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Gov. Wes Moore spent Friday afternoon on the Eastern Shore, meeting with local officials as well as nonprofit and agricultural leaders."It's great being back here, it's the 18th time that we've been on the Shore since I've been the governor," Moore said. "... I believe deeply that if this is going to be Maryland's decade, it means that the Shore must also be able to live up to all of its promise."
He made his first stop at the Caroline County Sheriff's Office for a tour of the facility that opened in 2021. Sheriff Donald Baker showed the governor everything from the department's inventory of supplies to its men and women working daily to protect residents.
"We absolutely treat our citizens the way they should be treated," Baker said to the governor.
The two talked about low homicide rates in Caroline County, collaboration between neighboring police and the task of policing in such a large state where policies are different county-by-county. Moore asked about the county's approach to other forms of policing and community safety.
"We definitely believe in community policing," the sheriff said.
Moore took the short ride from Denton to Ridgely to visit Martin's House & Barn, a homeless shelter that provides a food pantry and thrift shop for those in need.
He met with staff and board members of the organization, lauding the work they do for the homeless population.
"We've prioritized everything from funding going toward the Shore, health care … but also organizations like this one that are doing remarkable work," Moore said.
Moore donned a baseball cap for his final stop of the day at Twin Maple Farm in Ridgely. Dave Tribbett Jr. introduced the governor to his team and the farm's planting of miscanthus grass, an environmentally friendly product that can be used for bedding in chicken houses and the creation of biodegradable to-go containers.
Visibly impressed by the environmental benefits of miscanthus grass, Moore asked about building infrastructure to process the grass, as well as the challenges of growing it.
The governor didn't mind getting up close, walking through the farm's fields and getting a close look at the water filtration system and the ground beneath the crops.
Representatives and members from the Maryland Department of Agriculture, Mountaire Farms and USDA were present for Moore's last stop. Travis Hedrick, CEO of North Carolina-based AGgrow Tech, provided Moore insight into the benefits of miscanthus.
Hedrick said miscanthus is especially great for small farmers since it doesn't require equipment to replant it every year. There are around 3,000 acres of the crop on the Shore, he said.
If sent to other farms in the area, Hedrick and others emphasized it could create a mini-industry of growing and processing jobs.
"You had me at jobs," Moore said.
Before his three-stop tour, Moore's team held a cabinet meeting with the Caroline County commissioners.
"I just told the commissioners — and as they've seen — our belief in them and our commitment to their success is real and this is an administration that believes deeply in making sure the Shore succeeds," Moore said.

title: Caroline Commissioners Talk Flooding, Medford House
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline commissioners talk flooding, Medford House

 April 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: News 
 
 649
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Denton — The Caroline County Commissioners met on April 23 and discussed many issues, including the Medford House Agricultural Interpretive Center and stormwater flooding in Federalsburg.Medford HouseThe commissioners expressed reservations about a plan to fund renovations to the Medford House, an agricultural and historical house that the Historical Society of Caroline County has plans to use for educational tours.
On March 26, members of the historical society came before the commissioners with a bond bill for $150,000 from the state. Due to a technicality with the property's ownership, the state initially refused to release the funds to the historical society.
The historical society owns the Medford House itself, but the county owns the land it sits on.
The Historical Society wanted the county to act as the recipient of the funds from the state and passing those funds along to the society. The commissioners had some time to think about it and stated reservations with that plan on April 23.
"They had approached this board about having the county be the grantee of this bond and the pass through. As far as the financial aspect, it is very in line with prior block grants that we have received where essentially we are the grantee," said Daniel Fox, deputy administrator. "The county is the financial entity and would be the one called back if the money wasn't spent accordingly… As far as the state's eyes, we are the awardee of that $150,000 and would be responsible for making sure they comply with spending and requirements of the bond bill."
He asked if there were any comments or reservations about this bond and the county's responsibility to pay it back.
Commissioner Larry Porter said, "My reservations are twofold. Number one, it is the obligation of time and staff power that we are going to have to expend on this. Number two, the point about people handling money being bonded. I am not impugning the people, it is the position, not the people. You cannot have people who are going to be handling sums of money in excess of $150,000 unless they are bonded."
Porter said though he supported the Medford House project, he feared other entities may to come to the commission looking for them to sponsor a bond or grant.
"We are just going to continue having these things thrown in our lap, and I don't know if we can continue to handle them as a sub-recipient," Porter said.
"We need to get the word out that if you are going to apply for a grant where the county is going to be a sub-recipient, we are going to come looking to you to spend some money on your own to make sure these things work… We have limited staff," Porter said.
Fox noted that it can take all day to deal with a block grant that has federal and state wage requirements.
As the current location of the Medford House is in the public's eye, Commission President Travis Breeding said he wanted to work something out to get the house moved.
He said to Fox, "If you feel like you can handle that one, I would like to see something done with that house."
Federalsburg FloodingCommissioners discussed stormwater and heavy rains that they said has reached the second step on some apartments in Federalsburg. There's a few houses where the flooding has been so bad that they have to raise the house and the bottom of the house is rotted out.
As a potential solution to the flooding, the commissioners discussed evaluating drainage ditches in the area.
Breeding said that the GIS (geographic information system) would be interesting to look at to determine which drainage ditches in the county are the county's responsibility to maintain.
"Who is responsible for maintenance? Is it the property owner? Is it the county?" Breeding asked. "From a GIS standpoint, where are those tax ditches? And where would other ditches be that maybe nobody is really responsible for maintenance?"

title: Local legislators reflect on General Assembly
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Local legislators reflect on General Assembly

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 629
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — On Wednesday morning, the Caroline County Chamber of Commerce hosted a Legislative Wrap-up Breakfast with Maryland senators and delegates from the Eastern Shore.The meeting provided a summary and discussion of the recent Maryland state legislative session, the General Assembly. Topics discussed included DAF residual legislation and solar energy.
Sens. Stephen Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline) and Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), along with Dels. Jay Jacobs (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), Steven Arentz (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), Christopher T. Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Jefferson Ghrist (R-36, Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), were in attendance.
Jacobs spoke on his work on the Environmental and Transportation Committee and the work both delegates and local leadership in Caroline County had on regulating dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals.
"I really do appreciate the fact that all three county commissioners and Caroline County were there because it had a huge impact on the committee in Annapolis," Jacobs said. "With an issue that meant that much to the county, all three county commissioners showed up and gave very compelling testimony as to the real problem."
DAF is a method for processing wastewater from food processing plants. The method leaves behind a sludge-like byproduct, or DAF residuals.
House Bill 991 and its pair, Senate Bill 1074, aim to establish a food processing residuals utilization permit authorizing the Department of Agriculture to issue the permits, develop a fee schedule and inspect any site where food processing residuals are utilized.
This bill is significant to the residents of Caroline County, who have raised concerns about the storage of dissolved air flotation residuals and other waste materials.
The Caroline County Commissioners introduced legislation on Feb. 6 to establish four moratoriums related to DAF residuals, vegetable processing wastewater and the storage of biosolids not permitted by the Department of the Environment.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter said he met with Del. Sara Love (D-Montgomery); Alan Girard, Eastern Shore director at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation; and a Caroline County Department of Planning and Codes representative to discuss the draft legislation.
The bill is awaiting final approval by Governor Wes Moore to sign into law.
SOLAR DEVELOPMENT
Delegates expressed concerns over legislation they said took away a vital part of the comprehensive solar development planning process, giving local communities less determination over solar expansion.
Jacobs spoke on Senate Bill 783, or the Brighter Tomorrow Act, which would lower the cost of developing Maryland solar projects and increase the value of solar energy for consumers across the state.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter, who was in attendance, argued that if counties are forced to have more solar, they should be able to negotiate and charge what they want from solar facilities. SB 783 attempted to limit taxes charged to commercial solar facilities.
"I made a comment in the committee: If solar was as good as we are told it's good … Why doesn't everybody in this room have it?" Arentz said. "We're pushing so hard for something we can do. And I think the General Assembly has to, at some point, wake up."
The state's Renewable Portfolio Standard had already established a nation-leading mandate to deploy solar that equals 14.5% of Maryland's electric demand by 2030. Maryland has fallen behind the pace to meet that goal, only meeting 55% of the policy's intermediate 2022 target.
After the delegates had reflected on this year's legislative session, Arentz expressed his appreciation to his fellow delegates for the work that was accomplished during the legislative session.
"I appreciate the time. You guys are wonderful. And as these guys said, this is kind of a love fest. We do it here. We do it up in Cecil County. And we're very, very lucky because we have a lot of like-minded people to communicate, we talk, and we work well together," he said.

title: Caroline Commissioners Enact DAF Storage Legislation
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Commissioners enact DAF storage legislation

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 838
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners voted unanimously to adopt four resolutions designed to give them time to study the issue of storing dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals and other materials in the county.About two dozen people attended a public hearing on the matter Tuesday, Feb. 27, at the Health and Public Services Building in Denton.
The commissioners considered four moratoria that had been reviewed, amended and approved by the Caroline County Planning Commission Feb. 14.
The five-member Planning Commission determined if each were in accordance with the county's comprehensive plan and water and sewer plan. The resolutions also were revised on the counsel of County Attorney Stewart Barroll.
The set of moratoria addresses issues the County Commissioners learned about in December, when residents complained of possible illegal storage of DAF residuals.
"This was totally going on without any knowledge or consent or permitting by the county at all," Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding, a member of the Planning Commission, said Feb. 14.
Breeding called the issue a "huge gaping hole in storage where it's unregulated." The new legislation, which is in effect until Nov. 1, gives the County Commissioners time to research and "generate local regulations to fill that hole," Breeding said.
The legislation comprises temporary moratoria prohibiting the use of land or structures for the discharge or storage of four types of materials.
Resolution 2024-004 deals with the storage of bio-solids, Resolution 2024-005 addresses the "vegetable processing waste/wastewater and other specified substances," Resolution 2024-006 focuses on the storage of "materials other than livestock manure" in a "structure designed and/or permitted for the storage of livestock manure" and Resolution 2023-007 deals with the storage of "food processing residual and/or DAF residual."
Two industry spokespersons who had voiced their concerns to the commissioners in previous settings again spoke.
Mark Cropper of Ocean City, representing Denali Water Solutions LLC, asked the commissioners to restore the commencement date of Jan. 1, 2023, a provision that had appeared in the original Resolution 2023-25, "and if you do that, then you will hear no complaints from Denali," he said.
"We are here to help if you want our help," Cropper said. "But we think it's imperative that you do try to distinguish between those that have been storing and land-applying DAF without concern to neighbors from those that do otherwise."
His concern was echoed by Holly Porter of Denton, who is executive director of Delmarva Chicken Association, "the trade association representing the backbone of Caroline County, and that is our chicken community here," she said.
She also requested that "This moratorium shall not apply to the use of structures or land which had been used for the storage of food processing residual and/or DAF residuals prior to Jan. 1, 2023" be restored to Resolution 2024-007.
"We really just want to make sure that those 60 (or) 70 farmers throughout the state who have been using these food residuals properly and responsibly can continue to do so while we also have safeguards on those who are not," Porter said.
The commissioners did not restore that language.
County resident Russ Yates who, along with his wife, owns Holiday Park Campground near Greensboro, which now provides short-term rental units for 35 families, spoke up. He said he was "very upset" about the prospect of a neighboring former dairy farm's structures being used to store DAF, and the "adverse effect on our business."
Nick Carter, of Greensboro, also voiced his concerns about the defunct dairy operation. The receiving pits and structures "appear to have some materials in them," he said. He had recruited Choptank Riverkeeper Matt Pluta to take drone photos.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter called on Yates to answer additional questions.
Craig Yohn, nutrient management planning coordinator with University of Maryland Extension in Caroline County, arrived after Director Dr. Paul Rickert, asked him to provide his expertise if needed. Rickert had attended the commissioners' budget roundtable earlier.
Porter asked Yohn questions about the composition of DAF soil amendments and how they were tracked from point of origin to application.
Yohn said nutrient management plans, including those written by Denali and Synegro, both waste recycling companies, are confidential, prompting murmuring among the attendees.
Yohn told the commissioners that nutrient management plans are confidential, prompting those attending the hearing to murmur among themselves.
The commissioners voted on each resolution separately because each addresses "individual issues that have arisen," Breeding said.
"The goal to do them individually was so that they would stand on their own should we have to defend (them)," Breeding said Feb. 14. "It's much simpler. It seems convoluted, but you put all of this into one document, (and) it's really going to overwhelm us."
Each resolution explicitly highlighted health and quality of life concerns that were expressed at a previous public hearing that attracted hundreds of residents Jan. 23. Those concerns were "foul odors, insect infestation and adverse health effects in residential areas."
The resolution cited the commissioners' "power to adopt and enforce rules and regulations on any nuisance or cause of disease in the County" according to the Annotated Code of Maryland.
Each resolution was enacted unanimously by the commissioners.
The resolutions are available at carolinemd.org.

title: Meetings Set to Discuss DAF Moratoria
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Meetings set to discuss DAF moratoria

 February 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News

title: Commissioners Introduce DAF Storage Legislation Package
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Commissioners introduce DAF storage legislation package

 February 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 973
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — In an effort to address citizens' concerns about the storage of industrial waste products, the Caroline County commissioners introduced four resolutions establishing temporary moratoria.The moratoria, commissioners said, will give them time to study the issue and establish county regulations.
At their Feb. 6 meeting in Denton, the commissioners introduced the four pieces of legislation, each addressing a particular aspect of a problem that surfaced at the end of 2023 and culminated in a Jan. 23 public hearing that attracted hundreds of citizens and special interest groups.
The four resolutions have a common purpose of protecting "the public health, safety and welfare of Caroline County residents and visitors."
Legislative timelineCounty Attorney Stewart Barroll explained the lengthy timeline that includes two readings and a public hearing.
Each of the temporary moratoria have an effective date of 10 days after their adoption, or March 8, to be in effect until Nov. 1.
Public hearings on each moratorium will begin at 11:30 a.m. Tuesday, Feb. 27, at the Health and Public Service Building, Room 111, 403 S. 7th St., Denton.
The proposed moratoria also will be reviewed by the Planning Commission at 6 p.m. Wednesday, Feb. 14, at the same location.
"We have to go through a legislative process to make sure that this stands up should we be challenged in court," Commission President Travis Breeding said, admitting the process is "painstakingly slow."
While state legislation was introduced Feb. 5 in Annapolis to establish an industrial sludge utilization permit through the Maryland Department of the Environment, the language of House Bill 991, cross-filed with Senate Bill 1074, was not discussed during the commission meeting.
Four moratoriaAt the Jan. 23 public hearing on the first iteration of legislation to address the issue, most attendees were concerned with their health — breathing the "stench" emitted from stored DAF residuals, pathogens possibly leeching into well water and waterways, and the increase of flying insects and the possibility of their carrying diseases.
Resolution 2024-004, finalized on Feb. 5, focuses on a temporary moratorium on the "certain use of land or structures for storage of biosolids in Caroline County not permitted by MDE (Maryland Department of Environment)."
Biosolids is defined as "treated sewage sludge that meets the standards" for two classes of sewage sludge, according to the Maryland Code of Regulations.
Resolution 2024-005 addresses the "certain use of land or structures previously permitted for the discharge or storage of vegetable processing waste/wastewater and other specified substances."
The commissioners are authorized "to impose a moratorium on any activity governed by Zoning Chapter 175" or other chapters regarding the "issuance of permits or zoning certificates."
The commissioners also want to review the County's comprehensive plan and public laws "to consider the re-purposing of land or structures previously permitted for the discharge or storage of vegetable processing waste/wastewater for storage of any material or substance not generated on the lot for public health and safety concerns for the storage of this material."
Concerns had been raised by citizens about material being trucked in from outside the county and stored. This resolution addresses land and structures "previously permitted for discharge or storage of vegetable processing waste/wastewater, vegetable plant residuals/residue, non-contact cooling water and boiler blowdown for the storage of any material or substance not generated on the lot," defined in Chapter 175 of the Caroline County Code.
The focus of Resolution 2024-006 is the storage of "any material or substance other than livestock manure in a structure designed and/or permitted for the storage of livestock manure in Caroline County" and "the use of land or structures to store livestock manure which is generated at another location."
"This is not an argument with the poultry industry. This is not an argument with the many, many people who grow chickens on their farms," Commission Vice President Larry Porter said. "But in my opinion, delivering material that's generated at a poultry processing plant that is not even located in this county and bringing it here as a way to dump it and get rid of it is not what we're going to do."
Resolution 2024-007, revised Feb. 2, will supersede the original draft Resolution 2023-025. It tracks the same language in the original moratorium on the storage of food processing residual and DAF residual.
The commissioners again cited a Maryland Code of Regulations regulation to define food processing residual and DAF residuals, which is an "organic byproduct material created at an animal processing facility or rendering facility."
This moratorium "shall not prohibit storage at the processing location where legally created, nor a farmer or farming business from temporarily storing food processing residual and/or DAF residuals in a mobile, closed container for no longer than 45 consecutive days during the application process, provided that the stored material is applied to the same land on which it is stored."
State vs. county rolesPorter said it was "amazing" to him that "no government agency claims responsibility for storage of this material."
"You can't put a blow-up pool in the state without somebody telling you how many feet it has to be from somewhere, but this falls through the cracks," he said.
"Some residents are concerned as to why we are researching," Breeding said. "Well, some of the research is around what state agency regulates different aspects of this industry, and we have to make sure that we're not occupying a space that's already occupied by a state agency or we will be preempted."
Porter assured the public "Caroline County is an agricultural county. It always has been, always will be. I don't want anyone to leave here thinking that, with all these moratoriums … we're going to wave some kind of magic wand, and you're never going to smell anything again. When it's planting season, you are. We're going to address this important situation, but there are going to be noise and odors and traffic and combines. That's Caroline County."
To read the proposed House legislation establishing an industrial sludge utilization permit, visit mgaleg.maryland.gov/2024RS/bills/hb/hb0991F.pdf.

title: Caroline Commissioners Clarify Aims of Jan. 23 DAF Hearing
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Commissioners clarify aims of Jan. 23 DAF hearing

 January 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 854
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — With the DAF storage moratorium attracting attention among residents, the Caroline County Commissioners clarified the purpose of the Jan. 23 public hearing towards the close of their weekly meeting Tuesday, Jan. 16.Commission President Travis Breeding said he noticed there was "some misinformation and uproar going around" the town of Ridgely about the hearing.
A flyer distributed to Ridgely residents alleged that the "Holding Company that purchased the Hanover property on Peaviner Road plans to start DAF processing in various ravines located on the property." The flyer author said the same holding company owned property on River Road and "have already started processing this sludge."
The author urged residents to attend the public hearing and sign an online petition created by Nancy Boone. By press time Jan. 16, the petition had garnered 138 signatures.
The purpose of the 6 p.m. public hearing Tuesday, Jan. 23, is to "receive comments on the storage of dissolved air flotation, or DAF, in Caroline County that was brought to our attention several weeks ago," he said.
The hearing will be held at the Health and Public Services Building, 403 S. 7th St., Denton.
Breeding said the commissioners would issue a formal statement, but stated several points he wanted the public to know "to bring everybody up to date."
The commissioners learned "that the livestock manure storage facilities — essentially manure storage pits from dairy or beef cattle operations — had been repurposed for and (were) being used for the storage of DAF. The storage was causing a nuisance to neighbors, so the county put a moratorium into effect. County officials have used the past few weeks to gather information about DAF," Breeding said as he read from his draft statement.
"This was brought to our attention by the fact that it was being used by someone who did not go through the permitting and approval process, and we're dealing with that as well," Porter said.
While "it seems evident that the state only regulates the product, the production and the application of DAF, … it is the county's responsibility to regulate the storage," he said.
"In my opinion, the state kind of dropped the ball here and left it up to us without even notifying us that this was going on. And naturally, the producers and then the haulers and the appliers didn't come and ask us for permission, so we were totally oblivious to what was going on. So essentially, the county is ready to create those regulations, and it's seeking public input into that process," Breeding said.
The objective of the hearing is to for the public to share comments, but the commissioners cautioned that the county was focused on DAF open pit storage, not the application of DAF as a soil amendment nor fertilizing with manure, both of which are legal agricultural practices.
Breeding said he's learned in his relatively short tenure as a county commissioner "that if regulatory territory is occupied by the federal government or the state, we are preempted, and therefore we don't have the ability to change those requirements. But what we have found is that this is totally the Wild West," he said. "It is up to us to come up with a reasonable storage solution here."
"I believe that I do not want any open air storage, and I want it only in the I-2 Industrial Area, because I believe it's an industrial product," Breeding said.
"We have to be really careful about banning it and not making a reasonable accommodation, either, and setting reasonable rules, so we don't get challenged," he said.
"I think I agree with that," Porter said. "I think I would even like to say that even if it does go into a zoning classification … I still want there to be public hearings."
I don't want anybody walking out of that meeting thinking that this is going to be some kind of a magic wand — that they're not going to smell anything again," Porter said. "This stuff has been used in fields for a long time. … It is a soil amendment that is beneficial to farmers. … We are only talking about the storage of this material."
Breeding said he was "fine" with a provision that DAF could be stored "for a maximum of 45 days on a property that it is actively being applied to, … but otherwise, (it) needs to be in a closed container and in the I-2 Industrial Areas of the county. So that's my position right now, and that's what I want to present to the public on Jan. 23."
"This is the ironic part," Breeding said. "The town of Ridgely and residents over there would have no idea that this was even a possibility had we not brought it up. So, we are actively trying to address this issue by even letting them know, 'Hey, this is a possibility of something that could happen out there.'"
"So, we're trying to get ahead of it. The firestorm was created by us and now we're the ones getting burned by it," he said.
Porter said Ridgely officials had been proactive, as well, because they are aware of the potential DAF storage problem "and the complications."

title: 'Respect your neighbors' - Caroline Commission passes temporary moratorium on DAF storage
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
'Respect your neighbors' - Caroline Commission passes temporary moratorium on DAF storage

 December 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: A1 | Section: News 
 
 1013
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - The Caroline County Commissioners upheld a resolution introduced at their Dec. 12 meeting, but only after revising some language in a temporary moratorium on DAF storage in the county.Following what was at times a contentious, nearly two-hour debate among local residents and poultry industry representatives from out of state, the three commissioners adjourned to go into closed session to further refine the resolution for another 90 minutes.
About 30 people attended the 9 a.m. meeting, and chairs had to be brought in to accommodate them in the small meeting room in the Caroline County Courthouse.
The commissioners adopted Resolution 2023-025 as a "temporary moratorium on certain use of land or structures for storage of food processing residual and/or DAF residuals in Caroline County" for 60 days, starting Dec. 19.
However, the moratorium doesn't apply to structures or land used for storage of those residuals prior to Jan. 1, 2023.
"In other words, we're not addressing the legality or not of such facilities," County Attorney Stewart Barroll said. "We are stating that future uses of land or structures are subject to the moratorium. So, this does not directly attack a preexisting facility." The poultry byproduct treatment system in question is dissolved air flotation, otherwise known as DAF.
A DAF pit is located on River Road outside Ridgely.
At the Dec. 12 Commission meeting, neighbors living near the pit reported the stench and flies emanating from the open-pit DAF were unlike manure since the DAF contains poultry processing byproducts.
Although it does not own that DAF storage tank, three representatives of the Arkansas-based Denali Corporation, "a specialty waste and environmental services company," according to its website, attended the meeting. They requested a 60-to 90-day delay in enacting the moratorium.
The company operates on Delmarva and "specialize (s) in repurposing DAF skimmings, transforming them into nutrient-rich soil amendments." Denali attorney Mark Cropper requested the delay, citing the holiday season and only having a few hours to review the resolution.
"I don't think there is an urgency that necessitates a moratorium," Cropper said.
"But I fully welcome and fully support the investigation you want to undertake." Several attendees who live on River Road, Cedar Lane and Peaviner Road alluded to the "one bad actor," whose River Road operation contains openair DAF holding tanks that produce a stench and flies, negatively affecting neighbors' quality of life.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter asked several times, "If there are ways to control the odor and the flies, why hasn't it been done?" Glenn Dowling, a senior environmental manager with Denali Water Solutions in Georgia, said Denali can respond to a problem when they are made aware of it. He said he would appreciate a "60-to 90-day reprieve" for "time to help create a solution that could become a model for the future." Barroll challenged the Denali representatives. "I'm a little curious that you're surprised by the complaints about odor and fly infestation, when Denali's been sued in multiple states in the last several years for exactly that. And you sit here telling us you didn't have any idea that that was happening here." The commissioners reiterated several times that their main concern was how DAF residuals from the Delmarva poultry industry are stored, not how they are applied.
They also reiterated their concern that materials are trucked into the county, stressing county road infrastructure.
They questioned why the poultry processing plants were not building DAF storage on the sites of their plants.
Dowling called the timing of the resolution "pretty curious." "Because it's being considered at the inception of the 2023-2024 winter nutrient application ban in Maryland and Delaware, it's difficult to accommodate when that storage of those materials is essential to the continuity of service of businesses," Dowling said. "It is allowed by the state (of Maryland) to store those materials specifically to protect natural resources and water resources on the Eastern Shore." The purpose of the temporary moratorium is to give the commissioners time to research the issue of DAF storage and "enact appropriate legislation." "I want to make it clear that I am pro-ag, but this needs to be cleaned up," Commission President Travis Breeding said.
Addressing his remarks to the poultry industry representatives, he said, "You need to carry that message back that we are not going to have this go on in our county. This does not mean that I'm not willing to vote to put a moratorium on the entire operation because, frankly, I am. But I think we need to sit down at the table.
It needs to be addressed, and we need to be a part of it. And the citizens of this county need to be a part of it, and they need to be heard by the producers, by the haulers and by the applicators." The Maryland Department of Agriculture "needs to be doing a better job, but they don't have to do a better job; if the applicators do a better job, then we don't have as many complaints," Breeding said. "So, stick to the regulations and make sure that they're enforced." The resolution also stated that county staff, Boards and Commissions are directed and requested to act in a manner consistent with the provisions of the moratorium." "We have directed staff to prioritize enforcement of our permitting process on non-permitted structures at this point," Breeding said.
"I'm ready to put the clamps on, so you guys need to come to the table," Commissioner Frank Bartz said.
"And respect your neighbors.
Respect this community," Breeding said.
A public hearing on the subject of the moratorium will be held 6 p.m. Tuesday, Jan. 23, in Room 111 of the Health and Public Service Building (HAPS), 403 S. 7th St., Denton.
The Dec. 19 meeting can be viewed on the Caroline County website at carolinemd.org/667/Live-Meetings. Click on the County Commissioners Meeting link for Dec. 19 or click on the video link.
