title: Candidates Present Issues, Goals at Forum
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Candidates present issues, goals at forum

 November 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1B | Section: News 
 
 1104
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO - Although he is running for mayor unopposed, Greensboro Town Council Member David Spencer showed up for a town council candidate meet and greet Thursday evening, Oct. 26, along with two incumbents, a former mayor, one first-time candidate and one making a follow-up bid.Current Town Council Members Robert Harrison and Pete Brelia defended their records and explained their goals. Joe Noon, who served as mayor from 2011 to 2019 before he was sidelined by a serious illness, wants to get back to work for the town.Greg North, who lost the Sept. 26 special election, was back to claim one of two seats on the council. Jessica Tamika Ortiz was new to the roster of candidates, as is Megan Lord, who did not attend the Oct. 26 forum.Moderating the forum held at the Greensboro Volunteer Fire Company Community Hall was Public Works Director Brandon Cunningham, with help from Community Outreach Coordinator and timekeeper Amanda Weaver and Town Manager Tammy Kelledes.Spencer's mayoral run created an extra vacancy on the council to fill the two remaining years of his term.The two candidates with the highest vote counts will serve a four-year term, while the candidate with the third highest count will serve the two-year term, Kelledes explained.The only Greensboro native, Spencer led the forum by summarizing his 44-year career in law enforcement and his history serving the town and in wider statewide associations.He was elected mayor 2007 and served as a council member for 12 years.Spencer said he would like to see more people attend council meetings and commended Greensboro Police Chief George Paugh and Lt.Lenox Trams for stabilizing and modernizing the police force.He said he wanted to see the town of 1,900 residents as a "clean and safe, family-oriented small community." Ortiz followed Spencer, describing how she moved from her native Philadelphia to Greensboro a few years ago and "fell in love with this little town." She said she wants "to keep the changes going" and help more people "understand what's going on." As an employee with Choptank Community Health System, Ortiz said, "I do speak Spanish, and I would like to be able to help the ones that cannot understand and know what's going on. I've been out in the communities, and I've been seeing that there's a lot of needs with (those with) Creole and Hispanic backgrounds." Both Ortiz and Brelia said they wanted to encourage small businesses to establish and continue in the town, but Brelia said he wanted to see careful control of growth so it doesn't happen too fast.North, a self-employed businessman who has been based in Greensboro since 2019, said, "I love the town of Greensboro." "I have seen a lot of improvements in town," he said. "I still think there's a lot more that we can do We have a lot of very wonderful events, but I just think there's ways we can make them bigger to attract more people to Greensboro." Calling himself "outspoken and strong-willed," North said he would apply the strategic thinking he employs as a business owner and "be a voice for every citizen." North promoted exploring solar panels to lower the cost of powering the wastewater treatment plant, and voiced an idea to investigate the possibility of purchasing electric vehicles for town employees.Town Council President pro tem Robert Harrison has lived in Greensboro for 32 years. He was succinct in his bid for reelection, piggybacking on improvements Spencer listed."I'd like to stay for another four years just to continue the things that we are working on with the town council and town employees," he said.Some of the priorities Harrison listed were resolving issues, overseeing the charter to "make sure that things are being run right," keeping employees happy, obtaining grants, and carefully creating an effective, well-researched budget.He said he feels good about phase one of the Kinnamon Meadows subdivision starting up, but is concerned about town water and sewer issues."We don't want to raise taxes," Harrison said. We have to budget things, but everything - just like everybody else knows - is increasing. We haven't raised water rates for over four years. Taxes have gone down.Doesn't sound like a lot when you're talking pennies on the 100 - it's still lowering the taxes." Harrison said issues look different from the perspective of a council member and dealing with "all these numbers and all the issues that we have gone through over the years." He urged residents to "come to the meetings.That's all I can tell you.come to the meetings and see what goes on." Pete Brelia, who began his career of service as a busboy at the Riverside Hotel on North Main Street, is a graduate of North Caroline High School.A former town police officer, he is a shift lieutenant with Caroline County Emergency Services. He was appointed to serve the council seat vacated by Brandon Cunningham.Calling the town is a "bedroom community" with many residents employed elsewhere, Brelia said he "would like to stay on the council for the next four years to complete the projects" it has begun."We don't have the industry that will support the economy that we need today, so I think we should enhance that environment," he said."We have a lot of water problems.We have a lot of sewer issues. There's a lot of infrastructure under the streets that has to be fixed." Noon, whose cancer diagnosis in 2019 forced his resignation as mayor, received the all-clear from his medical team to run for office.That news was greeted by applause from the nearly two dozen people who attended the forum.A graduate of Queen Anne's County High School, Noon has lived in Greensboro about 20 years. He praised the current council for doing a "great job," especially with regards to town office communication and road paving."I'm not putting my name in the hat because I feel that somebody did something wrong," Noon said."I'm doing it because I love Greensboro." He said he believes strongly in "happy employees, happy citizens.I've always believed that we have to get our employees to their fullest potential." To that end, Noon said, "It's time now to put somebody at the wastewater treatment plant" because of the town's current and future housing growth.He advocated sending "some people to school and get them to be a grant writer.Let's get this free money out there. Let's lower the spending out of taxpayers' pockets." For more complete biographical information on the candidates, visit the Greensboro, MD Facebook page or contact the town office.

title: Caroline Commission Shares Top Requests With Mid-Shore Delegation
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Caroline Commission shares top requests with Mid-Shore delegation

 October 4, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 23 | Section: News 
 
 1104
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - The Caroline County Commission met Tuesday, Oct. 3, with five of the seven-member legislative team for state districts 36 and 37 to advance its annual "bill requests and discussion items" ahead of the 446th Maryland General Assembly Jan. 10 to April 8, 2024.The short list of priorities they asked legislators to support were:■ Providing supplemental funds for emergency medical transports.,■ Licensing for barbershops and beauty shops to allow one-site sales and consumption of alcoholic beverages under restricted circumstances.■ Allowing liquor-tasting and sampling in the county in addition to wine and beer tasting.■ Continuing local funding of legislative bond initiatives.■ Devising a better method of assessing electric vehicle use instead of imposing a mileage tax.The three-member commission met with the legislators for about an hour in the Health and Public Services Building in Denton.The meeting agenda was reversed, with commissioners' unanimously approving the consent agenda shortly after the 9 a.m. start time while they waited for Del. Jeff Ghrist, R-36-Caroline, to arrive. The annual presentation of the consolidated transportation program occurred at about 10:30 a.m.Besides Ghrist, attending the annual delegation meeting were state Sen. Johnny Mautz, R-37; Del. Jay Jacobs, R-36-Kent; Del. Steve Arentz, R-36-QA; and Del. Chris Adams, R-37B. Sen. Steve Hershey, R-Upper Shore, and Del. Tom Hutchinson, R-37B, were absent.Commission Vice President Larry Porter led the discussion by describing the county's critical need for help in funding emergency medical transportation.The Emergency Service Transporter Supplemental Payment Program addresses the difference between the cost per emergency transport versus the Medicaid reimbursement rate. Providers receive a supplemental payment to make up the difference, but it's not enough to cover the actual cost.Porter pointed out that "Caroline County is a long county. It's about a two-hour turnaround time for us to pick up a patient, transport them, get them into the emergency room in Easton or Dover or Seaford, and turn around and come back."Because the "program reimburses at a higher rate, we're able to keep our revenue coming in, so that we can buy the new ambulances, new equipment," Porter said.EMS Division Chief K.J. Marvel explained that Caroline County reimbursement for ambulance transportation per Medicaid patient is increasing from a $100 to $150. She said she was worried about the lack of clarity in the expiration date of the grant program, which was originally set to expire in 2025.ESPP is a federal program sponsored through the Maryland Department of Health, Marvel said. "It's actually been very beneficial for us because we have a lot of Medicaid transports with our population here," she said.Private insurance companies and Medicare pay the rate established by the Maryland health care system."It's very important to us," Commission President Travis Breeding said. "We do not have an emergency room in the county."Medicaid does not pay for transportation to urgent care or Choptank Community Health, nor for transportation back home from an emergency room, so county EMS ambulances and drivers must transport patients to hospitals and, often, back home.Marvel and Deputy County Administrator Daniel Fox told the delegation the county is not looking for an increase in funding, but a continuation of the program.The financial benefit was $723,000 last year, Marvel said. Fox said losing those funds would be "devastating.""That's what? Two, three ambulances," Breeding said.He said the commission wanted to make sure "that our federal representation understands how important it is, and then also make sure that the state continues to have the regulatory and the grant writing structure in place to pass that funding through."The commissioners put forward requests to make three changes in the county liquor code, as recommended by the Caroline County Liquor Board. Assistant Director of Codes Crystal Dadds explained the requests.The board recommends allowing hair salons and barbershop to provide one 5-ounce glass of wine or 12-ounce beer per customer during a hair appointment, if the business were approved for an annual license fee of $100.Two other changes in the liquor code were proposed. Currently, beer and wine tastings and samplings are allowed in the county, but not the tasting and sampling of spirits. The number of two-ounce drinks per day for sampling would increase from six to nine to accommodate the typical number of three-sample flights.The commissioners requested support from the delegation for the Rural Maryland Council for fiscal year 2025. The state council, supported by the MidShore Regional Council, is requesting $9 million for rural development and projects. The funding request remains unchanged from fiscal year 2023.Though not included in the published bill requests, the commissioners voiced their concern about a proposed state mileage tax that would "disproportionately hurt rural residents because we travel more, and residents who travel in other states," Ghrist said.He said the state is "trying to figure out how to capture a use tax for EVs, but that's not the answer." Rather, "the better answer would be a titling tax when somebody purchases an electric vehicle.""Well, I think each day we find unintended consequences of this green energy agenda," Porter said. "Whether it's danger to our firefighters and first responders or the reduction in Highway User Funds, I think it went from $4 million to $400,000. This is just another unintended consequence of this ridiculous mess."A discussion about rural transportation needs, infrastructure needs and costs, and differences between urban and suburban versus rural mobility ensued."Something to keep in mind is, no matter what they do with EVs, as far as how we address that issue, they're still heavily subsidized," Arentz said. "The poor are the ones who are really going to get hammered by this. And we are not wealthy counties."Adams said the talk of a new tax prompted a blip on his wristwatch heart monitor. A politician who would even try to propose a new tax "with a recession coming on and inflation going through the roof" would have to put forth a convincing argument, he suggested."You can expect every person sitting at the table who represents Caroline County to push back and push back hard when it comes to raising taxes," Adams said."We need to be mindful of the economy on Main Street, not just on Wall Street," Mautz said.

title: Here's where Easton leaders stand on growth
author: Konner Metz
content:
Here's where Easton leaders stand on growth

 August 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Headlines 
 
 309
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It's a classic debate: build more housing or curb growth?Since joining the The Star Democrat in June 2024, I've seen the housing-growth debate consistently occupy the minds of elected officials, town planners, developers and residents. If you ask a Town Council member or a longtime resident the number one issue that Easton faces, I'd venture to say the answer will be growth-related more times than not.
There's hundreds of housing units in the town's pipeline — 1,127, to be exact. But at the same time, it's well-documented that Easton and Talbot County have an affordability problem, leaving many employees to commute daily from Caroline or Dorchester counties.
So what are the plans to pare down already-heavy traffic and keep the Easton Volunteer Fire Department from transitioning to a paid agency? And at the same time, how can the town still pursue some level of reasonably-priced housing for those that need it most?
It's a complex set of questions I asked the town's top officials, from the mayor, to elected council members, to a surprisingly powerful, six-member volunteer planning board.
The answers aren't clear. Some say slam the brakes. Others believe letting off the gas here and there will do.
There is, however, an approach gaining steam: focus on building from the inside-out, rather than annexing more county land into town or approving sprawling, single-family home developments. Most officials I spoke with endorse that strategy.
No "silver bullet" has emerged or will emerge, many town leaders told me. But a combination of items on the horizon — including a comprehensive plan update, zoning reform and a pause on annexations — will work to manage the town's growth without forgetting about those that seek an affordable place to live.
To hear specifics from town officials, or to find out where Easton's 1,127 units in the pipeline are located, check out my story below.
Thanks for reading.
— Konner Metz

title: Caroline County Employees and Residents Voice Concerns About Chaberton Solar
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County employees and residents voice concerns about Chaberton Solar

 June 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 398
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — Caroline County's latest battle against solar development took place during a public hearing for Chaberton Solar in Federalsburg on June 12 at Caroline County Public Library.The hearing was held amid an ongoing court battle between the county and the development company. Multiple county residents voiced their concerns for bringing Chaberton Solar into Federalsburg, citing housing options that could replace the proposed solar array.
"Well, I think it's good," Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said about residents coming forward. "The main reason that we were opposing this one was because it was in the R1 (residential) zoning district and we just felt that it was not in compliance with our comprehensive plan and we feel that the town could grow with the availability of water and sewer and that land would be better used for potentially for housing."
Late last year, Chaberton Solar Pahar applied with the county to construct a 3.0 MW solar facility in Federalsburg. The application was denied because it did not meet zoning requirements laid out by the county.
The company requested to put solar panels down in a residentially zoned area, where such developments are prohibited by the county.
The applicant was informed by the county prior to submitting the application that it did not have a complete site plan and had omitted some necessary details from the application in addition to the zoning violation, according to County Attorney Stewart Barroll.
The county filed an intervention with a public utility law judge in December stating the application was not complete as a result of these factors, but other entities attested that Chaberton met all the requirements to construct the planned solar facility.
The Power Plant Research Program of the state's Department of Natural Resources filed a paper that said it had reviewed the application and the application was complete. In December, the public utility judge pushed the application through to the next stage.
According to Lauren Bachi, community engagement manager for Chaberton Solar, the proposed solar facility will cover 42 acres parcel, and 20 acres will be used for the placement of solar panels. Chaberton also plans to create an access road off the project location. The project's access to the site will be controlled via a locked gate with a seven-foot agricultural style fence around the perimeter.
While dates and locations have not been set, there will be more informational sessions on Chaberton Solar, according to county officials.

title: Greensboro Town Council Votes to Fight Solar Appeal Case
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro Town Council votes to fight solar appeal case

 May 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 554
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — With the mayor acting as the tiebreaker vote, the Greensboro Town Council voted to support the Board of Appeals in its fight against Halo Greensboro Property LLC, a proposed solar facility on Sunset Avenue.The Town of Greensboro Board of Appeals held a public hearing March 10, during which it consider an application filed by Halo Greensboro Property LLC for special exception approval to permit a private utility facility and major utility facility with capacity to produce 1.2 megawatts AC power with related equipment, transmission lines, utility poles, access areas, fencing and similar features.
The application was denied by the board. As a result, Halo Greensboro filed an appeal to the Caroline County Circuit Court. The Board of Appeals will be fighting the solar appeal.
Lindsey Ryan, town attorney, brought forward to the town council the option to support the Board of Appeals in the case or allow the court proceed with the case at hand.
Councilmember Joe Noon, who voted for the courts to proceed with the case without the council's support, emailed his decision to Ryan earlier in the week but wanted the public to know why he decided to make that decision.
"Just so the public knows, I do care about the solar panels, don't get me wrong. But I'm looking at everything else. I'm looking at the big picture too," Noon said. "Like the sale of the house, what we're going to use the money for... I'm looking at the big picture also. I'm not against fighting for the solar panels, but I'm looking at our bank. So, I'm not against fighting for our town to keep the solar panels out. I'm just trying to look at how we're going to pay for everything."
Councilmember Bob Harrison, who also voted in favor of letting the court make a decision without council input, agreed with Noon about saving money for the town.
"I agree with Joe," Harrison said. "Just let it go. How much money do we want to spend? If it's going to cost us more money, just let the judge make the decision."
Councilmembers Pete Brelia and Christina Robinson both voted to support the Board of Appeals in the fight. Brelia's explanation for support brought applause from the residents in attendance of the meeting.
"The Board of Appeals had a hearing, and they opposed it. These people are filing an an appeal, and I think we should do whatever takes to back our Board of Appeals," Brelia said. "... To have the Board of Appeals have to hearing, go through this and then all of a sudden us just say, 'Well, let's just see what the courts do. Just sit here and tread water waiting.' That's not very supportive. Those people come out of out of their homes, they took a lot of time, they listened to everything, and they're acting in our best interest. I think that we should support them."
Brelia made the motion to support the Board of Appeals, which Robinson seconded. Harrison and Noon opposed the motion, which meant the decision needed to be made by the mayor.
"Let's vote to fight it," Mayor David Spencer said.
According to a press release, a virtual public hearing for Halo Solar case will take place on Tuesday, June 10, at 6:30 p.m. To sign up to speak on the public hearing, residents can go to psc.state.md.us.

title: Chaberton Solar Case Provides First Public Hearing
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Chaberton Solar case provides first public hearing

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 481
 Words

 DENTON — Caroline County's newest battle with renewable energy has been over Chaberton Solar.A virtual public hearing was held Monday on the Chaberton Solar case, in which Caroline County is fighting a permit it alleges was issued in violation of local zoning laws.
According to Caroline County Attorney Steve Barroll, an application for a 3.0 milliwatt solar facility near Federalsburg, filed by Chaberton Solar Pahar LLC, did not meet requirements laid out by the county.
The company requested to put solar panels down in a residentially zoned area where such developments are prohibited by the county.
The applicant was informed by the county prior to submitting the application back in December that it did not have a complete site plan and had omitted some necessary details from the application in addition to the zoning violation, Barroll said.
The county filed an intervention with a public utility law judge in December stating the application was not complete as a result of these factors but other entities attested that Chaberton met all the requirements to construct the planned solar facility.
The Power Plant Research Program of the state's Department of Natural Resources filed a paper that said it had reviewed the application and the application was complete. In December, the public utility judge pushed the application through to the next stage.
According to Lauren Barchi, community engagement manager for Chamberton Solar, the proposed solar facility will cover 42 acres parcel, and 20 acres will be used for the placement of solar panels.
Chaberton also plans to create an access road off the project location. The project's access to the site will be controlled via a locked gate with a seven-foot agricultural style fence around the perimeter.
Public hearings, including the hearing Monday, need to be held before the project can receive final approval.
While no public comment was presented at the hearing Monday evening, Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding spoke on Caroline County's stance against the proposed solar field.
"I should express that Caroline County respectfully opposes this application because it is R1 residential zone property," Breeding said. "It's directly contrary to the county zoning code in our comprehensive plan."
"The county spends a significant amount of time and resources to review and analyze its zone code and comprehensive plan. And it shouldn't be disregarded by solar developers or the state.
"This property in particular is inappropriate for solar because it borders the town of Federalsburg and has access to infrastructure such as water and sewer."
Barchi spoke in favor of Chaberton facility in Federalsburg, stating the benefits of the project proceeding in Caroline County.
"In total over a dozen neighbors and landowners have been spoken to with no opposition to the project," Barchi said. "This community solar project will benefit the local community in many ways, including tax revenue to the state and county."
A second public hearing will be held in person on June 12. The location will be determined at a later date.

title: Caroline County Emergency Cannabis Bill Moved to Introduction
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County emergency cannabis bill moved to introduction

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 384
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At their Tuesday meeting, the Caroline County Commissioners discussed an emergency cannabis bill that would allow the county to set zoning regulations for cannabis facilities.The emergency bill is proposed to allow Caroline County to get on track with regulations and requirements of from the state.
It would also create parameters for dispensaries, growers and processors and where they can grow, process and sell cannabis in the county.
The adjustments are being made as a result of House Bill 805, a 2024 bill that established zoning requirements for cannabis businesses that are more restrictive than some that existed prior to the legalization of recreational cannabis in the state.
The state regulation mandates that cannabis dispensaries cannot be located within 500 feet of schools, child care center, programs, recreation centers, libraries, public parks or churches. Dispensaries will also not be allowed to be within 1,000 feet of another dispensary.
All state regulations are upheld in Caroline County's proposed emergency bill.
For cannabis growers and processors, Caroline County's proposed emergency bill will mandate growers and processors to be in the I2 industrial district of Caroline County.
The regulations will also mandate that growers and processors not be located within 1,200 feet of schools, religious facilities, public or nonprofit parks, recreation areas, playgrounds, civic centers, club, libraries, registered family daycares and group daycares. They also can't be within 300 feet of a residence.
Caroline County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter questioned if the distance in feet of the dispensaries, growers and processors could be increased to a further distance from the places the state suggested.
Caroline County Director of Planning and Codes Crystal Dadds responded, "For the processors and growers the distances, yes they can be increased, but for the dispensaries, no, they are covered by state law."
Porter made another suggestion that Caroline County make a color-coded map of the county to indicate areas where dispensaries, growers and processors can be located for when businesses put in an application.
"Yes, we can put something together to give a better visual where those areas are and what the setbacks look like," Dadds said.
The licensing of cannabis sales will be handled by the state. The counties have no control of applications, only the zoning of where dispensaries, growers and processors can be located.
The Caroline County Commissioners decided to move the emergency cannabis bill forward for introduction.

title: At Daysprings Townhomes, Poor Housing Conditions Persist
author: Konner Metz
content:
At Daysprings Townhomes, poor housing conditions persist

 February 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 1351
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Phillip Gibson often walks around the complex where he lives, checking in on his neighbors at the Dayspring Townhomes. He's recognizable and trusted by neighbors, many of whom call him "Pappy."Last October, the retired maintenance worker walked around the complex and into some of his neighbors' units, pointing out what looked like mold above the shower of a second-floor bathroom.
He repeated one word that encapsulates how he and many others view the living conditions at the low-income complex: "Unacceptable."
"I've only been living out here for eight months," Gibson said in October. "This is what I'm seeing. This is crazy. This is crazy, and I've been a maintenance man for 40 years."
Gibson isn't alone, as other residents of the Caroline County-owned complex have voiced similar concerns.
During recent months, dialogue surrounding the 46-unit operation has picked up among housing and social activists, disgruntled tenants and Caroline County officials. Property management has sought to collect unpaid rents while many tenants point to poor housing conditions and unresponsive maintenance requests.
Owned by the county, the property is run by East Coast Property Management, a Delaware-based company. In November, the Dayspring Townhomes filed 23 complaints against residents for failure to pay rent.
Shore Legal Access and Maryland Legal Aid took on cases for residents that accepted their legal services. Some cases were dismissed, while others were ruled in favor of the landlord. A number of tenants agreed to rent payment agreements.
County officials say only around half of the units are currently occupied and collecting rent. Some of the vacated units have extensive damage stemming from evicted tenants, Caroline County Administrator Katheleen Freeman said at a Feb. 4 county meeting.
While the county explores the possibility of selling the property to a qualified nonprofit, some residents remain confused and frustrated with lacking maintenance and communication.
Gibson said he wants the units fixed up, and that at times, property management has been putting "a Band-Aid on a little sore" when it comes to addressing issues.
"I can't let these people live like this," he said.
LIVING CONDITIONS
The Dayspring Townhomes complex is located just outside Ridgely on School Street. The initial property was built in 1994 by Interfaith Housing Development, a former local nonprofit that worked with the county, according to Caroline County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter.
That nonprofit ceased operations a handful of years ago, leaving the low-income housing complex in the hands of its owners, Caroline County, and the contracted property management company, East Coast.
In October, Caroline County paid for First State Inspection Agency, based in Milford, Delaware, to perform unit-by-unit inspections.
Of the complex's 46 units, inspection records showed common damages in a number of units: cracked window surfaces, doors off their frames and damaged outlets or light switch covers. Some apartments had damaged or worn stairs.
None of the units had smoke detectors in the bedrooms, which Caroline County and property management remedied in the days after inspection.
Manizh Brown, a former tenant, lived at Dayspring for more than a year with her two children. In her townhome, an electrical outlet was faulty, closet doors were broken and the ceiling leaked where the second-floor bathtub sits.
"Everybody else got similar … problems. Especially this," Brown said while standing in her then-apartment, pointing to the leaks. "This is really getting me."
Brown said many of the issues with her townhome existed when she moved in. Aside from her floor, which she said was upgraded, Brown said there weren't sufficient improvements.
"The health situation right here, the water and everything else. F. F-minus," Brown said. "Ain't no way I should move in, and there's mold already on my window sill."
Caroline County officials have labeled the Dayspring Townhomes as high priority, facilitating the inspections last fall and consistently checking in with property management and the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development.
"We want those units to be in good shape," said Porter, the Caroline commissioner. During recent meetings, the county has focused on facilitating renovation of heavily damaged units.
Some residents hold concerns about physical safety, as well. A non-fatal shooting outside of the complex last August intensified those worries. The county purchased security cameras, which were placed at the front of the complex.
Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker has remained in contact with Bridge Maryland Inc., a Baltimore County nonprofit that's held meetings for residents to air concerns and is assisting tenants with the court process.
Some tenants and nearby homeowners participate in neighborhood association meetings, during which they discuss their concerns about violence, drug use and large parties in or outside of the Dayspring Townhomes.
In October, resident Trina Ewell said the shooting was still affecting her peace of mind, and her son's as well.
"You're just at your own risk," Ewell said. "And I do know that my son has increased with panic attacks because of the shooting."
PROPERTY MANAGEMENT
East Coast Property Management, which manages the Dayspring complex, has more than 50 rental properties across Delaware, Maryland and Virginia, according to its website.
Despite repeated attempts to reach the property manager or a company representative, East Coast Property Management did not respond to The Star Democrat's requests for an interview or comment.
Residents have raised concerns about a lack of communication with property management, the property manager and maintenance workers.
"We have not heard from anybody, letters, emails," Ewell said last fall.
Brown said in order to place maintenance requests, she called the "maintenance man" or the property manager, as there was no standard maintenance order procedure.
"You ain't got to do no type of papers, no work (order), just tell them," Brown said. Often, she considered doing some of the maintenance fixes herself.
Rachel Wolpert, a chief attorney at Maryland Legal Aid who has worked with landlord and tenant issues since 2008, says it's an "incredibly relationship-based business."
Wolpert acknowledged it's a difficult task to be a property manager at any apartment or multifamily complex. She notes, though, that clear communication and follow-through from property management are critical.
"I see successes when the on-site manager is accessible and responsive to tenants," Wolpert said. "And then you see real troubles where tenants feel like the on-site manager is not accessible, not responsive."
Recently, tenants were notified monthly rent rates would increase. Porter said since there are no rent subsidies, but also an income threshold tenants must be below, a tight window exists of those who qualify but can still meet rent payments.
Bridge Maryland Board of Directors President the Rev. Angelique Mason said in an interview that rent payments and fear of eviction both play a role in how outspoken residents feel they can be.
"We do know that some of them are not being vocal because they might be behind in their rent," Mason said. "They had this idea that they might be evicted if they speak up. And that's really why Bridge is being the voice for the people, because some of them do have fear of eviction."
WHAT'S NEXT?
While Caroline County owns the property, the option for that to change is up in the air.
"Our position at this point that we're going to express is the possibility of selling that property to a qualified nonprofit organization," Porter said at a November county meeting. "The question we need to have answered is the mortgage amount."
Porter calls it a "tough situation" because of that mortgage conundrum. The state has involvement with the property, he said, binding the county to have at least a portion of ownership and the apartments to be low-income in order for the mortgage to remain deferred.
As the county has been in consistent dialogue with Maryland Housing and Community Development, many tenants faced court proceedings at the end of 2024.
Bridge Maryland organizer Hannah Freeman, who has facilitated community meetings, assisted many tenants during the court process. She said while some owed thousands in rent, others owed less than property management alleged.
Freeman says she remains focused on helping those who need it most.
"There's people just out homes," Freeman said. " … These are people with kids, with legitimate complaints about management."
Ewell acknowledged that amid her concerns regarding safety and the complex's living conditions, there isn't always another option.
"You got to live somewhere," Ewell said. "Right now, during this time with everything, you have to. You have to live somewhere."

title: Caroline Zoning Appeals Board Denies Hartland Holdings Grain Silo Variance
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Zoning Appeals board denies Hartland Holdings grain silo variance

 January 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 1365
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Over the course of two meetings and four hours of testimony and deliberation, the Caroline County Board of Zoning Appeals voted against granting a zoning variance to a agricultural operation near Greensboro.Benjamin Flahart of Quarryville, Pennsylvania, whose Hartland Holdings LLC owns the 160-acre farm in question, was denied a 43-foot variance for already-constructed grain silos at 14010 River Road.
His attorney, Brendan Mullaney of McAllister, DeTar, Showalter & Walker in Easton and Brett Ewing of Lane Engineering represented him at the Board's Nov. 19 meeting and attended the Dec. 19 meeting with Flahart. Both meetings were held at the Health and Public Services Building in Denton and were attended by about a dozen Caroline residents.
Board of Zoning Appeals Chair Karen Hardy, Vice Chair Ben Butler and Member Kevin Parks voted unanimously to deny the variance, claiming that Flahart knew, or should have known, that setting up grain bins within the county's 500-foot road setback requirement was a violation of the county code.
"It's the principle to me," Hardy said at the Nov. 14 meeting. "If … we just say, 'Okay, no problem, come on into Caroline County, put up what you want, and then whenever it doesn't go your way, just come on and bring your attorneys and … we'll give you your variance' — I don't want that to be something that happens here."
Several times during the course of both meetings, Hardy said Flahart had "created his own hardship."
Butler said he felt "the same way," although moving the grain bins would cost "a lot of money."
"But I really feel like he created this situation, and I just feel like he should have to move it," Butler said.
Flahart bought grain bins from Mountaire in Greensboro and moved them to the River Road location. Three of the bins are located within the setback limit. At the Dec. 19 meeting Flahart estimated demolishing and relocating the three bins would be "close to $1 million."
"I know that the financial hardship is severe, and I do understand that, but it is somewhat self-created," Hardy said after the unanimous vote. "I don't feel good about that decision. Unfortunately, we could not do it any other way."
The Board of Zoning Appeals considered two items related to Flahart's River Road operation. The first item considered at the Nov. 14 meeting involved a public hearing and an extended debate addressing Hartland Holdings LLC's application for a special use exception in accordance with the Caroline County Code.
Flahart's operation, permitted in 2019 to store his own grain, evolved into an "agricultural products processing plant" when it began storing grain from other farms and selling it, which required a special use exception.
Mullaney explained Hartland Holdings LLC "owns a significant amount of land" on the Eastern Shore — "1,000 acres in Cecil County, over 2,000 acres in Dorchester and over 1,500 acres in Caroline."
He added that "in Pennsylvania and many other counties, you don't have to permit things like grain silos and agricultural barns."
Despite the additional structures' being added to the grain operation without permission, Mullaney said he believed all the variance criteria were satisfied. He said he and Ewing had worked together to submit permit applications "to get all this stuff cleaned up with Planning and Codes, the building permitting department and the Office of Health."
According to Matt Kaczynski, assistant director of development review for Caroline County, in 2019 Flahart hired engineering company Red Barn Consulting, which, in turn reached out to the planning department for the requirements to establish an agricultural products processing facility.
Kaczynski said the timeline required by the county prompted the Red Barn engineer to scale back the operation "to basically one grain tank."
"It was our understanding … that (Flayhart) would come back later for an expansion," he said. "Fast forward to now … What was constructed and what is shown on the site plan now was not what was reviewed and approved as part of the building permit process, so we had received some complaints from neighbors in the area about what was going on onsite."
Kaczynski said Flahart may not have been aware of Red Barn's process, as Flahart maintained during the Dec. 19 meeting.
However, Hardy said on Nov. 14 Flahart should have been aware "to some degree what's happening. … At the end of the day, it just makes me question the integrity of the man who's moving into this."
She brought up briefly "the elephant in the room" that wasn't under consideration: Flahart's dissolved air flotation, or DAF, pit, which has been a source of controversy and was a concern addressed at the Dec. 12 Caroline County Commission meeting.
Several people spoke up during the public hearing.
Local farmer James Lewis, who is the extension agent for Caroline County, said he has hauled his grain to the River Road facility the last couple of years. He said the operation benefited the community and that he was concerned about the carbon footprint involved with tearing down and moving the bins 43 additional feet from the road.
Caroline County farmer John Saathoff said he was "mainly concerned about the precedent" that would be set, although he liked "the option of having another grain facility."
In 2019 Flahart didn't own 1,500 acres in the county, Saathoff said. "He owned one farm, and that one bin was able to accommodate that farm."
"Everybody knows initially his plan all along was to go commercial," but "it was going to take too long." Because Flahart had also erected a scale and scale house, "that was clear evidence, in my opinion, of his original intention."
"Those of us down here in the trenches (who) have been here all this time — we're bound by the law," Saathoff said. "Those of us who have been here for generations, every time we want to do something, we come in your office and we apply for a permit, and we do what we're supposed to do. And these people who hire their attorneys, they get to do whatever they want. I don't think that's how we want this county to be."
Brett Meyers, a farmer who lives next door to Flahart's River Road property, said the permitting process is "not negotiable."
"I find it hard to believe a man with enough wherewithal to buy all these farms (and) put these grain tanks up wouldn't have understood that there was a permitting process involved to build what he wanted to build and to have to adhere to a site plan," Meyers said.
Although the 43 feet was not "going to make too much of a difference," Meyers said, "I feel like you're going to open Pandora's box. Where does it stop with the grain and the tanks. How big is it going to get? … If you okay this, how far is it going to get?"
Mike and Suellen Woodward, whose property adjoins the operation, voiced several concerns, including the increased heavy truck traffic and the lack of communication to neighbors that would allow them to present concerns earlier about the operation's expansion.
"We've seen this happen from the beginning," Mike Woodward said. "I don't understand how he got all those grain bins up with no permit at all. I don't care about the grain operation. That doesn't bother me at all. But the part of the permitting process — something was skipped somewhere, whether he didn't follow through or somebody else didn't follow through."
"And that happens all the time," Kaczynski said. "More often than you would want to know. We issue building permits. We go out onsite to do final inspections, and we find that they've constructed various other things without permits."
The board considered the benefits to local farmers hauling their grain to a nearby facility, but noted Flahart's business expansion that ventured beyond the approved site plan.
After almost two hours of testimony and discussion Nov. 14 the board deliberated, voting unanimously to approve a special use exception with the conditions that the applicant receive final site plan approval from the planning director or commission prior to issuing a permit and/or zoning certificate.
A further condition required the applicant and county entering into a development rights and responsibilities agreement to work with the Department of Public Works to address wear and tear on county roads affected by Hartland Holdings LLC's truck traffic.

title: Commissioners Mull Moratorium On Poultry Byproduct Storage
author: Connie Connolly; Cconnolly@Chespub.Com
content:
Commissioners Mull Moratorium On Poultry Byproduct Storage

 December 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; Cconnolly@Chespub.Com | Page: 13 | Section: News 
 
 914
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - Following a sometimes spirited discussion of a controversial poultry byproduct treatment system, the three Caroline County Commissioners went into closed session Tuesday, Dec. 12, with the county's attorney to refine language for a temporary moratorium.Crystal Dadds, director of the Caroline County Department of Planning and Codes opened the discussion that focused on a "possible moratorium on the onsite storage of dissolved air flotation, otherwise known as DAF."
Dadds said the department and the commissioners had heard concerns from citizens about the recent construction of a concrete storage pit used to store DAF, or raw food waste.
"And there's some concern that the county does not have any specific regulations to address agricultural storage tanks," she said. At issue is the waste products being trucked into the county from poultry processing plants located elsewhere.
Concerned citizens, an agricultural expert and a trade association spokesman weighed in during the nearly hourlong discussion.
Grayson Middleton, government affairs manager with the Delmarva Chicken Association, argued that DAF is "an agricultural product because it's coming from a product that's being manufactured agriculturally on the Shore, and it's being applied to the Shore in an agricultural manner."
"If there's no place to store this, it makes it extremely hard for application," Middleton said.
However, Commissioner Frank Bartz claimed there was a distinction between a farmer being paid to store a product or being the end user of it.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter was more blunt. "We're not going to become a storage ground in this county for things brought in here from somewhere else and then everybody else is going to have to sit around and deal with it," he said.
The DAF pit is located on River Road outside Ridgely.
Neighbors reported the stench and flies emanating from the open-pit DAF were unlike manure since the DAF contains poultry processing byproducts.
"The smell smacks you in the face," said John Hammer, a farmer and poultry producer who lives about a quarter-mile from the DAF facility.
Sue Ellen and Mike Woodward live on Marblehead Road, and their property borders the land on which the facility sits.
Mike Woodward said the smell is so sickening, he can't work at his sawmill outside, and the flies are "just outrageous. I mean, they just cling right to our house."
Commission President Travis Breeding cited another concern. Hauling the materials in 18-wheelers and tanker trucks "is increasing the weight in traffic and potential damage to roads that, frankly, we struggle to keep up with now," he said.
Bartz placed the responsibility for storing byproducts on the poultry plants.
"It's up to them to expand their holding facilities and processing facilities where they are, instead of sending it to wherever they can just find a room and just to stick it temporarily," he said.
Caroline County Extension agent Jim Lewis said DAF is part of the nutrient management program and regulated by the Maryland Department of Agriculture, but "they very rarely issue fines" for violations.
The Maryland Department of the Environment deals with biosolids and can "pull their permits, they can fine them, shut them down," Lewis said.
However, at this point DAF is not considered a biosolid, but rather a "soil amendment" which should be worked into the soil within a day, Lewis said.
"If you do incorporation, then you're exposing soil to the surface rather than leaving a cover crop with no till," he said. DAF is untreated, Lewis said. "It's a decomposing meat, fat, blood product that potentially, I would think, would carry foodborne diseases.
The residents who commented said the DAF pit in their vicinity is not the only one in the county. The commissioners and planning department have heard of other storage facilities.
Porter asked Middleton if Caroline County had any poultry processing plants.
Middleton said no and added that the county has chicken houses.
"I'm fully aware that we have chicken houses," Porter said. "Are the chicken houses bringing material to these pits directly?" "This is the kind of thing that irritates me to no end," Porter said. "We're not going to subject our citizens to this."
County Attorney Stewart Barroll told the citizens who complained about the DAF pit, "What you've described to us is clearly a nuisance and not protected by the Right to Farm law." He asked if they had sought legal counsel. They answered that they couldn't afford an attorney and were afraid of retaliation.
"I don't know if I can handle that fight, let alone the expense of going through a long, drawn-out process of me trying to prove what the stink is like in the air, or how many flies are around my window or what's in my ditch," Sue Ellen Woodward said. "I don't have the resources or the emotional part to fight that. That's why I come to you."
"I think we're going to attempt to address the issue for you and try to come up with reasonable expectations and guidelines for the storage and application of this product," Breeding said.
The commissioners went into closed session with Barroll to determine the language to place in a resolution to declare a temporary moratorium.
They plan to introduce a resolution at their Dec. 20 meeting.

title: Caroline Commissioners Talk New Regional Detention Center
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline commissioners talk new regional detention center

 October 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 333
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Oct. 15 the Caroline County Commissioners discussed a plan to build a new regional detention center in Queen Anne's county.The financial burden would be split between Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties, but it is still unclear how that would be managed or what would happen to the detention center on 101 Gay Street in Denton, commissioners said at the meeting.
The new facility is being designed to hold 338 beds for men and women. The current Denton jail holds 130 inmates.
The warden of the Caroline County Detention Center, Charles Scott, said there are mental health needs among the inmates that could be better managed with a designated space, which could be incorporated into the design of the new facility.
"There should be a wing just for mental health. Juveniles and mental health are just piling up in the jail," Scott said.
He said there is plenty of land in Queen Anne's County to build this new detention center. The new facility will be located in Church Hill on the site of the Eastern Pre-Release Unit.
Commission President Travis Breeding cited the economies of scale and how the new detention center could serve the needs of the counties for less money.
The commissioners discussed who would be the authority on this tri-county project. Right now, one county commissioner and one county administrator oversee the jail in Denton. The commissioners said they wanted more clarity on how that would work in a tri-county context.
The commissioners also discussed the employment possibilities for current Caroline County Detention Center employees. Employment decisions would factor in tenure and managing workers who have fulfilled this amount of time as they work in a new county.
Scott said it is hard to find correctional officers, so everyone's job should be safe.
County Administrator Katheleen Freeman said the new facility will offer better services at lower costs, but the devil is in the details.
The commissioners agreed to discuss this further at the next meeting on Oct. 22 at the Health and Public Services building.

title: Greensboro Moves Toward Monthly Utility Billing
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro moves toward monthly utility billing

 October 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 256
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Town of Greensboro presented two ordinances that would change some of the towns billing from quarterly to monthly at the Greensboro Town Council Meeting on Thursday.The council introduced a resolution to change trash billing from quarterly to monthly at $16.50 per month per single-family residence, including multi-family units.
A second resolution was introduced to establish water and sewage rates effective Dec. 1, changing from quarterly to monthly billing.
"The benefit for residents, of course, is better budgeting, improved usage awareness, too, and fewer surprises," Town Manager Cindy Yost said to the Star Democrat on Oct. 3 when the proposed water bill changes were first discussed at a town meeting. "So if they fill a pool up or if they have a leak on their commode or something like that, this is going to pick it up a lot faster."
The proposed change from either monthly to quarterly or quarterly to monthly has been discussed around Caroline County throughout this year.
The town of Federalsburg is in discussions to change water and sewer billing from monthly to quarterly.
According to Yost, the benefits for the town would be enhanced cash flow and improved public works procedures.
"Enhanced cash flow, I mean, that's a given." Yost said. "You're going to get paid on a monthly basis. Faster leak detection, which is going to be huge for us, and a stronger customer engagement because we're going to be out there on a monthly basis interacting instead of the quarterly."
A public hearing was scheduled to discuss both proposed ordinances at the Nov. 6 meeting.

title: Greensboro Faces $300,000 Sewer Line Repair Cost
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Greensboro faces $300,000 sewer line repair cost

 October 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 372
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — The aftermath of a sewer main pipe break will cost the town of Greensboro around $300,000 to fix, but the town plans to be reimbursed for the cost.At around 3:30 p.m. last week, the Town of Greensboro received a call about sewage water in the road on Route 313 and Bridgetown Road, town officials said.
Upon arrival, Greensboro Public Works found a sewer main pipe break on Bridgetown Road. Greensboro Town Manager Cindy Yost said the sewer line runs from Greensboro to Goldsboro. Friday evening, she said the town asked Goldsboro residents to use less water while repairs were underway.
After investigation, the town discovered that a subcontractor from Sure Shot Drilling was boring on the property. Yost said the subcontractor for Cherrywood Solar hit the main sewer pipe, then covered the pipe with plywood, put orange netting around the pipe and left the scene without contacting the town.
Now almost one week after the main pipe break, the town still continues work at the site to resolve the broken pipe 19 feet underground.
According to Yost the town called Spring and Associates, a horizontal directional drilling, to begin the process of fixing the pipe on Friday. The plans state that this particular pipe is 19 feet underground and while drilling down and getting to 17 feet, the road began to slide.
The town signed a contract with Spring and Associates on Saturday night. After the contract was signed Spring and Associates began to bring more equipment into Greensboro, but equipment delivery was delayed until Monday because of the wind storm this past weekend.
After more difficulties on Monday, Spring and Associates are still bringing in equipment from Virginia.
Yost said the town has two pump trucks operating around the clock at the Goldsboro pump station to prevent any issues for the town of Goldsboro.
Yost said that with the costs for contracting with Spring and Associates, Premier, the State Highway for guard rail removal, power companies for telephone pole removal, flaggers and their town staff, the repair will run up to $300,000.
The town is fronting the bill and has reached out to CherryWood solar contractors, NextEra to request they cover the cost, but has not yet received a response and plans to reach out to confirm.

title: Subcontractor strike causes major sewer line break in Greensboro, town says
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Subcontractor strike causes major sewer line break in Greensboro, town says

 October 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 357
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — At around 3:30 p.m. Friday, the Town of Greensboro received a call about sewage water in the road on Route 313 and Bridgetown Road, town officials said.Upon arrival, Greensboro Public Works found a sewer main pipe break on Bridgetown Road. Greensboro Town Manager Cindy Yost said the sewer line is connected from Greensboro to Goldsboro. Friday evening, she said the town had asked Goldsboro residents to use less water while repairs were underway.
"We've had to go in and shut down the pump station to Goldsboro, and hopefully that'll keep it from coming forward," Yost said. "Then we've got some trucks coming in, too, to help with that load. So, hopefully we can manage that with Goldsboro and not create any issues for them at the current time."
She said the town hoped to have the issue resolved by the morning.
After investigation, the town discovered that a subcontractor from Sure Shot Drilling was boring on the property. Yost said the subcontractor hit the main sewer pipe, then covered the pipe with plywood, put an orange flag around the pipe and left the scene without contacting the town.
According to Yost, the town contacted Sure Shot Drilling after discovering the break, and the company said workers had contacted Miss Utility, the company responsible for marking the location of power lines, sewer lines and water lines ahead of construction work.
The town manager said Sure Shot Drilling officials told her the area was not marked, so the contractor boring in that area was unaware the pipe was there.
Sure Shot Drilling could not be reached for comment due to the office being closed at the time the Star Democrat called.
Yost said the town was not contacted by Miss Utility ahead of Friday's construction work and was unaware of boring being done in the area that that day.
"This is a huge sewer main. We should have been contacted. We were not," Yost said. "So, right now we've got emergency crews out here. We've got our local police out here on the road. We've called MDE because of the sewage going into the creek. So, we're hoping that we can get this fixed tonight."

title: Denton Approves Sharp Road Park Playground's First Phase
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Denton approves Sharp Road Park playground's first phase

 October 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 392
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Town of Denton approved the first phase of Sharp Road Park's playground construction at the Denton Town Council meeting on Monday.Phase one of the playground features equipment that's designed to look like first responder vehicles. The hope for the park as a whole is to honor first responders and veterans of Caroline County.
"We've got a lot of first responders that live in our community, and we want to make sure that we've got a place to acknowledge them. So that's something we're really excited about," Mayor Abby McNinch said.
The council approved a proposal in the amount of $294,699 from Kompan Inc. to furnish and install playground equipment at Sharp Road Park.
The town received $300,000 in grant funding from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources Community Parks and Playgrounds program for phase one of the project.
The DNR grant funding will be used to fund $274,426.86 of the playground costs, and the remaining grant funding will be used to fund engineering costs related to the project. The Town will fund the remaining $20,272 for playground surfacing.
Denton has additional play equipment planned for a second phase of construction, but the town will need to secure additional funding from the state to complete phase two.
The park is expected to receive multiple upgrades in the near future, which started with a mural honoring first responders on the basketball court created by Terae Warner, a local business owner and basketball coach, and artist Shelton Hawkins.
More additions expected at Sharp Road Park include an outdoor exercise circuit, flag court and highly anticipated dog park.
"It seems like everybody's most excited about the dog park," McNinch said. "We've heard the community about that, and that's something we're looking forward to putting in as well."
The flag court will include flags representing different branches of the military.
Caroline County has started construction on the baseball field, softball field and multipurpose field at the park with hopes of the fields being finished by December.
McNinch said that the upgrade of Sharp Road Park has been a goal of hers since she entered office.
"You'll have the dog walkers, the people that are walking the trail, then the little kids that are playing, the kids that are playing soccer, basketball, all of it. It really becomes a community asset and kind of what we've envisioned for a long time, so we're excited," McNinch said.

title: Transportation Officials Tour Eastern Shore to Discuss Funding and Project Statuses
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Transportation officials tour Eastern Shore to discuss funding and project statuses

 September 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 975
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Members of Maryland's Department of Transportation came to the Eastern Shore on Tuesday to meet with county and city officials and give updates on current projects.MDOT officials traveled through the Mid-Shore to discuss the agency's Draft Consolidated Transportation Program for fiscal years 2026 to 2031, which details a $21.5 billion, six-year capital budget investment in the state's transportation network.
Three separate meetings were held with MDOT officials Tuesday, one each in Talbot, Dorchester and Caroline counties. The meetings are part of the department's tour visiting every Maryland county.
TALBOT
Meeting with local officials at the Talbot County Community Center, acting Secretary of MDOT Samantha Biddle presented a draft of the Consolidated Transportation Program, emphasizing efforts to enhance safety, maintain systems and drive economic growth.
Biddle and other MDOT representatives shared status updates for several transportation projects in the county.
The Route 50 corridor project from Dutchman Lane to Lomax Street in Easton is in the final design stages, with construction expecting to begin in 2026, Biddle said. This project includes signalized pedestrian crossings at the Route 50 intersections with Dover and Matthewstown roads.
State Highway Administrator Will Pines reported that the State Highway Administration upgraded and improved 38 crosswalks across Talbot County in fiscal year 2025.
The county will receive a Kim Lanpheir Bikeways Grant for bike racks as part of the Easton Community Bicycle Parking Initiative. Director of Local Transit Support Travis Johnston said that MTA will provide Talbot County with $1 million in operating grants and preventative maintenance for local transit operations.
St. Michaels Town Manager Don Richardson requested the restoration of two crosswalks, which District Engineer Kenny Fender said would be completed in the next two weeks.
Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) raised concerns over a funding issue for the Oyster Recovery Program, which he said is designed to mitigate damage from port activities and has been the backbone of oyster restoration.
Biddle responded to Mautz's concerns with good news, saying funds are secured for this fiscal year to continue that work. But the conversation escalated at the Dorchester County meeting later Tuesday, when Mautz expressed he felt the secretary had presented conflicting answers throughout the day.
DORCHESTER
Mautz worried transportation officials weren't following through on the details of the contract between MDOT and the Department of Natural Resources. That contract outlines that the agencies together will provide $2 million in funding this fiscal year for the oyster program, Mautz said, among other specifics.
Biddle ensured that the departments would hit the $2 million "target," adding that she will "stay very close" on the matter as her agency works with DNR.
Meanwhile, transportation officials told the Dorchester County Council and residents on Tuesday that a long-awaited roundabout project in East New Market is moving forward.
During MDOT'S stop in Dorchester, Pines said the department's six-year capital funding plan fully supports the roundabout design for the intersection of Routes 392 and 14 in East New Market next to Dockins Service Station.
According to the draft plan, estimated cost is $4.65 million for the improvement. Pines said Tuesday the design should be completed in 2026.
Dawn Stanley, who was in an accident at the intersection two years ago and pushed transportation officials on the matter at last year's annual meeting, clapped when Pines spoke and thanked him.
"Knowing that that roundabout is coming is really essential," said Dorchester County Council Vice President Mike Detmer. "Talking with responders from Station 21, this has always, always been a problem. This is gonna be a triumph of making the roads safer."
SHA District Engineer Mark Crampton touched on efforts to fix culverts at Route 336 as it goes over Worlds End Creek. The road is one of limited access points for residents in southern Dorchester County.
Crampton said temporary improvements have been done and estimated a three-week construction timeframe to begin this summer once school is out. State transportation leaders will meet with the county next week to look at the detour route, Crampton said.
Other areas discussed included:
Warwick Elementary School. Biddle said officials have worked to improve safety on the roads in front of the school in Secretary.Route 392 sidewalks. Biddle said the sidewalks on the portion of the state road in Hurlock were completed this year.
CAROLINE
MDOT came to the Health and Public Service Building on Tuesday morning to hear Caroline County's requests for projects and answer questions from the County Commissioners.
The commissioners also listened to MDOT's plans to ensure federal funding possibilities are still available for the county.
"Our team specifically at the State Highway Administration is looking for opportunities to look where we can apply federal funds for critical safety and state of repair projects here in the county," Biddle told the Star Democrat in an interview after the meeting.
"So, as many projects as we can identify that are federally eligible, it allows us to stretch limited state resources even further to be able to do more projects such as, the intersection improvements referenced by the commissioners today or just safety and resurfacing project where those are helpful and necessary parts of keeping our system in a state of good repair," Biddle said.
Here are the current projects in the county under construction, in progress or requested:
Bridge replacement and rehabilitation at Maryland Route 16 and Harmony Road. The project is already under construction.Intersection capacity improvements from Maryland Route 16 and Harmony Road to Greenwood Road. A planning study is underway.Additional striping or re-striping at the intersection of Maryland Route 317 (Burrsville Road) and Maryland 313 (Greensboro Road). This was requested by the county.Signal change for the traffic lane at Maryland Route 16 (Harmony Road) and Maryland 404. This was requested by the county.Additional lighted intersection at Maryland 404 and Gay Street. This was requested by the county.Consideration of the 16 E school in Greenwood and 404 as a major breakout point. The commissioners requested this change, calling the road as a "major disaster."
Reporters Ahmad Garnett, Konner Metz and Lily Tierney contributed to this report.

title: Sharp Road Park Construction Underway
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Sharp Road Park construction underway

 September 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 341
 Words

 Denton — Construction has officially started on Sharp Road Park in Denton.The park is expected to receive multiple upgrades, which started with a mural on the basketball court created by Terae Warner, a local business owner and basketball coach, and artist Shelton Hawkins.
Now Caroline County has started construction on the baseball field, softball field and multipurpose field at the park.
"It's a unique build, and we're doing it a la carte," said Jamie Beechey, director of Caroline County Recreation and Parks. "It's only so much money, so we're making sure that we get the right materials for the right price each step of the way and then decide like what we can afford and what we can't afford."
The construction starts with moving dirt for an access road and making sure the road has a good foundation for construction trucks. The next step is stormwater management.
The county has set up lighting and irrigation contracts, all of which have yet to be approved by the county commissioners. A fencing contract of $84,873 for the playing fields was approved by the county commissioners on Tuesday.
While the hope is for the fields to be finished by December, the county has plans to make the fields safer by adding nets, which could push the completion date back.
"My strongest hope is that we get finished by December, but that may not be everything," Beechey said. "One of the things that we are looking at because of the proximity of the fields, we want to put a netting up at least on one of the fields so the foul ball situation doesn't cause a safety issue for people."
The county is very excited for what the field could offer to Caroline County and other surrounding counties with games under the lights.
"It's going to be really remarkable to have a so-called it 'Field of Dreams,' where our kids go outside of the county and they get to experience these games under lights and now both the boys and the girls will get to experience that here in Denton," Beechey said.

title: Superintendent and Commissioners Discuss Lockerman
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Superintendent and commissioners discuss Lockerman

 July 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline 
 
 474
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners and Caroline County Public Schools Superintendent Derek Simmons discussed Lockerman Middle School at the County Commissioners meeting on Tuesday.At the last commissioners meeting, the commissioners discussed their role, responsibilities and preferred location for the new Lockerman Middle School.
The superintendent came to the commissioners meeting to discuss the approval of its fiscal year 2026 budget. After the discussion the commissioners talked about Lockerman Middle School and the next steps.
"I think it'd be good for us to say that we are working together on the Lockerman Middle School construction," Commissioners President Travis Breeding said. "We were asking questions about what role the commissioners officially play in siting and construction, they were just questions that we were asking. It wasn't like the Board of Ed's going to run all over us and make crazy stupid decisions and we're going to be stuck with it. It was just what influence do we have over the process."
Breeding explained the consensus the commissioners have come to on their personal choice for the new school location.
"I think we talked about it, and our consensus is that the most logical place to put it is probably next to North Carolina High School for us," Breeding said. "We understand that there's a whole process that has to be going through, fact finding, the Board of Ed will review that and make their decisions based off of that. But we were just saying that that questioning what influence we actually had over the process."
Simmons clarified they understand the commissioners wanting understanding of their role and told the commissioners how the process will go.
"Board of Education selects the site," Simmons said. "The feasibility study, which was presented to the board on July 1st, indicated North Carolina High School was the better of the two locations. We did review the two sites that we were asked to review that were basically the county-owned, which is cost efficient way to do it.
Simmons said the board received the feasibility study that night and should be making its decision on a site at the August meeting. He added the site selection does not include picking what the design of the building will be.
After looking over potential designs for the new Lockerman Middle School, Breeding suggested having athletic facilities have their own location and not sharing fields.
"One of the major things that stuck out with me was, relocating the athletic facilities around there," Breeding said. "If we can get dedicated facilities so we're not sharing space like we have been doing forever, where lacrosse or soccer is using the outfield of the softball and the baseball field, if we can actually get dedicated space, that would be a priority of mine."
He noted that facilities in surrounding counties should be studied.
"We've got one bite at the apple here, let's get it right," Breeding said.

title: Greensboro Will Not Bring Northern Towns onto Wastewater System
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro will not bring northern towns onto wastewater system

 June 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 440
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Greensboro — Caroline County is creating a plan to address septic system concerns in Henderson, Marydel and Templeville by building a wastewater treatment facility, but there is still a long way to go, officials say.The county has been brainstorming ideas since the May 6 commissioners meeting, where Commission President Travis Breeding announced the town of Greensboro would not take the towns onto its wastewater treatment system.
Greensboro Mayor David Spencer said the Greensboro Town Council came to that decision because of the wear and tear the facility would take by adding three new towns.
"I don't know that the council had absolutely said that they didn't want to be involved in the process. I think that they preferred not to be because of the additional responsibilities and potential expenses that may incur on our residents," Spencer said in an interview with the Star Democrat on Monday.
"I know that they were going to come back and give some more numbers... I don't know that the door has been absolutely closed, but I don't think the council had any appetite to try to move forward at this time," Spencer said.
The discussion arises after multiple north county residents complained about problems with their septic tanks. One resident brought their concerns to the county commissioners in April.
"My mom's property started flooding with the rain, and she is on a septic, and it's been drained three weeks ago," Kia Pierce said at an April meeting. "But the flooding is causing her septic lines to back up to the point where we cannot flush the toilet, and it's coming through the sinks now."
The commissioners are working on a plan, Breeding said, but it all depends on government permits and funding.
"We're talking to Maryland Department of Environment about other options, whether it be individual plants for each town, which we don't think is feasible, or one new plant in a centralized location that all three towns, Templeville, Henderson and Marydale, could connect to," Breeding said.
"We are looking at options as far as locations of a potential plant and what kind of discharge permit MDE would be willing to give us... Then also we're looking at what kind of funding MDE or (U.S. Department of Agriculture) may have available to help us construct a new plant up there."
While the county is working with MDE and USDA, Breeding said there is no time table for when the county will have a solidified plan.
"It's all pretty much funding-dependent, and one thing I've learned in the two years I've been in the office, it takes a lot longer than you think it's going to take," Breeding said. "So, we're working through it."
