title: Commissioners Discuss Potential Water and Sewer Issues in Caroline County
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Commissioners discuss potential water and sewer issues in Caroline County

 April 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 609
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At the April 15 Caroline County Commissioners meeting, Kia Pierce spoke about her mother's property in Ridgley."My mom's property started flooding with the rain, and she is on a septic, and it's been drained three weeks ago," Pierce said. "But the flooding is causing her septic lines to back up to the point where we cannot flush the toilet, and it's coming through the sinks now."
The discussion prompted the county to consider options for the future of northern Caroline County's water and wastewater infrastructure.
Commission President Travis Breeding said Tuesday that the county has set up a meeting to walk through the neighborhood and look at the drainage on that road.
Breeding also reported he had met with North County Water Authority, the entity behind an agreement for the northern towns in the county established more than a decade ago.
The agreement, which aimed to end the use of failing septic systems in the county's four northernmost municipalities — Goldsboro, Henderson, Marydel and Templeville — established a new sewer system.
Eventually, Greensboro built a new sewage treatment plant because the existing plant was flooding. Greensboro's plant began to serve Goldsboro residents after the upgrade.
Rates for Greensboro's waste water treatment have been rising rapidly, commissioners said, and residents of Goldsboro have had issues with the rates.
"Essentially under the the current agreement, those municipalities really don't have any say in the operation of the plant," Breeding said. "The rates that they pay or any real input into the maintenance operation and they're kind of just silent re-payers."
Tuesday, the county weighed whether to continue to have Greensboro's plant serve residents of other towns or whether to set up a county-run wastewater treatment plant at the north end of the county.
"We discussed each individual town having their own system or plant, which we believe is probably cost prohibitive, and we put them in a situation where they would all be competing with operators or competing to find an operator to operate the plant for them," Breeding said. "We also discussed option where there was one plant to service all three towns, Henderson, Marydell and Templeville. And what that would look like would either be the establishment of an authority or the county potentially stepping in and managing the plant for them."
While all options are on the table, Breeding presented this to the commissioners not expecting a definitive response.
"My question is just throwing this all out there for you guys to think about. I guess we don't need an answer right now, but is it time that Caroline County got into the water and sewer business or start to investigate that?" Breeding asked.
The commissioners concluded that if they were to consider an agreement with the towns to run their own water and sewage facility, the commissioners would need to go through multiple hurdles to do so.
"I'm certainly willing to talk about it," Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said. "My concern is if we want to talk about an exponential jump in costs and start operating a wastewater treatment plant, that's a whole different ballgame."
"The only way I would entertain it is if the people connected covered the cost to operate it," Breeding said. "If it's not a cost-effective, if there's not enough grant money that can be obtained, then it's tough to go. But I wouldn't want to subsidize it with any money from the rest of the county."
The commissioners plan to reach out to the Greensboro Town Council and see if the town is willing to push its wastewater treatment out of town limits. If the town is not willing, Henderson, Marydel and Templeville will need some sort of plant to service those residents.

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners discussed their Capital Transportation Priorities list and drafted a letter to send to the state at their April 15 meeting.The priority list is presented to the state every year to receive funding for road work projects within the county that the commissioners and town officials believes are a priority.
The state will ultimately determine which projects it funds.
PRIORITY A
Priority A for Caroline County is maintaining and improving existing infrastructure. The county asked for a comprehensive resurfacing of Route 313 from Route 404 to Federalsburg, including repairs to pavement, shoulders and stormwater infrastructure.
Next is the completion of the resurfacing project on Route 16 from Lake Drive to Route 404.
Lastly, Caroline County asked for general resurfacing, shoulder repair, drainage improvement and signage upgrades across Caroline County's state road network. Timely investment in these areas will help avoid further deterioration, reduce maintenance costs and significantly improve travel conditions for our residents and businesses, the county said.
PRIORITY B
The county requested Route 404 be widened from Harmony Road to Route 16 East.
Previous phases of this project have led to improved traffic flow and reduced accidents, demonstrating the importance of completing the corridor, the county said in its priorities list.
PRIORITY CCaroline County requested help with rebuilding and resurfacing Route 454 (Crownstone Road) from Marydel to Templeville.
Route 454 is a vital connector for residents in the western part of the county and serves as a gateway to Queen Anne's County. This route has seen substantial wear and requires resurfacing and structural upgrades to ensure safe and dependable travel, the county said.
PRIORITY DThe county requested state assistance with rebuilding and resurfacing Route 313 from Greensboro to Goldsboro.
This is a major north-south route within the county and is essential for local mobility and emergency response, the county said. It added resurfacing and drainage improvements are necessary to restore safe travel conditions and extend the life of the corridor.
PRIORITY ERounding out the county's priority list is an effort to restripe Route 317 and add a right turn lane.
"We propose restriping MD 317 (Burnsville Road) at the intersection of MD 313 to add a right turn lane. This improvement will help enhance traffic flow and improve safety for all drivers," the county said.

title: A Public Hearing Will Come for Potential Regional Detention Center
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
A public hearing will come for potential regional detention center

 January 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 449
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County wants to hear the public's opinion before making any big decisions on the potential regional detention center agreement with Kent and Queen Anne's counties.The Caroline County Commissioners discussed the draft agreement for the potential facility for the second week in a row at their weekly meeting Tuesday.
County Administrator Kathleen Freeman and County Attorney Stewart Barroll attended a meeting with Queen Anne's County officials about the draft agreement for the detention center Monday, bringing with them a list of concerns from the commissioners.
Freeman was not in attendance for Tuesday's commissioners meeting, but Barrol and Deputy County Administrator Daniel Fox presented an update on what was discussed in the meeting Monday.
Last week the commissioners' concerns largely dealt with the power Queen Anne's County would have over the regional detention center, and Queen Anne's County ability to throw Kent or Caroline County out of the agreement with no warning.
The majority of the authority over the center will be in Queen Anne's County hands, according to the draft. All decisions and disagreement must go through Queen Anne's County Commissioners, and if they may have a disagreement it will be mediated.
Under the draft, Queens Anne's County could decide after a certain amount of time to remove Caroline or Kent county from agreement, regardless of the amount of money that was put up. To remove one or both of the other counties from the agreement, according to the draft, Queen Anne's County must give the other county a two-year notice to take all their prisoners and house them somewhere else.
Those issues were discussed at the meeting on Monday, but Queen Anne's county has yet to send back the new revised draft bill.
Queen Anne's County was not receptive to all of Caroline County's requests at the Monday meeting, Barrol said, particularly a proposal to create a three-county authority to oversee the facility.
"I finally got it out of them that no, Queen Anne's will never part with any part of the title to the campus," Barrol said.
But Queen Anne's County verbally agreed to draft the agreement so that it can no longer exit the deal or force Caroline or Kent county out of the deal.
In addition, Caroline and Kent county will have the right to exit the deal if they please.
Another proposed change from Caroline County is allowing Caroline County employees positions at the regional detention center as opposed to having staff provided by just Queen Anne's County.
"From what I gather, from talking with Kathleen, that has pretty much been resolved that our employees would be able to be absorbed into the workforce," Commission Vice President Larry Porter said.
A date for a public hearing on the agreement has not yet been set.

title: Caroline County Looking to Make Security Upgrades at Courthouse
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County looking to make security upgrades at courthouse

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 481
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Upgraded security measures may soon be installed at the Caroline County Courthouse in Denton.On Nov. 26, the Caroline County Commissioners approved sending out an application letter for state funding to install 16 new bulletproof windows.
Circuit Court Administrative Judge Heather Price brought the proposed security upgrades to the commissioners at the county's most recent public meeting. She indicated a review from the state noted window and front door security as weak points for the courthouse.
As originally presented, if awarded, the county would receive $118,724 from the state to make the improvements to the windows and door. Price's ask was that the commissioners approve a memorandum of understanding between the county court and the county commission.
"This is a reimbursably-based grant," Price said. "So the commissioners would hopefully agree to front the money and then be reimbursed for that by the state. We're not guaranteed that we'll be picked for this."
During the meeting, Price said she has received death threats due to her job, including multiple that resulted in the person making threats serving jail time.
While the commissioners were on board to apply for funding for the new windows, they did not motion for the Circuit Court to apply for funding for a new door.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter raised concerns about removing the current door. He emphasized the historical nature of it and said he could foresee the Caroline County Historical Society having similar worries.
Price said she had "anticipated that concern" and already talked to Kathy Mackel of the Historical Society. Price said Mackel was agreeable to the request for new door funding "on the basis that we would save the old, historic door that could be reinstalled if the secure door was no longer necessary."
Commissioner Frank Bartz, however, felt if the door was removed and stored, it could become lost or forgotten.
"If you take the door out (and) say 'Hey, we're going to save it, we're going to put it back,' it gets stuck in a corner somewhere," Bartz said. "Twenty years from now, 'Where'd this door come from?'"
Porter said the photos he's seen of the potential door replacement aren't up to historical standards, likening one photo from a door quote to a Dollar General entrance. Commissioners asked that Price and the county go back and search for door replacements that fit within the courthouse's nature, even if they are more expensive than anticipated.
"I'm not saying that I won't support improving the safety of the door, but not with what the design that I've seen so far," Porter said. "It's got to comply more with the historic character of the building."
Commission President Travis Breeding agreed with his fellow commissioners, saying it's best to go "back to the drawing board" with the potential door replacement. Commissioners unanimously voted to approve funding 16 new windows with the potential of receiving money from the state's courthouse security application, which closed Dec. 3.

title: Transportation Departments Share Projects During Caroline County Meeting
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Transportation departments share projects during Caroline County meeting

 October 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 538
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Tuesday morning, the Caroline County Commissioners gathered to discuss the state's Consolidated Transportation Program. Members of the Maryland Department of Transportation shared an annual presentation that included various infrastructure projects and funding challenges.Representatives from MDOT, Maryland Aviation Administration, Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration, Maryland Transit Administration, Maryland Department of Transportation State Highway Administration and Maryland Transportation Authority shared information affecting local transportation as well as statewide transportation.
LOCALWill Pines, administrator for the State Highway Administration, shared various transportation projects in Caroline County, both pending and completed.
"We understand the fiscal challenges Maryland is facing," Pines said. "However, I want to assure you of two things. First, SHA will continue to do big things moving forward, multimodal projects that improve safety, and accessibility and equity. And second, safety will always be our highest priority."
According to Pines, the newly constructed bridge on Maryland 16 over Mill Creek was reopened to traffic in September.
Additionally, Pines said two county priorities are the focal point of the fall. The first is the construction of pavement widening and signalization upgrades to provide a dedicated left turn lane from Maryland 328 to Maryland 404. This $2.1 million project is anticipated to be completed near the end of 2025.
The second is the conversion of the flashing signals at Maryland 313 and Maryland 317 to full color signals. This improvement will facilitate safer traffic movements at the intersection.
SHA hosted the second public meeting for the Maryland 404 Planning and Environmental Linkage Study. The meeting was well attended, according to Pines, and the study is anticipated to be completed by the end of the year. Once completed, SHA will work with Caroline County to identify potential breakout projects along the corridor, pending available funding.
SHA has begun a pipe replacement project on Maryland 328, near Salisbury Road. Construction crews will work daytime hours this week for site preparation, then switch to overnight hours to minimize the impacts to traffic.
Travis Johnston, local transit support director for Maryland Transit Administration, said MTA provides nearly $1 million in operating and capital grants to support local transit operations provided by Delmarva Community Transit in conjunction with Kent and Talbot counties. In addition to continued preventative maintenance, the funds will also provide one new small bus.
Earlier this month, Gov. Wes Moore announced additional grant funding to the county aimed at helping the Caroline County Sheriff's Office and the Denton Police Department address speed impairment and aggressive driving.
Finally, Atkins Arboretum was awarded nearly $180,000 in recreational trails program funding to support the bridge deck replacement, the creation of a new trail and the necessary accessibility and maintenance improvements for its "Over The Creeks and Through the Woods" project.
STATEWIDEPaul Wiedefeld, secretary for MDOT, presented updates and plans for statewide projects.
According to Wiedefeld, major projects include working on the Howard Street Tunnel in Baltimore, major construction on aviation courses and connections, future growth of Southwest Airlines at BWI Airport and bringing the FBI headquarters to Green Belt.
Commission president Travis Breeding, took the time to thank Wiederfield and the rest of the representatives for their continued work for the county.
"Thank you, Secretary Wiederfield, for visiting Caroline County today with your entire leadership team," Breeding said. "Thank you for your continued investment in MDOT infrastructure within Caroline County."

title: Caroline Commissioners Discuss Dirt Road Paving
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline commissioners discuss dirt road paving

 September 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 445
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners convened on Sept. 24 to discuss several issues, including funding to pave dirt roads.Daniel Fox, deputy administrator; Robin Eaton, director of public works; Megan Gallagher, GIS specialist; and Leslie Grunden, assistant director of planning at Department of Planning and Codes, all came before the commissioners.
Fox said they are collecting the data to look for funding to upgrade and pave some of the roads in the county. There are county priorities and there are federal Protect Grant priorities. Where those two intersect is where funding can happen, he said.
"What we are trying to do is take a whole new look at dirt roads as a whole. Try to put as much information together and start to figure out where we can look for funding to start upgrading and possibly paving certain areas throughout the county," Fox said. "With the spreadsheet that we have outlined, we can really start to score and put metrics together with areas that bode well with different grant applications."
The group showed the commissioners maps of dirt roads in the county and data-rich spreadsheets about the dirt roads. The measured many things like how many homes per mile and the road's condition. They also plugged all that data into a GIS map so the commissioners could see exactly which roads needed help.
Trunk Line, Bates and Gregg Roads were identified as the most expensive dirt roads to maintain. Fox noted Gilpin Point, Blades Road and Noble Road have been identified by Public Works as needing work.
A few citizens who live on Trunk L ine Road came to speak about how dusty the road is. School bus driver Robert Smith said he had to wash his tail lights clean every time he drove on the dirt road.
American Rescue Plan Act funds could be used to pay for dirt road paving, Fox said.
The Department of Transportation also offers a PROTECT (Protect Resilient Operations for Transformative, Efficient and Cost Saving Transportation) grant. It could be a two-year process to get the funding said Fox.
"Last year the notice for funding opportunity came out in September. This year is it will probably come out in November. There is usually a month to a month and a half from the funding opportunity to the deadline for the grant. We are big believer in well begun in half done," Grunden said.
She wanted to know what the county priorities were before they proceeded to ask for the grant.
Grunden said the minimum these planning grant can offer is $100,000 and the minimum for a resilience grant that could include some construction is $500,000. She said there was no ceiling of what the county could ask for.

title: Proposed Software to Streamline Septic, Well Permitting in Caroline County
author: Tom McCall
content:
Proposed software to streamline septic, well permitting in Caroline County

 September 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 395
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At the Caroline County Commissioners meeting Sept. 3, three public health officials announced that they are looking to streamline the Caroline County Health Department's website's functionality. They want it to be easier to use, have more internal efficiency and feature enhanced collaboration.The system being considered by the department is called the LAMA System, an integrated local government interface. The Health Department plans to use the system to streamline the county's septic and well permitting process. According to the department representatives at the meeting, the system could be employed at no cost to the county.
"We are here to request approval for Caroline County Health Department's well and septic permitting to be added to the current Caroline County Planning Code LAMA system," said Robin Cahall, Caroline County health officer. "It is used to manage permits, licences, planning projects and code enforcement."
It can review environmental health services permits, planning reviews and code enforcement. County residents could pay fees through a portal and check the status of well and septic, and water and sewer.
The system even allows for mobile inspections and sends the inspection in for real-time reviews.
The department officials said it would take time to deploy the system and train the staff to use it. They hope to have it in place by the next fiscal year, which begins in July 2025.
"You are going from paper files to actually being able to utilize a tablet or smartphone to complete things... We want to start out small and then push it out to the public that this is what is going to happen," Cahall said.
Josh Parker, director of the Environmental Health Division, said, "The transition on our side is when, as Robin said, there is double work that is a big bottle neck in our office. On site, in the field approvals is really going to alleviate a lot of paperwork on our side and an immense amount of time scanning, uploading, verifying. It just won't need to be done anymore."
She said the department is committed to doing a mini campaign to let residents know the process is changing. The commissioners agreed that anything to make the process more efficient is welcome.
After lots of discussion about the potential efficiency of LAMA, the commissioners gave it the OK.
"It sounds good. I think we are good to move forward with this. Good luck," Commission President Travis Breeding said.

title: Commissioners Discuss Landfill Agreement, Upcoming Detours
author: Tom McCall
content:
Commissioners discuss landfill agreement, upcoming detours

 August 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 429

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners met on Aug. 20 and discussed a wide range of topics, including a River Road detour, an agreement pertaining to the waste transfer station and the tabling of the food processing residual storage bill.RESIDUALS BILLThe commissioners decided to hold off on the third reading of a Food Processing Residuals Storage bill that has garnered a large amount of public comment during previous hearings.
Commissioners stated this was so they could have a full board present to vote on the bill. Commissioner Frank Bartz was absent from the Aug. 20 meeting.
The bill requires the use of closed-top storage tanks for food processing residuals, going a step further than state regulations passed during this year's General Assembly.
The commissioners decided to hold the third reading until their next meeting, which will be Sept. 3.
RIVER ROAD DETOURThe commissioners discussed the upcoming replacement of the culvert pipe on River Road in Ridgely and traffic problems that may ensue. Central Avenue and Holly Road will be covered by the Sheriff's Office to keep traffic moving.
Through Oct. 1, Holly Road will be closed between Central Avenue and Route 404 between 2:40 and 3:15 p.m., which will reroute the traffic of North Caroline High School. Traffic will be directed north of Central Avenue up to north of 480 to access 404.
LANDFILL AGREEMENTCounty Administrator Kathleen Freeman brought up the County Administrator's report on the landfill agreement between several Mid-Shore counties, which was signed by all jurisdictions.
Mid-Shore II Regional Landfill, located in Caroline County, is governed by a four-county agreement between Queen Anne's, Kent, Talbot and Caroline counties.
Caroline County is hosting the current landfill and, under the original arrangement, would be off the hook at the end of 2030 when Queen Anne's County would take over the responsibility of host. However, the partnering counties have agreed to allow the landfill to stay in Caroline County for 12 years longer than initially planned.
"We are not expanding it. We are filling it to its full capacity," Travis Breeding said.
DETENTION CENTER REPAIRSThe Regional Detention Center has a leaky roof that is jeopardizing electric operations, according to county officials who spoke at the Aug. 20 meeting. An emergency repair was requested at the detention center for the leak.
A bid from Dynamic Roofing was $67,000 to fix it. The commissioners will take the money out of remaining American Rescue Plan Act funds. The commissioners voted to approve the purchase order to fix the roof.
"The money for this is not in the capital budget. We are still spending down some of the ARPA funding," said Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox.

title: Water Woes Hit Federalsburg Again
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Water woes hit Federalsburg again

 February 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 365
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — A downed tree behind Holland Drive uprooted a main water line, causing a "massive leak," according to town officials Tuesday, Feb. 20.Crews worked from mid-morning to late afternoon, trying to determine the cause and seal off the line at the break.
At mid-morning Tuesday, Feb. 20, town officials posted on the Town of Federalsburg Facebook page, "We have received reports of low/no water pressure and Public Works is currently investigating the cause. We will post more information as soon as it becomes available."
Shortly after 10 a.m., an update was posted: Public Works discovered an issue with Well 5 this morning. "Well 5 handles the capacity of all 3 of the other wells. It appears to be working properly now and pressure is returning, though it will take some time to fully return to normal. Staff is working to do everything possible to assist in this process."
In a 12:30 p.m. text message to The Star Democrat, Mayor Kim Abner said, "We were made aware of low water pressure early this morning and Public Works staff is working diligently to get it resolved."
"A Well Specialist has been called in to assist. Right now they are still troubleshooting. Town Manager Marshall is actively working the situation and we are hopeful it will be resolved as quickly as possible," Abner wrote.
Another update posted at 3:40 p.m. stated "the exact problem has not been determined." Bottled water was available at the town office until 6 p.m.
At 5:14 p.m., town officials announced, "Water pressure should now be back to normal. A massive leak was found in the woods behind Holland Drive where a tree came down and uprooted a main line. We turned off the line with the break which is restoring pressure to the rest of the system."
The town recently experienced problems with the system on Friday, Jan. 26, with a water shutdown that lasted until Tuesday evening, Jan. 30. Then a sinkhole developed Tuesday on Maple Avenue.
A power outage at the town's water and sewage plant in January caused the town's water pumps to fail, depleting the water in the system and leaving air in the lines.
The town's population is about 3,000, according to the 2020 census.

title: Caroline Commissioners Pass Bills, Approve Roads Projects
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Commissioners pass bills, approve roads projects

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 532
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Road paving projects, legislative picks and pans, and zoning decisions formed the bulk of the Caroline County Commission meeting at 9 a.m. Tuesday, Feb. 13, in Denton.After a lengthy discussion with Deputy County Administrator Daniel Fox and Roads Superintendent Bryan North, the commissioners settled on beginning paving projects for two county roads.
Wolf Road near Henderson and a short dirt section of Jones Corner Road at Concord will be paved with tar and chip, and paid for with leftover American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 funding.
Two roads affected by flooding are awaiting better weather and materials. Fox said he will be getting a purchase order to the commissioners next week for $122,000 to buy the precast concrete needed to improve the River Road site. Unusually high tides have prevented work on Gilpin Point Road, although the replacement pipes are on hand.
Legislative actionsThe commissioners introduced legislation to change zoning requirements for solar energy systems in the R-Rural District, repealing subsections in Section 175 of the county code, and "reenacting the same with amendments." The legislation is Bill 2024-003.
Originally proposed in October 2023, public comment prompted the county Planning Commission to recommend changes. Screening requirements, including working with a licensed landscape architect and providing for a variety of buffers were not changed.
Also unchanged was the restriction on placing commercial solar on the portion of acreage that was used for transfer development rights. Road right-of-way setbacks were increased.
The second reading and public hearing for Bill 2024-003 is set for Feb. 20 at the County Commission meeting. The third reading is scheduled for March 12, with an anticipated effective date of April 26.
Two other pieces of legislation were read for the third time and enacted unanimously. Legislative Bill 2024-001, authorizes additional projects to be funded from the proceedings of the Consolidated Public Improvement and Refunding Bonds of 2019.
The projects are roof replacements for Federalsburg Elementary School, North Caroline High School and Preston Elementary School, as well as a new HVAC system for the Fretterd Center in Denton.
The bond proceeds were reallocated since the commissioners are not pursuing the renovations of the county detention center, anticipating the eventual construction of a regional detention center.
Legislative Bill 2024-002 revised stream buffer requirements for both perennial and intermittent streams, increasing them from 25 to 50 feet.
State legislation
Commission Vice President Larry Porter and Public Information Officer Jennifer Reibly have attended Maryland General Assembly legislative session updates with various groups.
The commissioners will send letters of opposition and directives to the lobbyists to oppose bills that "take away local autonomy" such as House Bill 1407, which would preempt a county's authority to decide if and where to place solar arrays, Porter said.
Porter recommended opposing a statewide school emergency response bill, consulting with the Recreation and Parks Department regarding legislation that would require counties to replace certain playground surface materials and opposing funding cuts to community colleges.
Because the county "has been a catalyst" for lithium battery safety, Porter recommended supporting House Bill 468/Senate Bill 530.
The commissioners discussed other pending legislation. To view the meeting of the commissioners, watch the video posted on the commissioners' website, usually within 48 hours of the meeting.
Agendas, videos and transcripts of commission meetings are posted at carolinemd.org.

Denton leaders discuss resilience, upgrades

 DENTON — Among the agenda items discussed during the Denton Town Council meeting Thursday, Feb. 1, were flood resilience, expanding water and sewer to West Denton and providing town law enforcement officers with enhanced portable radios.Two ordinances were introduced and received unanimous consent to move forward.
Ordinance 751 would amend the code's subdivision code to allow shared access for minor subdivisions and improved right of way, which is not a component of the town, county state or federal road system.
In Ordinance 752, the town council amended the town code with two updated official zoning maps that align with the Comprehensive Plan adopted Dec. 11.
In December, the town council adopted the 2020 Comprehensive Plan, following a process that had been held up during the Covid pandemic.
The council green-lighted the first step in working with the Federal Emergency Management Agency in Philadelphia to receive free technical assistance through a memorandum of understanding.
Town Administrator Wayne Getchell said his "key takeaway ... will be that (FEMA) will come on site and do a needs assessment in our areas that we struggle with flooding in and around the Choptank, and develop an action plan that would be consistent with their grant program."
The second step would be to apply for FEMA money "to make whatever improvements are found to be made," but the 3-year MOU "was required by them to get started," Getchell said.
Crisfield is the only other town on the Eastern Shore who is working on a similar MOU with FEMA, he said.
The council approved the purchase of new portable radios for the Denton Police Department.
Bacorn asked the council to approve the purchase of 16 Motorola portable radios, 13 for officers, two for office staff and one to have on hand as a spare.
The radios will replace the 6-year-old BK Technologies radios "which have been failing regularly and without warning, which causes safety concerns," McNinch said.
Bacorn said the old radios were unreliable, and "as of late, they have been feeling, and they don't give any warning. We've had officers out on traffic stops who couldn't be contacted, on calls where they couldn't be contacted."
Bacorn said up to 75% of the $107,425 pricetag could be covered by grant money from the US Department of Agriculture. Even so, Getchell said ARPA (American Rescue Plan Act) funds were available, enabling the town to commit to ordering them. It will be Bacorn said the "backbone of Caroline County's radio system is a Motorola system. The compatibility is just better, the features are much better. title: Federalsburg Works to Resolve Water, Sewer Issues
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Federalsburg works to resolve water, sewer issues

 January 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 472
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — Following a water shutdown that began Friday, Jan. 26, the town of Federalsburg announced Tuesday evening that water service was restored.However, another difficulty challenged town officials before 1 p.m. Tuesday when a sinkhole developed on Maple Avenue, caused by "an issue with the sewer main," according to the town's official Facebook page.
"Further details to be determined once the water is drained and the pipe can actually be observed," the post stated. "The crew is working on the repair as we speak and no services to residents will be affected." The 300 block of Maple Ave will be closed until the repairs are complete.
One resident commented on the post: "It's OK. We can't drink the water so we don't need the toilet. All good."
As for water service, the "system continues to replenish itself," the town announced on Facebook. Residents were asked to conserve water and to be aware of air bubbles or cloudiness in the water. "This is normal and will return to normal once all air is out of the line," the post stated.
The water problem began Friday night after a power outage at the town's water and sewage plant. The outage caused the town's water pumps to fail, depleting the water in the system and leaving air in the lines.
Mayor Kim Abner said an alert system did not go off Friday night when one of the town's water pumps failed to work. She said Monday that all three pumps were up and running, pumping 600,000 gallons to fill the system.
The Maryland Department of the Environment recommended Monday afternoon that the mayor and town council post that "regular and bacterial testing is in process and results will be posted as soon as this info is available."
Bottled water was available at the Federalsburg Fire House until 7 p.m. Tuesday, Jan. 30. The Maryland National Guard also provided a tank of water for residents to fill their own containers.
Town staff delivered meals at Federalsburg Volunteer Fire Company, as well as bottled water available for pick up. Caroline County Public Schools provided bottled water to Federalsburg Elementary School and the Judy Center.
On Monday morning, the town had posted on its Facebook page, "All three wells are back online and pressure is coming up. We are now pumping 500 gallons a minute, but we need to fill the water towers and lines that were empty. It will take time, but we are making progress."
In a Tuesday afternoon text message to The Star Democrat, Abner said town officials "will be having a debrief on the event with staff and external entities as to how we can prevent something like this from happening again if there is another power outage."
"We want to thank all of the neighboring Towns and agencies for their assistance," Abner's text message said.
Star Democrat reporter Tom McCall contributed to this story.

title: Greensboro may get funds to move pump station, restore site of old wastewater treatment plant
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Greensboro may get funds to move pump station, restore site of old wastewater treatment plant

 January 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 655
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Though she wasn't on the agenda, Caroline County Assistant Director of Planning Leslie Grunden reported a positive development in protecting a stream flowing into the Choptank River north of Greensboro.Leading off the Jan. 23 meeting of the Caroline County Commission, Grunden said state funding was available to shore up "erosion at the town's pump station at the site of the old treatment plant located on a small tributary that feeds directly to the Choptank River," she said.
Greensboro Director of Public Works Brandon Cunningham alerted Commission President Travis Breeding about the "severe erosion" after recent significant rainfall.
"When he called me, and I went to look at it, I was like, 'Oh, yeah, this is a big deal,'" Breeding said.
Grunden said Cunningham told her he noticed "some erosion had been increasing" over the past several months.
"I think that was part of the old outfall for the old treatment plant, but the sides and the bottom are lined all the way down to the river — under the overpass into the river," Grunden said. "And over time, because it was probably put it in in the '60s, … it's broken up and starting to collapse and that's exacerbating the erosion."
A short-term solution in the form of an emergency grant was already in the works to add rocks and rebar and help hold the bank in place "while we went looking for funding for the long-term solution," to move the pump station farther uphill, Grunden said.
The aim is to remove the infrastructure and convert the stream location to a natural floodplain.
"Bringing the pump station up the hill (on town property) keeps it out of harm's way from erosion but also from eventual rising water from the Choptank," she said.
"This pump station takes flow from the town to the plant, so for that to be in jeopardy kind of keeps me up at night," Grunden said. The north county wastewater treatment plant is located on State Route 313, just north of Greensboro Volunteer Fire Company's community hall.
Grunden said her usual funding sources could support either the infrastructure or stream and floodplain restoration but not both. "So, I kind of put the word out saying we need money for both," she said.
However, the Maryland Department of the Environment gave her a call a week or two ago, "essentially (saying), 'We think we found the money to do both,' which is … almost a miracle," Grunden said.
MDE had "actually never done this grant. It's a grant they get from EPA that they've never had interest in," she said. "They would actually be the recipient, and then the county would be the sub-recipient. (MDE) would actually have to do all the reporting up to EPA, and I would provide them status reports and invoices."
She is currently putting together a project budget. Preliminary estimates put the pump station relocation at $1.3 million, and Grunden's guess is removing the structures would be half a million, with stream and floodplain restoration another half a million.
"And then I always have a contingency plan because nothing ever goes the way you want," she said. "So, we're at about $2.4 million. (The Department of Natural Resources) has reached out to say they'd be interested in helping with the stream and floodplain component, which would give us more money if we need more to deal with on the pump station side."
Grunden said she was "pretty confident" that enough funding would be available for the two-phase project, "where the first phase would be moving the pump station and demo-ing the old buildings, and the second phase would be going in and doing the stream and the floodplain restoration."
Although the project is "not a sure thing," she said MDE reaching out to her was "a really good sign that they're serious about providing the funding."
"I can't think of a better move that we can make there environmentally other than to get that stuff out of the floodplain," Breeding said.

title: County Council Approves Vehicle Weight Limit On Black Dog Alley
author: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub.Com
content:
County Council Approves Vehicle Weight Limit On Black Dog Alley

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub.Com | Page: B3 | Section: News 
 
 426
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Talbot County Council on Tuesday approved legislation establishing a vehicle weight limit on Black Dog Alley to reduce heavy truck through traffic.Resolution 351, which received unanimous support from council members, will prohibit vehicles over 17,000 pounds from traveling on Black Dog Alley, which runs between Cordova Road and Dover Road.
Some vehicles are exempt from the restrictions, including vehicles owned or operated by government entities and their employees, vehicles involved with agricultural production or operations, emergency vehicles, vehicles belonging to those whose land is located on or is only accessible via Black Dog Alley and vehicles providing services like heating oil delivery, trash pickup or property improvement.
Vehicles over the weight limit can use U.S.
Route 50 as an alternate route, which is better equipped to handle oversized vehicles and higher traffic volume.
The need for the legislation stems from maintenance and safety issues along the narrow roadway.
The concept of a weight limit on the road has previously been considered by the county.
The council introduced similar legislation in late 2019, but the resolution did not progress.
During the legislation's public hearing Tuesday, Talbot County farmer Keith Shortall, who lives off of Black Dog Alley, said while he does utilize the road for agricultural purposes during harvest season, he's noticed many trucks hauling grain from the Port of Baltimore down into Hurlock in Dorchester County year-round.
Shortall emphasized the need for advance signage for the change in vehicle allowance.
He also stressed the need for other improvements on the narrow parts of the road that don't have shoulder lanes.
" Regardless of what you do with this, the work that needs to be done on Black Dog Alley still needs to happen," he said.
Design for improvements to parts of Black Dog Alley is in progress, said Ray Clarke, the county engineer.
Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble echoed safety concerns, noting that Black Dog Alley is the most accident-prone road in the county.
Gamble also raised a flag to future traffic problems once the new regional medical center is constructed, saying Black Dog Alley will likely see more emergency vehicles coming from southern Caroline County utilizing the road.
Gamble said the sheriff 's office would start enforcement of the new restriction on Black Dog Alley in an educational way at first.
Citations are more likely to be handed out after an adjustment period.
John Trax, a Talbot County farmer and the "self-proclaimed mayor of Black Dog Alley," expressed full support for the resolution. He adding that he wished more could be added to it, namely ways to further address traffic and speeding.
The resolution took effect upon adoption.

title: Highway Administration Hears from Public on Route 404
author: Maggie Trovato; trovato@chespub.com
content:
Highway Administration hears from public on Route 404

 December 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; trovato@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 738
 Words

 DENTON - The Maryland Department of Transportation State Highway Administration gave Caroline County residents the opportunity to share their thoughts on state Route 404 between Harmony Road and Greenwood Road at a public open house held at Denton Elementary School on Wednesday.SHA Project Manager Carmeletta Harris said the purpose of the open house is to get feedback from the public on what they would like to see regarding Route 404."We are not presenting any concepts tonight," Harris said. "We want them to tell us what else is out here that we haven't seen yet." At the open house, poster boards lined the school cafeteria to show SHA's findings from its Planning and Environmental Linkages Study.The purpose of the study is to assess transportation needs.Information was broken down into seven sections: Study overview, PEL process, environmental overview, transportation needs, mapping, Title VI and safety.At the mapping station, residents could place post-it notes with their concerns on a map of Route 404.According to the information displayed at the event, the top five dislikes, gathered from stakeholder interviews so far, are congestion, uncontrolled intersections, danger from high speeds and trucks, accidents and that there is not a dual lane all the way through.Harris said SHA wants to listen to residents before presenting any concepts. Currently, SHA plans to develop preliminary improvement concepts this winter and present those concepts for feedback in the spring. It also plans to finalize its study recommendations and identify any potential stand-alone projects in the spring.Harris said the project is not funded for anything outside of the study."Not construction and things of that nature," she said. "That could come down the line But right now, we're tasked to do this study and develop some concepts." Bruce Pepper, who lives on Mitchell Road, said he's most interested in seeing the concepts that the SHA comes up with.One of Pepper's main concerns is traffic. He said that he has noticed Legion Road getting beach traffic."They run 60 miles an hour down that road," he said. "It's hilly, winding.And they think they're getting ahead, but they're not. But the GPS tells them it's a shortcut." Pepper's neighbors, Alyssa and Jamie Taylor, said they have concerns with safety and the accidents."We have only been here for about two and a half years," Alyssa Taylor said. "And we have walked up to, I would say, at least three - I can think of four or five accidents that we hear happen." The Taylors are especially interested to find out if Route 404 will be expanding."I would love to know if 404 is going to be in my front yard," Alyssa Taylor said.If that does happen, the Taylors would consider moving. They said it would affect property values and be a safety concern."Even though my front door right now is probably 160 feet from the centerline - If they do dual-lane, I don't want tractor trailers, cars, motorcycles, whatever, going 80 miles an hour now 60 feet from my door, 80 feet from my door," Jamie Taylor said.Alyssa Taylor said she was happy that SHA wanted to hear from residents and said that they had written down "everything that we're saying." John Booze said everyone from SHA was receptive and willing to listen."Tough forum too because everybody has their own issue," he said."I don't envy them. But they gave everybody a good listen and I think it'll be positive going forward." Booze said traffic volume and getting across Route 404 are some of his major concerns."Getting across the road," he said. "Whether it's somebody coming from a home. Whether it's somebody coming from business The folks that have frontage right on 404 I really am concerned about." Like Pepper, Booze has noticed more drivers taking roads that connect to MD 404."Because of Waze and GPS and Google Maps, people are starting to go farther out on the back roads to get where they want to go," he said.Booze said those drivers are driving fast and its causing the traffic problems to spread outside of Route 404."So you need to take that into consideration as well," he said. "That was one of the things that I wanted to make sure I shared with them when I came."

title: Commissioners Prioritize Roads, Bridges Projects
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Commissioners prioritize roads, bridges projects

 November 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 3A | Section: News 
 
 666
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - A list of projects to repair and maintain the county's dirt roads and to open closed bridges was presented to the Caroline County Commissioners Oct. 24 by then-Caroline County Director of Public Works Ryan White and Roads Superintendent Bryan North.As of Nov. 8, White was no longer the director, but no further information was available as of press time.The number of houses on the roads determined the priority of attention to them.Applying that standard, Commission President Travis Breeding set aside Alms House, County Farm and Dead End roads east of Denton as low priority.Concerns about the amount of traffic and the distance road crews must travel to maintain the roads were also considered, along with the amount of truck traffic and school bus routes."A truck on a muddy road, it just kills it," White said. "So that's also something we took into account when we figured this out.Breeding and Commissioner Frank Bartz agreed that Mitchell and Wolf roads were priorities because of the number of houses. White said he considered property density rather than the number of houses.Participating remotely, Commission Vice President Larry Porter suggested beginning work on Wolf Road east of Henderson and reaching out to residents for feedback on Mitchell Road south of Denton, who had expressed concerns in the past about increased traffic if the road were tar-and-chipped.Tar-and-chip paving increases the speed on those roads about 10 to 15 miles per hour.Beck Road connecting State Routes 404 and 313 (Federalsburg Highway), Trunkline Road north of Henderson and Jones Corner Road between Concord and American Corner were also considered.Dirt roads are inspected about once a month and scraped as needed, White said.The commissioners determined that Beck and Wolf roads were priorities, which are in line for gravel, then tar-andchip paving, with Mitchell on the list after calls to residents.White said he's reached out to the Maryland State Roads Administration about funding the culvert pipe replacement on River Road.In the meantime, White has "given (SHA) the green light to go ahead and try to get us at least an 80-20 (state and county funding) split on Bloomery Road" north of Federalsburg Road, he said. "That does not sound like it's going to be an issue at all." Issues concerning the approach to the bridge on Long Swamp Road generated some discussion about the extent of the county's ownership of certain rights of way, something County Attorney Stewart Barroll suggested discussing in a closed session."If we can get 100% funding, are we interested in having a discussion about reopening some of the older bridges that have been closed?" Breeding asked. Bartz and Porter agreed.Regarding reopening bridges, property owners will be contacted for their opinions.The attention turned to River Road west of Denton. "I don't think anybody misses that bridge being closed from a traffic standpoint," Porter said."No, but where I'm coming from is the proximity to the high school, the waterfront and the potential for economic growth out there," Breeding said. "It's close to our growth area in the county, it is waterfront property with higher potential property values and it's right in the center of the county as well. If we have a discussion about opening one, i think that one makes sense to talk about.Other closed bridges are on Poplar Neck Road west of Preston, Bloomery Road and Back Landing Road which runs from Preston into Dorchester County. White said he was waiting to hear back from SHA about available funding for reopening the bridge on Gregg Road.According to the county's website, the roads division "is responsible for maintaining over 450 miles of roadway and 39 bridges or crossings in Caroline County." Over 70 miles of those roads are dirt roads.

title: County to Consider Vehicle Weight Limits on Black Dog Alley
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
County to consider vehicle weight limits on Black Dog Alley

 November 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 4 | Section: News

 EASTON - The Talbot County Council on Tuesday introduced a resolution that would establish a vehicle weight limit on Black Dog Alley to reroute some of the road's through traffic.According to Mike Mertaugh, the assistant county engineer, Black Dog Alley has essentially become a bypass around Easton for traffic going to and from southern Caroline County and Dorchester County.That traffic volume, along with heavy trucks, are causing maintenance issues along the roadway, Mertaugh said. Restricting heavy trucks from traveling on the road would extend its lifespan and improve safety on the road.Some parts of the road are narrow, and the southern part of Black Dog Alley does not have a shoulder lane.While the county roads department has worked to keep it maintained, heavy vehicles on the edge of pavement without support can cause the road to "crumble away," Mertaugh said.The restriction wouldn't burden trucks, he said - U.S. Route 50 almost runs parallel to Black Dog Alley, and the highway is designed for that type of traffic.The legislation, if passed, wouldn't impede local traffic or farmers, and exceptions would be made for agricultural businesses and government vehicles.The county already has a similar weight restriction in place on Dover Neck Road, which experienced similar issues.The council unanimously introduced the legislation, known as Resolution 351. A public hearing will be held on Tuesday, Dec. 12, at 6:30 p.m.

title: MDOT Updates Caroline Leaders on Project Plans - Officials Outline Six Year Draft Budget, Provide Key Project Updates
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
MDOT updates Caroline leaders on project plans - Officials outline six year draft budget, provide key project updates

 October 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 988
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - Maryland Transportation Secretary Paul J. Wiedefeld and other representatives of the Maryland Department of Transportation met Tuesday, Oct. 3, with Caroline County officials to discuss the department's six-year draft FY 2024-2029 Consolidated Transportation Program.The spending plan "calls for a $21.2 billion, six-year investment to create a safer, cleaner, efficient and accessible transportation system connecting Marylanders to jobs, schools, recreation, health care and essential services," according to a MDOT press release."Delivering safe, reliable, equitable and sustainable transportation is critical to Maryland's economic health and the vibrancy of neighborhoods across the state. This draft CTP is inspired by that mission," Wiedefeld said."We know there are challenges ahead, and we are committed to fiscal responsibility and collaboration with local communities, stakeholders and elected officials as we deliver the transportation network Marylanders need and deserve," he said.In addition to Wiedefeld, officials attending included State Highway Deputy Administrator for Project Development Matt Baker; Motor Vehicle Administrator Chrissy Nizer; Maryland Transportation Authority Planning and Program Development Director Melissa Williams; Maryland Transit Administration Local Transit Support Director Travis Johnston; Maryland Aviation Administration Regional Aviation Director Ashish Solanki; and District 2 Engineer Ken Fender.At the meeting, transportation officials offered details and updates of several projects and programs affecting Caroline County.Baker said the agency is planning for potential improvements along three miles of state Route 404 from Harmony Road to Greenwood Road. A study looking at pedestrian and bicyclist safety improvements and traffic operations, as well as truck and agricultural traffic, is anticipated to be completed in spring 2024. An in-person open house meeting planned for this fall. In addition, a public survey to gather feedback on the study is available at mdot-sha-md404-harmony-rd-to-greenwood-rdco219b11-maryland.hub.arcgis.com/Baker said the State Highway Administration will advertise a $1 million contract for improvements at the state Routes 404 and 328 intersection, which will add turn lanes for safer traffic flow.Some interim improvements have been made to help reduce intersection conflicts and improve traffic flow during peak school bus times.Transportation officials noted other allocations for Caroline County in the draft CTP, including more than $1.1 million in operating and capital grants to support local transit operations provided by Delmarva Community Transit. In addition, Delmarva Community Service will receive a $123,000 Statewide Transit Innovation Grant to install a propane station for propane-powered vehicles, enabling Delmarva Community Transit to transition to a low-emission fleet.As "a charter member of the Ken Fender Fan Club," Caroline County Commission Vice President Larry Porter thanked the District 2 engineer for his responsiveness, especially with improving traffic flow at the Goldsboro Volunteer Fire Company and traffic light timing at the intersection of River Road (State Route 328) and State Route 404, calling the latter a "tremendous benefit." Porter cited concerns with highway user funds being slashed to $400,00 from a high of $4 million, and a proposed mileage tax for electric vehicles.Wiedefeld said addressing changes in policy affecting EVs "is a challenge that's coming at us. We don't have any answers yet." Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding brought up the "four old timber bridges that were built in the '30s and '40s that are on our list that need to be replaced." Breeding said someone from MDOT "actually reached out to us to start the conversation about potentially pursuing some federal funding because these bridges are probably a million dollars or better a piece to replace, and that would just be too large of a hit on our (county)." Commissioner Frank Bartz thanked the State Highway Administration for repaving Route 578 between Harmony and Bethlehem but expressed concerns about future traffic detours when the Williston bridge is eventually replaced on state Route 16.Other concerns brought up by the commissioners were the long transport times for emergency services and the effectiveness of DCT's fixed routes versus a mobility-on-demand model.The draft CTP includes funding to maintain existing transportation facilities, expand transit opportunities, invest in Maryland's economic growth and support the state's long-term goals for mobility, safety, equity, environmental stewardship and economic growth.The program allocates funding for electric vehicle infrastructure, as well as investment in the transition to zero-emission transit buses and other carbon reduction and resiliency programs, "establishing Maryland as national leader in addressing climate goals," the press release stated.The program includes funding to promote Transit-Oriented Development to spur economic growth in transit corridors, and for projects to support Complete Streets - an initiative to make Maryland's roadways safer and more accessible for all users, and help reduce the number of roadway fatalities and injuries.The program outlines investments in each mode funded by the Transportation Trust Fund: Maryland Aviation Administration, Maryland Port Administration, Maryland Transit Administration, Motor Vehicle Administration, State Highway Administration and The Secretary's Office, as well as Maryland's investment in the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority.The plan includes an additional $2.7 billion investment planned by the Maryland Transportation Authority. Receiving no funds from the Transportation Trust Fund, the Maryland Transportation Authority's toll facilities are fully financed, constructed, operated, maintained, improved and protected with toll revenues paid by customers using those facilities.Motor Vehicle Administrator Nizer discussed the state's Vision Zero initiative - the goal of achieving zero fatalities on Maryland roadways. She noted that jurisdictions and organizations are encouraged to apply for safety grants through the Maryland Highway Safety Office to use for enforcement and education efforts.The Caroline County meeting was part of the Maryland Department of Transportation's tour of all 23 Maryland counties and Baltimore City to discuss the funding plan and receive input from local officials and the public. The tour continues into November.Following the tour, the draft fiscal year 2024-2029 Consolidated Transportation Program will be finalized and submitted in January for consideration during the 2024 General Assembly session.To view the full the program, visit ctp.maryland.gov.

title: Broadband Internet Project Ahead of Schedule
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Broadband internet project ahead of schedule

 September 28, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 4 | Section: News 
 
 670
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Choptank Electric Cooperative and Choptank Fiber presented the Dorchester County Council last Tuesday evening on the broadband internet project that will bring broadband to about 704 locations in the county."We believe that this entire project will be done by the end of 2024," Valerie Connelly, vice president of government affairs and public relations for Choptank Electric, said. "We are moving much faster than we thought." Choptank Fiber, a broadband internet company, is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Choptank Electric. Its goal is to "serve the unserved." Connelly said a broadband project of this kind is often expected to take about three years."The first year is all engineering and design, the second year they start to do the construction, the third year [is] connecting members," she said. "We've been able to build out most of what we're doing in 14 months or so. We're very pleased." The $8.3 million project, which runs below Federalsburg and into Northeast Dorchester County, builds on a recently finished broadband project in Caroline County. Funding for this Dorchester project comes from the Maryland Office of Statewide Broadband, Choptank Electric and Choptank Fiber and Dorchester County.The Office of Statewide Broadband is contributing $4.08 million, Choptank Electric and Choptank Fiber is contributing $3.7 million and Dorchester County has pledged $500,284 of American Rescue Plan Act funds."The grant money that was contributed by the county and by the state allows us to bring on contractors and keep them working continuously," Connelly said. "So we're moving them from one project to the next trying to get to everybody who is unserved here on the shore." Connelly said construction has started for the project and most of the engineering has been completed. She added that because the project has been divided into zones, some areas are opening up for service as the project continues."We're not waiting until the entire project is built out," she said. "We're, weekly, announcing areas that we're opening for service for members who live there." Connelly said the question everyone asks as soon as they hear about the project is, "How much is it going to cost?" Choptank Fiber offers different speed packages. These include: Up to 100 Mbps for $84.95 per month Up to 450 Mbps for $99.95 per month Up to 1,000 Mbps for $139.95 per month Up to 2,500 Mbps for $279.95 per month Connelly added that there are three affordability programs that could bring down these prices for customers. The first program is a $15 discount per month if the customer qualifies for energy assistance.The second program is a $30 discount per month if the resident is eligible for certain programs, like income programs.Connelly said residents must log onto the Federal Communications Commission website to get qualified for this program.The third program is an additional $15 discount per moth for those that qualify for the second program."They automatically get the state program," Connelly said.Connelly said Choptank Electric thinks these programs are important."We don't want anyone to have to make the decision not to take broadband when we get there because of an affordability issue," she said. "We are doing more this fall to really promote that and make sure that families know that all these options are available." After Connelly's presentation, council member Ricky Travers asked what the company needs from the county to continue moving forward with this project - "other than money," he joked.Connelly said council members should continue to keep track of residents that reach out to say they don't have good service or they don't have any service.Council Vice President Mike Detmer called some of the areas in the county "drastically unserved." "So I know that it's going to be a very welcomed thing for the citizens of this county," he said of the project.

title: Sale of Daysprings Townhomes Will Come Soon Caroline County Says
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Sale of Daysprings Townhomes will come soon Caroline County says

 October 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 326
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners have discussed the sale of Daysprings Townhomes throughout 2025, now the sale looks like it may happen.At the Caroline County Commissioners meeting on Tuesday, County Administrator Kathleen Freeman said that paperwork with legal teams are being prepared and negotiations are ongoing on the potential sale of Daysprings Townhomes.
"We're down to just what I would say wording, not much left to get that contract finished and I don't need to speak for Stewart, but he's drafted up the letters to notify the tenants and all of those things. So we're making really good progress on Daysprings," Freeman said.
The Dayspring Townhomes complex is located just outside Ridgely on School Street. The initial property was built in 1994 by Interfaith Housing Development, a former local nonprofit that worked with the county.
That nonprofit ceased operations a handful of years ago, leaving the low-income housing complex in the hands of its owners, Caroline County, and the contracted property management company, East Coast.
According to Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding, the decision to sell is due to a lack of funding to properly repair the complex.
"There's limited state money available to renovate the apartments that are there, and it's very difficult to get a hold of the money. So really the the best path moving forward is to sell it to a private company and just have them renovate as needed to make it fair market value housing," Breeding said.
According to Freeman, once the contract is signed, the county will notify tenants of the sale and advise them with an option to extend their lease for one year. The apartments will be sold to a private entity who will rent the units at market rate.
According to Freeman, the purchaser intends to renovate the apartments, but the timeline is unknown. The county will offer relocation assistance to all tenants.
The county will follow state requirements with the sale of Daysprings Townhomes and the movement of the tenants.

title: Town of Greensboro Receives Almost $400,000 in Grants
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Town of Greensboro receives almost $400,000 in grants

 July 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News

 GREENSBORO — On Tuesday, the Town of Greensboro announced it received multiple different grants for improvements around the town that total almost $400,000.The biggest grant received was a $250,000 grant from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources and the Maryland Board of Public Works to revitalize Jesse Sutton Memorial Park for Community Parks and Playgrounds Improvement, Phase 1.
"We are working in conjunction with the Department of Natural Resources to revitalize that park because right now it's nothing. I think at one point it was a ballfield and they removed everything out," Town Manager Cindy Yost said in an interview with the Star Democrat.
While there are plans to restore the park, Yost said she has ideas that could not be shared until after conversations with DNR are complete.
"We're going to try to look at something a little bit different that maybe DNR will go with, and we can make this park into something that the kids will enjoy and that the residents will really enjoy too," she said.
In addition, the town received a received $1,000 grant from Critical Area Commission and a Waterway Improvement Fund grant for $75,000 for improvement of the boat ramp in town.
The town also received two police grants, a State Aid for Police Protection Fund for $30,649 and Body Armor for Law Enforcement grant for $1,035.

title: Caroline County Passes Fiscal Year 2026 Budget
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Caroline County passes fiscal year 2026 budget

 June 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 413
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners adopted the county's fiscal year 2026 operating and capital budgets at a meeting Tuesday.The commissioners and county employees have been working on the budget for about six months and have balanced a $2 million shortfall. The revenue total for the county sits at $79,208,471.
Allocations to some departments and agencies dropped compared to years prior. Some organizations and nonprofits completely lost county funding in this year's budget. Among those organizations are the Human Service Council, His Hope Ministries and Big Brothers Big Sisters of the Eastern Shore.
While Commissioners President Travis Breeding wanted to cut all nonprofit funding to avoid picking and choosing organizations, Commissioners Larry Porter and Frank Bartz chose to give to certain nonprofits.
"My thought process was that that there are a lot of good nonprofits in the county, and we don't have the funding ability to support them all," Breeding said. "So, I didn't really want to get in a situation where we were picking and choosing which ones. I advocate for people to donate to all of those nonprofits, but it just didn't feel like a core responsibility of Caroline County to provide funding there."
During the end of the budget process, changes from the state impacted the proposed budget. In the income tax line item, the county's original $1 million loss due to the state allocating more cost to the county went down to only a $200,000 loss. In the disparity grant section, the legislators passed a bill to make the disparity grant gap cover 90% instead of the normal 75%.
The county decided to add money to the tar and chip fund in the infrastructure line item of the capital budget. This move left over $1 million for the county to allocate in the capital budget.
The county put $100,000 to Public Works for tree trimming and $980,994 toward a fund to purchase radios for emergency services.
In addition to the budget being passed, the county S&P grade has increased from an "AA minus" grade to an "AA." This grade is what allows the county to bond or borrow money.
The commissioners thanked county employees, Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox and Grant Coordinator Stacy Seward for their hard work balancing the budget and the grade upgrade.
"In an environment where a lot of government agencies are seeing reduced credit ratings, we have managed to see an increase here. I think its a testament to staff, tight budgeting and managing every dollar to make sure its used appropriately," Breeding said.

title: Caroline County Retains Tax Differentials, at Least for This Year
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County retains tax differentials, at least for this year

 May 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 546
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners held their last fiscal year 2026 public budget hearing Tuesday evening.While the commissioners received multiple recognitions for balancing the budget, municipalities brought questions about property tax rates and real property tax differential rates.
Ridgely Commissioner Brad Sears asked the county commissioners what the extended outlook was for municipal tax differentials.
"Just in terms of looking forward from my town's perspective, I would like to get your overall sense of where this might be headed, if that's appropriate," Sears said.
In Caroline County's proposed budget, the property tax rate sits at 98 cents per $100 of assessed value. For towns incorporated within the county, tax rates can sit between one cents to six cents lower than the county's rate.
The differentials were put in place to keep resident of towns from being taxed twice for services provided to these residents by the municipality instead of the county.
"This is something that was in play when I came into office, and it's been a real subject that I battle with over the years," County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said. "What this means is it does not affect the town's budget, it affects the money the county collects in their county property tax rate.
"I will say tonight that this will be the last year I would support the property tax differential, I know its gonna be a very controversial subject... In this year's budget, we did not collect about $600,000 in the property tax differential. We're able to balance the budget this year. Going forward, I don't have a clue."
Porter advocated for eliminating the differentials in coming years, pointing to cost shifts from the state that he says will make it more difficult for the county to balance future budgets.
"We will not be able to forgo $600,000 revenue in the next year, I don't think we will," Porter said. "I see nothing but cost being shifted every year, the Blueprint number just keeps exponentially going up every year... I'm not sure where the road is going to take us."
The situation is similar to one being seen in Dorchester County this fiscal year.
In an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit, Dorchester County has proposed multiple tax increases in its draft fiscal year 2026 budget, including the removal of tax differentials for Cambridge and Hurlock residents.
The Cambridge City Council has voiced opposition to the county's elimination of the differentials. In a unanimous vote Monday, the City Council voted to adopt a resolution that requests the Dorchester County Council "develop and implement an annual tax differential or rebate model" to address the "tax burden" of county property taxes on Cambridge residents.
While Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding does not fully agree with Porter, he said he understands Porter's point.
"My position is a little different than Commissioner Porter. I believe that there are redundant services that are provided by the municipalities," Breeding said. "I know the formula that generated the tax differential was generated for police protection.
"....I don't know what the fiscal situation is going to be next year, we may find ourselves in the same dilemma that Dorchester county is in this year, I don't think we will…. I am still at the maintain point, but I certainly understand Commissioner Porter's position. That's where I'm at right now."
