title: Denton Approves Budget with Lower Tax Rate
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Denton approves budget with lower tax rate

 May 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 530
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Denton Town Council presented and approved its fiscal year 2026 general fund budget and appropriations with a 2% lower property tax rate."We were able to lower the tax rate 3 cents," said Dallas Lister, a Town Council member, "which is a commitment that we've been trying to make each year, is to try to be as efficient as possible and not let the taxes increase where we can. This has been a lot of work on the staff, we really didn't have a lot of hard lift this year. We just set some priorities and staff made it happen, so it's spectacular."
The tax rate decreases from 69 cents per $100 of assessed value to 66 cents per $100 of assessed value on properties taxed within the boundaries of Denton. Town officials credit increased property values in Denton for being able to lower the rate.
"Because our property rates were higher, if we had stayed the same, people would have had the same tax rate but they would have been paying more money because of the percentage," McNinch said. "That's when when we decide to go down, the impact is, $40,000 roughly on our budget."
According to McNinch, the officials understand that some fees might increase, but they felt lowering the tax rate was the best decision for the town residents and for the council.
"We're aware that other taxes and fees might increase, but we need to hold our line ... we want to make sure we're providing the best services to our public and other things that might go up are county, state, utilities, that we don't have control over," McNinch said. "But with us trying to reduce and trying to put these things in place. We understand it's tough out there right now. It is for us too."
Denton tax revenues will increase by close to $150,000, while license and agencies revenues will decrease next fiscal year, according to the approved budget.
While a majority of the expenditures saw minor increases and decreases, Park and Recreation received the biggest decrease, dropping by $60,000.
"We've gotten things done," McNinch said. "We've gotten the Fourth Street Park done, we're partnering with the county, and the Sharp Road Park looks different. We've had park plans in place and and we've been able to get things done. So yes, that impacts the budget positively."
Tourism Visitor Center received a $14,000 increase, and Main Street received about a $4,000 increase in the budget. According to Mayor McNinch, Denton being named the first American Discovery Trail Town has an "impact on the decision."
"We want our visitor center open as much as possible," McNinch said. "We've been able to help support that a little bit more over the course of the last couple of years. We see the benefit of tourism for economic development.
"Things like the American Heritage Trail, we do see an increase in visitation to our visitor center. Those things are important, and we also increased the Main Street budget a little bit, because again that all works in trying to provide a community that people want to visit and want to live."
For more information on Denton Town Council fiscal year 2026 budget, go to dentonmaryland.com/departments/finance/tax-rates.

title: Counties Approve Chesapeake College Budget Request, Shift Cost of Tech Center
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Counties approve Chesapeake College budget request, shift cost of tech center

 April 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 526
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WYE MILLS — In a joint meeting Thursday, officials across Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot counties approved a shift in county cost shares for Chesapeake College's new technical building.During the meeting, which was held at the college's main campus in Queen Anne's County, the five counties approved a total $9.02 million budget request made by the college for fiscal year 2026. The school's budget is $1.31 million higher than its fiscal year 2025 budget.
Part of the $9.02 million budget request included a $952,560 request for the design of a new technical building. Chesapeake College Vice President for Administrative Services Karen Smith said the new building will have areas for a variety of programs, including agriculture, electrical, welding and fabrication, construction trades and advanced manufacturing. She said the cost for the design phase could be lower depending on state approval.
Although the five counties approved the request for funding for the design, the decision came with a shift in contributions toward the project.
Dorchester County's share of costs for the design phase will be taken on by Queen Anne's County. This means Queen Anne's County's responsibility for the project will jump from 28.9%, or an estimated $275,290, to 47.8%, or an estimated $455,324.
During the meeting, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer and Vice President Mike Detmer outlined their council's concerns regarding paying for the project.
Although other counties hope to use the new technical building for career and technical education at the high school level, Dorchester County has a career and technology center it is still paying off, they said.
Through its budget process, Dorchester County has struggled to eliminate an estimated $6.2 million deficit.
Pfeffer said Dorchester County takes in about $45 million in property and income taxes and will have to give Dorchester County Public Schools $26.6 million for fiscal year 2026.
"So we're trying to run the rest of the county on half of that," he said. "So while in conceptual context, we believe in the project, fiscally our citizens and our staff are saying we don't know how we're going to be able to participate."
At the Chesapeake College meeting, Queen Anne's County Commissioner Jack Wilson Jr. shared his county's decision to cover Dorchester County for the project design costs.
"We all know what happens if we let this money go back to the state," Wilson said. "It's going to go somewhere else in this state, and it's not going to be here. We got this far. And Lenny, listen, I feel for you guys. I know what you're going through. But I think we just need to keep it on the rails at least through the design phase and see what the state's going to help with."
According to documents from the meeting, the state will support 75% of project costs, and the counties will support the remaining 25%.
After the counties voted to approve the amended capital budget, Kent County Commission President Ron Fithian said he understands the position Dorchester County is in, mentioning the Blueprint for Maryland's Future and "unfunded mandates" by the state.
"I think we all understand any one of us could be in your same position very easily," Fithian told the Dorchester County Council members.

title: Caroline County Officials Discuss Fee Changes for Fiscal Year 2026
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Caroline County officials discuss fee changes for fiscal year 2026

 March 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett | Section: News 
 
 599
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners discussed potentially raising some fees as the county looks for ways to close a $2 million deficit in its fiscal year 2026 budget.""We really wanted to get into the fee schedule today and highlight a couple items that the board has brought up in conversation through past meetings that they wanted to either look at that will possibly change," Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox said at the Caroline County Commissioners meeting Tuesday.
County officials presented the draft FY 2026 fee schedule at the meeting, highlighting some main focuses the commissioners wanted to discuss.
The Liquor Commissioners fees were looked at by the county commissioners. While majority of the licenses and fees for the board are set by state legislation, there are three line items the commissioners can adjust: the application fee, advertising cost and TIPS alcohol awareness certification class.
The commissioners focused on the application fee.
"The reason for bringing this up is really looking at the money that's being brought in from the liquor license," Fox said. "First, what the operation is costing us. So, we're budgeting to take in about $60,000, but last year, we spent about $99,000 to operate the the board. So there's about a $40,000 gap there that is being made up by the general fund."
The commissioners suggested raising the application fee from $175 to $500 to help the board break even.
Commissioners addressed similar concerns with Jonestown Water System.
The water system, which serves residents near Preston, hasn't increased its fees in over a decade, commissioners said at the meeting.
"We have to do surveys, outreach that are now required by MDE, and it's just just continuing to push that fund into a little bit of a bigger hole," Fox said. "…Based off the 52 users that are in the system and some quick math that we calculated on last year's operation, the fee would have to be about $476 to break even."
The current resident price to have a property connected to Jonestown Water System is $300.
"I think we have got to start coming up with some type of a gradual increase here," County Commission Vice President Larry Porter said. "We are going to at least start recovering some of this money because we cannot continue to operate the system on the same amount of money every year."
The commissioners suggested raising the price to $350 this budget term and removing the $150 unconnected charge.
The last fee the commissioners and officials discussed was the Office of Finance administrative.
"This is the fee that the county charges for the Office of Finance to conduct all tax collection or property tax collection for the municipalities," Fox said.
The adjustment of the fee is being presented to account for the larger towns that require more attention and interaction. The current cap is set at $15,000.
"This costing us money to provide. I don't want to gouge anybody, but if it's costing us a certain amount of money to process these bills, we already give a differential to the towns. We already provide significant services to the towns," Porter said. "… We are going to have to get away from this subsidizing services process here if we're going to go forward with balancing this budget."
The commissioners will phase the removing of the cap in to next years budget.
"I'm fine with with implementing this next year, but letting them know that the cap is going to be phased out and they are going to need to adjust their budgeting for to come of this cost," Porter said.
The commissioners will raise the cap to $22,500, and next year they will remove the cap completely.

title: How ARPA Funds Shaped Maryland's Mid-Shore
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
How ARPA funds shaped Maryland’s Mid-Shore

 March 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 884
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Delegate Jay Jacobs, who represents Maryland's District 36 — encompassing Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil and Caroline counties — has seen the region through economic peaks and valleys. But the COVID-19 pandemic presented a crisis unlike any other.At the same time, it brought a rare opportunity.
Through the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA), Maryland received $3.7 billion in federal relief funds. Jacobs estimated that roughly $88 million of that flowed into his district over the past five years.
"The money gave counties and municipalities a chance to get things done when they normally might not have had that opportunity," Jacobs said.
Across the district, more than 200 projects were funded through ARPA, aimed at bolstering local infrastructure, supporting nonprofits and modernizing essential services.
Rock Hall to Queen Anne's: Local Needs, Local SolutionsEach town took a unique approach, reflecting ARPA's flexible framework.
In Rock Hall, the town's aging wastewater system was a priority. Mayor James Cook said of the $1.3 million received, $300,000 went toward replacing the headworks at the sewer plant — a key filter that removes debris such as grease and rags from wastewater.
Chestertown formed a task force led by Ward 2 Council member Tom Herz to ensure transparency and community input. Of the $4.25 million allocated, local nonprofits were invited to align funding requests with the town's comprehensive plan.
In Galena, $570,000 supported road improvements designed to make parks more accessible and attract visitors.
Betterton directed its $311,000 toward modernizing its website to be ADA-compliant, enabling online payments, purchasing an air purifying unit, and upgrading pump stations with generators for resilience.
Millington received $504,821, though specific projects were not detailed.
Queen Anne's County saw one of the largest allocations: $16.3 million. Projects included installing 3,300 feet of water line at the Old Towne Shopping Center, investing $900,000 to upgrade affordable housing units, and expanding broadband access with $1.5 million. Six new consoles were also added to the county's 911 backup center, and cell phone boosters were installed in public schools to strengthen communication in rural areas.
Countywide Efforts and Broadband ExpansionIn Cecil County, where municipalities received a greater share of ARPA funds than the county itself, a major initiative focused on expanding high-speed internet. A $16.2 million broadband project combined $12.8 million in state funds, $2.5 million from internet service providers, and $900,000 in ARPA funds contributed by the county.
According to county officials, additional ARPA investments went toward two emergency medical services paramedic stations and a new training center for the Cecil County Sheriff's Office.
Rising Sun used $2,300 for infrastructure repairs, while the Town of North East applied its share to enhance police department operations.
In Caroline County, which received just under $6.5 million, part of the funding was used for infrastructure, while a portion supported reentry programs and post-release case management for individuals leaving the Ordnance Road Detention Facility.
Jacobs noted that ARPA's flexibility was one of its most valuable aspects.
"It was not one size fits all," he said. "Municipalities could use the money to meet their specific needs — with the only caveat being it must be spent by Dec. 31, 2026."
As ARPA Winds Down, Financial Pressure MountsNow, with the funding window closing, local governments are bracing for its absence. Jacobs said the drying up of ARPA funds is intensifying pressure on the state as the General Assembly works to pass the FY 2026 budget — which currently faces a $3.5 billion shortfall.
"Certain services were being relied on and now are cut off," Jacobs said. "ARPA funds possibly would have kept some of these programs afloat."
A notable cut is the reduction in senior care funding by the Maryland Department of Aging. Jacobs said the proposed $2.5 million budget — an 18% reduction — could translate to about $28,000 less per county. He warned this could destabilize staffing and services for vulnerable seniors, such as in-home care, transportation and meal delivery.
"These cuts will be felt, not by the lawmakers, but by ordinary hardworking folks who have to make decisions about affording food or putting gas in the car," he said.
Talbot County: Planning for LongevityTalbot County took a strategic approach. Officials distributed surveys to identify community priorities, which included broadband access, public health, and household assistance.
According to Cassandra Vanhooser, director of Talbot County Economic Development and Tourism, the county received about $7.2 million in ARPA funds. The goal, she said, was to ensure that projects wouldn't falter once federal dollars were gone.
"These are largely capital items, these are one-time items... a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity," said then Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher. "We need to be very careful about how this is done."
Among Talbot's allocations:
- $1.75 million to Easton Utilities' Connect Talbot project to expand broadband to rural residents.
- $105,000 to the Chesapeake Center in Easton to replace a failing septic system and connect to county sewer.
- $500,000 in grants for volunteer fire company equipment upgrades.
"People recognize that this is transformational money," Vanhooser said at the time of the funding discussion, "It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to be a driving force for change and to impact the lives of our citizens."
Looking AheadAs the Dec. 31, 2024 obligation deadline nears, and the Dec. 31, 2026 expenditure deadline looms, local leaders are focused on maximizing remaining funds while grappling with what comes next.
Jacobs is urging urgency from lawmakers.
"With less than 20 days in session," he said, "the Assembly needs to come up with solutions — and fast."

title: Caroline County Conduct First FY26 Budget Workshop
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County conduct first FY26 budget workshop

 March 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 635
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Caroline County Commissioners, Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox and grant coordinator Stacy Seward, who helps with the budget annually, tackled the first workshop for fiscal year 2026 budget at the county commissioners meeting on Tuesday.While the budget is a work in progress, Caroline County Commissioner President Travis Breeding cautioned that the work done at Tuesday's meeting is fluid and could be changed as discussions continue.
"I should point out that a lot of this is fluid and still up in the air," Breeding said, adding that the pending state budget could change things. "We still don't have a clear picture of what kind of fiscal situation were going to be in when they strike the budget."
The county is expected to bring in $77 million in revenue, while the proposed fiscal year expenditures are currently $79 million, leaving a $2 million shortfall.
For capital funding the county has $7.3 million allocated for capital funding. The requested amount for capital funding in FY26 is $10.4 million, leaving a shortfall of $3.1 million.
Both budgets need to be in balance when they are presented at a public hearing in May.
The commissioners discussed both the operating and capital budgets to account for the shortfalls in both budgets.
CAPITAL BUDGET
A number of items were discussed in the capital budget.
The Department of Corrections control panel for $120,00 is already being worked on but the requested new van is still in question. While the van is damaged the county took into account the mileage on the van is only 22,330.
"I think we should get the van looked at and evaluated," County Commissioner Frank Bartz said.
The Department of Emergency Services could receive funding for the 14 cardiac monitor replacement, but the commissioners discussed waiting one more year for purchasing a number of requested trucks.
Facilities requested a long list of items which the county commissioners discussed to fund the first seven and will discuss the rest as the budget workshop sessions continue.
The county commissioners discussed potentially cutting capital funds for these organizations.
All Circuit Court request for $272,000.DES $180,000 for EMS lieutenant and EMS division chief.Facilities proposal to receive $498,000 of requested $1,477,000.All Public Works requests except a six-wheel dump truck and a Husqvarna Zero Turn mower for $1,203,500.All Rec and Parks requests except a Skag 72-inch Zero Turn mower for $136,000All 4-H Park requests for $90,000.All Human Society requests for $85,000.
OPERATING BUDGET
While the operating budget has a $2 million deficit, the county must find cuts in many different areas. Companies in the expenditure category gave the commissioners the most discussion at the county commissioners' first workshop.
"I appreciate everything these volunteers organizations do," County Commissioners President Travis Breeding said. "There is a lot of other volunteers organizations and nonprofits in the county that we don't give money to, our job is public safety. My position is the same as its been the last two years, I don't think we should fund any of them."
While Breeding thinks they could potentially save funding here, Commissioners Porter and Bartz said that some nonprofits should be allocated some funds.
"I looked at some of the budgets to see whether the $5,000 will impact their budgets or not, some I thought I felt we could contribute to, some I struck off," Bartz said.
The commissioners also discussed the fire companies that requested a 10% increase in allocation, and a property tax credit. Breeding landed on a 5% increase, Porter at 10% and Bartz at 7.5%.
"Enter our different numbers I don't think we will come to a consensus today, we have one more public hearing," Breeding said.

title: Mid-Shore Counties Advocating Against State Cost Shifts
author: Konner Metz
content:
Mid-Shore counties advocating against state cost shifts

 March 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 371
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council sent a letter this week to the Maryland General Assembly expressing its concerns regarding more than $1 million in county money impacted by the state's Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act."The proposal to shift costs onto counties by sending invoices simply places the State's fiscal problem into other hands and threatens local services," reads the letter, which was unanimously approved by the council Tuesday.
Cost shifts are expected as the state aims to balance a budget with a nearly $3 billion deficit. Specific costs include contributions to teacher pensions and the state Department of Assessments and Taxation.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher said it's "simply a poor and inappropriate strategy for resolving the very real state budget crisis."
Lesher noted Tuesday that Talbot County isn't seeing the worst of the cost shifts — Dorchester County may be looking at more than $3 million affected, he said.
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said he testified at a Senate budget committee meeting in Annapolis and talked with members of the governor's staff.
Pfeffer says Department of Legislative Services recommendations to double the costs for counties to pay toward teacher pensions is particularly alarming. For Dorchester, it would cost $1.1 million compared to the previously estimated $550,000.
Gov. Wes Moore has said solving the budget crisis is an "enormous task" only made more difficult by constraints from the federal government. At a Feb. 28 Senate budget committee hearing, he emphasized that the budget bill is nowhere near final.
"While I still remain locked in on the destination, I come in moving in partnership to be flexible on the journey," Moore said.
Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding said the county may lose $1.1 million in income tax revenue if Moore's tax cut plan is approved.
Moore has maintained that giving middle-class families tax relief is a critical component to the budget and state's economic growth plan.
"Marylanders are being squeezed. They're being squeezed by rising prices," Moore said Feb. 28. "They're being squeezed by the rising cost of groceries, they're being squeezed by the rising cost of energy."
As session continues, Breeding says Caroline County has representatives in Annapolis fighting for relief from the potential cost shifts.
"We have a lot of heartburn with the proposed budget," Breeding said.

title: Caroline Public Hearing Reveals Bigger Shortfall and Property Tax Talk
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline public hearing revivals bigger shortfall and property tax talk

 March 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 372
 Words

 DENTON — On Tuesday evening, the Caroline County Commissioners held the first public hearing for the county's fiscal year 2026 budget.At the workshop, agencies presented their needs for more money for salary raises and equipment repairs and replacements. But the commissioners are facing tight budget constraints.
"We just want to take input from from all the agencies that are asking here straight from them," Commission President Travis Breeding said. "Learn what their priorities are ... to help us educate ourselves and make informed decisions on what they need."
At a Caroline County Commissioners meeting in February, the draft FY 2026 budget presented showed the county could be facing around a $900,000 shortfall this budget season.
After the first FY26 budget roundtable, that number has increased. The county is expected to bring in $77 million in revenue, while the proposed fiscal year budget is projected to be $79 million, leaving a $2 million shortfall.
"We gotta find $2 million in cuts somewhere basically," Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding said. "We still have tough decisions to make, well evaluate everyone's testimony and well do what we think is best."
While majority of the public comment Tuesday was thanking the commissioners for their work, the commissioners offered some insight on property tax rates.
"I don't think the property tax rate has been raised in nine years," Larry Porter Caroline County Commissioners Vice President said. "For the people who say my taxes go up every year, your taxes go up because of the assessment, we don't control assessments."
"The only number we control up here is the property tax rate and we have held the line for nine years, and my guess is we will hold it this year."
Residents may still have to pay more in property taxes regardless if the rate remains the same because if the assessment values have risen the rate is applied to those values.
While the property tax rate may not go up the commissioners understand that many changes must be made to keep up with the states requirements for the counties.
"Sooner or later I don't know if its reasonable to think planning, budgeting and looking at cost is gonna be enough, if the state keeps shoving expenses and cost down the line to us," Porter said.

title: Proposed Tax Breaks Could Mean Service Cuts in Lower-Income Counties
author: Paul Kiefer Capital News Service
content:
Proposed tax breaks could mean service cuts in lower-income counties

 March 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: PAUL KIEFER Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 963
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Gov. Wes Moore plans to change how Marylanders take deductions on their state income taxes, but officials in some of the state's poorest counties say that plan could force them to cut services."You mentioned that the federal government is creating chaos for our state government in an effort to balance their budget," Del. Jefferson Ghrist, a Republican representing Caroline, Cecil, Kent and Queen Anne's Counties, told Gov. Moore in a recent budget hearing. "It appears that your budget does sort of the same thing to our county governments."
Moore's administration, however, contends that the reforms will provide tax relief to a majority of Marylanders — including residents of lower-income counties — even if those county governments face a revenue loss.
"This proposal leaves more cash in the pockets of the majority of Maryland's households," said Budget and Management Secretary Helene Grady.
Lawmakers in Annapolis are weighing a two-pronged approach to tax reform intended to shift the scales in favor of low- and middle-income households.
Moore's proposal to double the state's standard deduction would provide a tax break to Marylanders who opt not to itemize their income tax deductions — many of them low- and middle-income. To account for the resulting revenue loss, the governor's office proposes ending the practice of itemized deductions, which would mean a larger income tax bill for many high-income Marylanders.
But county governments also collect income taxes, and a tax break for lower-income Marylanders would deal a blow to some counties' budgets.
Representatives from Allegany County appeared in Annapolis last week to ask lawmakers to soften that blow.
"Governor Moore discussed the idea that no Marylanders should be left behind," Allegany County Attorney T. Lee Beeman told lawmakers on Friday. "Ultimately, his proposal this year will do exactly that in Allegany County. It will leave Allegany County behind."
If the General Assembly moves forward with doubling the standard deduction, Allegany County would stand to lose $3.2 million in revenue next year, according to Maryland's Board of Revenue Estimates.
While the vast majority of county residents would receive a tax cut, "we'll be looking at probably cutting potentially each and every service we have," said Allegany County Administrator Jason Bennett. "We're pretty slim as it is."
Last year, the county laid off emergency services staff and scaled back employee health insurance in response to a $13 million deficit. Additional cuts could mean scaling back snow clearance operations in the winter, public transit service and support for the county's library service, he told Capital News Service.
If Allegany County raised local income taxes to the maximum rate allowed under Maryland law, he added, the county could only make up for half of the projected losses created by doubling the standard deduction.
Allegany County is not alone. Del. Malcolm Ruff, a Democrat representing Baltimore City, noted that doubling the standard deduction could undercut services in his district.
"Baltimore City would lose approximately $40 million over the next five years based on those changes," Ruff said.
The Board of Revenue Estimates projects that half of Maryland's counties and county equivalents would lose income tax revenue if the state moves forward with the proposed changes to deductions. Those include all but one of the 10 poorest Maryland counties as of the Census Bureau's 2023 American Community Survey.
"Contrast that with our friends in the beltway corridor," said Beeman. "Montgomery County stands to gain $300 million in income tax revenue over the next five years. It's a shocking contrast."
Meanwhile, some members of the Legislative Black Caucus of Maryland have expressed concerns that eliminating itemized deductions would have a disproportionate impact on majority-Black districts in the Washington suburbs.
Residents of Charles and Prince George's Counties itemize their deductions at higher rates than residents of any other Maryland counties. That presents a political challenge for someone like Sen. Michael Jackson, a Democrat representing parts of Calvert, Charles and Prince George's Counties. Residents in those districts are more likely than other Marylanders to see their tax bills increase under Moore's plan.
Jackson told CNS that he and other caucus members representing those counties are in talks with the governor to address their concerns.
But Moore's current proposals drew praise from some outside observers.
"Itemized deductions are regressive," said Miles Trinidad, a state policy analyst with the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan think tank. "These policies offer the largest benefits to higher income taxpayers and little if any benefits to low- and middle-income families."
Grady, meanwhile, notes that the governor's tax reforms would offer a tax cut to a majority of Marylanders, and that aid to local governments accounts for a third of general fund expenses in the proposed 2026 budget — aid that would support both public school systems and county governments.
The governor's office also underscores that Maryland's standard deduction is only a third of Virginia's, meaning that some poor and working-class residents who would pay no income tax in Virginia make enough to pay income tax in Maryland.
While Moore's proposal would still leave Maryland's standard deduction lower than those in Virginia and Washington, his office argues the change is in the interest of fairness.
However, given the dire state of Maryland's budget and the prospect of dwindling federal support, Grady also noted that the state may not be in a position to simultaneously offer tax cuts to most Marylanders and shield counties from the statewide budget crunch.
"Given the general fund challenge, it would be very difficult to insulate counties entirely from impacts," she said.
Senate President Bill Ferguson, a Democrat representing Baltimore City, echoed Grady's sentiment.
"I appreciate [the governor's] approach of bringing forth a proposal that attempted to balance state needs, local needs and our business climate," he said. "But we're dealing with an unprecedented situation, and so just as the state is having to tighten the belt. I think local jurisdictions are going to be in a similar place this upcoming year."

title: MACo Officials Say Cost Shifts from State to Counties Are 'Absurd,' Unfair
author: Konner Metz
content:
MACo officials say cost shifts from state to counties are 'absurd,' unfair

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 647
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Representatives from the Maryland Association of Counties minced no words when speaking to the Eastern Shore's state legislators Friday morning about the expected cost burdens being placed on counties this budget cycle."Shifting these costs onto counties at this point is absurd," said Kevin Kinnally, the association's legislative director.
Earlier this month, the Department of Legislative Services told the Eastern Shore Delegation that local governments across the state may have to pick up around $144 million in costs as the state legislature and Gov. Wes Moore grapple with tackling a near $3 billion deficit.
The governor's proposed fiscal year 2026 budget would shift costs in a number of areas, including teacher pensions and property assessments, according to MACo officials.
In Caroline and Talbot counties, projected local cost shifts are in the $700,000 range, per legislative services projections. Dorchester County is at $830,000, while Queen Anne's County leads the pack for the Mid-Shore at $970,000. Kent is the lowest of the five counties with a $300,000 projection.
Friday at the Eastern Shore Delegation meeting, Kinnally said the Shore's poorer counties, like Caroline and Dorchester, are being "railroaded."
Kinnally claims the state budget leaves counties with no choice but to raise property tax rates, going so far as to deem it a "state-mandated property tax increase."
"Two-thirds of Marylanders live in counties at the maximum local income tax rate, so the only place to go is to the property tax," Kinnally said. "Which is regressive, which everybody hates. But they're pushing us into a corner here, and that's not fair."
Michael Sanderson, executive director of MACo, said the organization took a closer look at how cost shifts would impact Dorchester County's fiscal situation.
After running the numbers, Sanderson said he believes Dorchester County may have to raise property taxes, a result he called "absolutely bonkers."
"I have no idea how Dorchester County manages this year's budget," Sanderson said.
SOLAR COMPROMISEAs legislators and industry leaders have eyes on a joint hearing Friday regarding the state's solar legislation, MACo is opposing Senate Bill 931 and its paired House bill.
The legislation is designed to expand solar energy across the state, a measure intended to work toward accomplishing Moore's clean energy goals for Maryland. If passed, the bill would give the state authority to approve solar energy projects — a significant harm to local siting authority, critics say.
Dominic Butchko, MACo's intergovernmental relations director, said the association opposes the legislation based on five impacted areas: safety, livability of rural areas, concerns for local taxpayers, affordable housing opportunities being stripped and inefficiencies in the legislation's requirements.
Butchko said the legislation strays from compromises MACo thought it reached last November.
But through recent discussions with solar industry leaders and environmental advocates, Butchko still sees a path to compromise.
"Those efforts have started to yield some fruit," Butchko said. "We believe we actually have amendments that revert the legislation back to where we were at or pretty close to where we were at in November."
MUNICIPAL LEAGUE
Friday, the Eastern Shore Delegation heard a brief update from the Maryland Municipal League, an organization representing local municipal governments.
The group has two legislative priorities this session: Senate Bill 390, which would allow local governments to have trained civilians issue speed camera citations instead of police officers; and House Bill 991, which would allow local governments to institute food and beverage fees.
Justin Fiore, the league's deputy director of advocacy and public affairs, said House Bill 991 could give flexibility to governments that are "heavily dependent on property taxes as (their) only revenue."
"We have 43 million visitors annually to the state of Maryland, and while they do pay a hotel tax if they stay, we really don't capture revenue from the services that they utilize," Fiore said.
The food and beverage fee bill is still waiting committee review and House approval before it moves to the Senate, while the speed camera citation bill was passed by the Senate earlier this month and currently sits in the House.

title: Caroline County Holds First FY26 Budget Workshop
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County holds first FY26 budget workshop

 February 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 480
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Tuesday, the Caroline County Commissioners held their fiscal year 2026 budget roundtable with all internal and external county agencies.While agencies need more money for salary raises and equipment repairs and replacements, the commissioners are facing tight budget constraints.
At the Caroline County Commissioners meeting last week, the draft FY 2026 budget presented showed Caroline County could be facing around a $900,000 shortfall this budget season.
Caroline County Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox presented projected operating requests and revenues for the upcoming fiscal year during the last week's meeting.
Fox acknowledged while the entire budget is fluid, the current requests total $79.7 million and the revenues total $78.8 million, up from the fiscal year 2024 operating budget, which was balanced at $72.3 million.
Some of those fluid items include income tax cuts proposed by Gov. Wes Moore and potential cuts to The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's education funding initiative.
The County Commissioners are concerned that the Blueprint cuts will leave the county in a bad financial predicament.
"There is no leadership at the top. There no leadership in the state," Commission Vice President Larry Porter said Tuesday. "We don't have anyone who is willing to stand up and say this Blueprint policy is a mistake."
On Tuesday, all internal and external county agencies presented their FY26 budget requests.
"We just want to take input from from all the agencies that are asking here straight from them," Commission President Travis Breeding said. "Learn what their priorities are ... to help us educate ourselves and make informed decisions on what they need."
The majority of the agencies experienced some of the same issues. Their fiscal year budgets were rising for multiple reasons.
Employee pay, overtime, and general equipment and technology updates were needed for many agencies.
"One of biggest challenges is hiring and retaining employees. It's getting increasingly difficult for us," Executive Director of Caroline County Public Library Jonah Owens said. "Queen Anne's County typically offers salaries 20 to 25% above ours, Anne Arundel County sometimes 50 to 100% higher salaries than what we offer for similar positions. We have become a farm team, as have all our agencies have."
For many agencies, every five to 10 years, equipment needs upgrades. Some upgrades fall on this fiscal year. Others will come in the following years.
But facing a budget shortfall, the commissioners are aware of potential cuts they will have to make and how honoring these requests from agencies will be difficult.
"We can't go out and and find any more money," Breeding said. "Our tax rates are as high, I think, as as we feel comfortable having them. I don't want to entertain any rate increases.
"I think the only thing we can do is search for efficiencies inside our existing budget and make sure we spend it as efficiently as we can, and prioritize spending in the areas that actually need additional funding."
Star Democrat Reporter Konner Metz contributed to this report.

title: Caroline County Commissioners Will Grapple with Shortfall to Balance Budget
author: Konner Metz
content:
Caroline County Commissioners will grapple with shortfall to balance budget

 February 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 509
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — A draft of the fiscal year 2026 budget presented Tuesday shows Caroline County could be facing around a $900,000 shortfall this budget season.Caroline County Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox presented projected operating requests and revenues for the upcoming fiscal year during Tuesday's Caroline County Commissioners meeting.
Fox noted while the entire budget is fluid, the current requests total $79.7 million and the revenues total $78.8 million, up from the fiscal year 2024 operating budget, which was balanced at $72.3 million.
"This is where we're at currently today," Fox said. "Obviously there's a lot of items still not set in stone."
Some of those fluid items include income tax cuts proposed by Gov. Wes Moore and potential cuts to The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's education funding initiative.
Caroline County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter expressed concerns about expected cost shifts from the state to local governments.
"I don't even know where to start on this because every indication we have is that it's worse than this," Porter said about finding a way to balance the budget. "The state shifts are going to be worse than this. I think at this point, I'm going to be looking at this as a zero budget."
Porter said he views it as a lack of leadership in Annapolis. Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding concurred.
"Nobody's going to tell the solar lobby or the teachers' union no," Breeding said.
"All your work that you've done is great, but I'm not sure at this point where we go," Porter told Fox.
In terms of revenue, Fox noted there are increases projected in income and property taxes, respectively, though Moore's plan to cut income taxes for many Marylanders may reduce that number if his proposals are passed by legislators.
Breeding said income tax reduction for Caroline County may be $1.4 million. He added he's not looking to raise the county's property tax rate, since increased property values are already hiking up those taxes.
"People cannot sustain a property tax increase, not with the way the assessments have gone through the roof," Breeding said. " … I'm not entertaining raising property taxes."
Breeding said given the tight fiscal situation, the commissioners will be pushing county department heads on why requested funds are absolutely necessary.
"It's not that we enjoy asking the hard questions or scrutinizing everything," Breeding said. " … But they need to be prepared for tough questions because I think we're going to have to scrutinize everything."
Fox presented a list of capital requests to the commissioners Tuesday. Those projects came from departments and agencies including Chesapeake College, the Caroline County Sheriff's Office and the Public Works Department, among others.
The requests totaled just over $11 million. Fox said around $7.3 million is currently available for capital projects, leaving a $3.7 million gap.
"Do know that this is fluid, so if there needs to be more money transferred out of operating to fund capital and vice versa … you can do so," Fox said.
Porter asked how this year's capital requests compare to previous years.
"It's high," Fox said. "This is probably the largest capital budget request we've had."

title: Assessments and Taxation Discussion at Caroline County Meeting
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Assessments and taxation discussion at Caroline County meeting

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 485
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Denton — In anticipation of changes to the division of costs for property assessment, the Caroline County Commissioners asked questions of Keith Bobbick, Caroline County supervisor of assessments and taxation, about some general operation of the department.A part of Gov. Wes Moore's proposed budget is a shift of more expenses for property assessment services to the county.
Counties will be responsible for 90% of operational costs for their assessment offices if the budget is passed as written, according to Commission President Travis Breeding. Currently, the county and the state split the cost of operation evenly.
The commissioners' questions dealt with how things were assessed and the process of assessment. In particular, the commissioners wanted to know what the process looked like for having agricultural properties reassessed for commercial uses.
The tax money paid for a property goes up when agricultural properties turn into commercial properties, making the taxes more expensive for the land owner and generating further revenue for the county and other taxing agencies.
"That happens once a year," Bobbick said. "It's usually in July, and it happens whenever the change actual starts from agricultural use to some other use."
By law, the towns and counties are supposed to provide permits about new operations in their area. A problem the assessment office faces is not receiving information on properties from the towns in a timely manner.
If the properties are not reported by the town, the assessments office will have no knowledge of the property, which could cause the reassessment to be delayed until after the July deadline, limiting the taxes that can be collected.
The county suggested the assessment office make a list of the towns it is having trouble with so the commissioners could encourage them to remain on top of reporting new developments.
Another big concern from the county is that a lot of taxpayers are showing up in the county tax office with assessment questions. The taxpayers are saying that the voicemail of Caroline County Assessment Office is directing them there.
"When you call our main line, it does have a bit in that in there," Bobbick said. "It says 'if you have a question about your tax bill, call the tax office.' When people come into our office, we try to help them as much as we can. If they have a question about their tax bill, we're gonna try to help them."
Commissioner Frank Bartz also questioned the assessment office's hybrid work schedule.
By state law, the assessment office employees are only required to work from the office three days a week.
Commissioner Frank Bartz questioned whether when the staff is working from home, they can accomplish all the necessary tasks.
"Anything we can do in the office, we can do from home," Bobbick said. Bartz responded, "expect answer the phone."
Bobbick informed Bartz that there is always someone in the office to answer the phone.
The county commissioners suggested that the language in the voicemail be changed to not confuse taxpayers.

title: Emergency Bill Drafted for Cannabis, Alcohol Tax Dollars
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Emergency bill drafted for cannabis, alcohol tax dollars

 December 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Local News

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners moved an emergency bill on for its third reading Tuesday to establish the Caroline County Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund.The tax sales of alcoholic beverages and cannabis will go to the fund, which will benefit low-income communities in Caroline county.
The emergency bill is being proposed by the county to comply with the Maryland Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article, which allows the sales tax of these items to be used for the county's benefit. The state mandated each county create its own version of this fund.
According to the draft bill, "The revenue paid into the CCCRRF shall be used only for funding community-based initiatives intended to benefit low-income communities, and community-based initiatives that serve disproportionately impacted areas, as defined in 36-101 of the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article of the State Code, and any related administrative expenses."
The Caroline County Commissioners are hoping to have exact answers for how this funding will be allocated before the third and final reading of the bill Jan. 7.
"An Allegheny County commissioner said that it was to be self-determined," Caroline County Commission Vice President Larry Porter said about allocating funds. "I think our decision is that we don't like doing self-determined things that might come back. So I would suggest that we either wait for confirmation on what areas or what zip codes the money can be spent, or we get confirmation verifying that it's self-determined and there will be no repercussions on where we spend the money."
The emergency bill's third reading and potential enactment will take place in a closed meeting Jan. 7. As an emergency bill, the bill would become effective on the day of enactment.
Public comments or concerns regarding the emergency bill should be emailed to info@caroline.org by Jan. 1 for review.

title: Legislators Talk State Budget Before Heading Back to Annapolis in January
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Legislators talk state budget before heading back to Annapolis in January

 December 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 557
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The state of the state's budget took up a large part of the conversation at a Dorchester Chamber of Commerce luncheon with state legislators on Dec. 4.The Lower Shore delegation answered questions from chamber members regarding concerns about Maryland's fiscal health, with a looming $2.7 billion state budget deficit predicted in fiscal year 2026.
"The reality is that if you continue to do the things that have gotten us into this deficit, it's only going to take us back there again," Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said. "There needs to be a structural, fundamental change."
Mautz and Dels. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico), Chris Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) all spoke at the chamber lunch. They, along with the rest of the state's legislators, will head back to Annapolis in January for the 447th session of the Maryland General Assembly.
In talking about the state's budget, Mautz also said there should be incentives in place to try to drive state agencies to save money.
Sample-Hughes said the state should do its fiscal homework and find out what it "really (has) to work with."
"But I do believe that we can still address and attack some of these goals that we have, whether it's education, whether it's climate, whether it's criminal justice," she said. "We can do it in a pragmatic way."
Adams said to solve the budget problem, the state has to leverage and grow its private sector.
"You do not do what we've done for the past two years," he said. He said the state and its leadership need to stop spending so much, own up to the problem and stop blaming it on COVID-19.
Hutchinson expressed his concerns with the transportation budget and the lack of funding for many infrastructure projects across the state.
"We've got to pay attention to our transportation budget," he said.
BLUEPRINTThe legislators also talked about the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a plan passed by the Maryland General Assembly in 2021 that aims to improve student outcomes and the quality of education across the state through increasing education funding by $3.8 billion over a 10-year period.
Sample-Hughes said although Blueprint's goals are important, the General Assembly's decision to pass the plan has contributed to the state's budget deficit. She later advocated for giving more resources to the nonprofits that already serve 3 and 4 year olds, rather than putting money toward expanding early childhood education in the state's public school systems.
Mautz said he thinks the project needs to be paused so that the plan's strengths and weaknesses can be better evaluated.
JUVENILE CRIMEThe legislators also talked about the state of juvenile crime in Maryland, with Sample-Hughes calling for the removal of Department of Juvenile Services Secretary Vincent Schiraldi.
Hutchinson said that with recent juvenile justice reforms going into effect Nov. 1, he doesn't think a lot of legislators are going to want to discuss juvenile crime this upcoming session.
"Because they'll say, 'We just put that in place. We haven't even been able to see the results,'" he said.
Adams said law enforcement is needed now more than ever and officers need to be able to do their jobs.
"If you want a society, if you want a City of Cambridge, if you want an Eastern Shore (or) State of Maryland, if you want a United States that is civil, there have to be consequences," he said.

title: Caroline Commissioners Hear from County Workers, Discuss School Budget
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline Commissioners hear from county workers, discuss school budget

 November 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 599
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners convened on Tuesday and several topics were discussed, including the Employee Advisory Board's desire to attract and retain workers, approving changes to the fiscal year 2024 Caroline Board of Education budget and a restructuring of the Department of Public Works.BOARD OF EDUCATION BUDGETDerek Simmons, superintendent of Caroline County Public Schools, and Jill Hignutt, CFO of The Caroline Board of Education, requested amendments to the Board of Education's 2024 budget.
"We are here to share where the budget adjustments needed to take place in the operating budget and align those with the actuals at the end of the fiscal year," Simmons said.
Hignett gave the commissioners a copy of her short presentation, then began detailing the request.
"Starting with prescriptive revenues, there is a change of $6,389,071 related to our grant funding. Many of our grants cross fiscal years, so we must adjust the revenues to match the expenditures that were actually seen at year end," Hignutt said.
Then she shifted the attention to expenditures like driver salaries for transportation. Between fuel costs and bus driver salaries, the school system overspent about $39,000. She also mentioned parking lot repavement projects and classroom renovations.
There was a $5,782,498 surplus noted in the total budgeted revenues. According to Daniel Fox, deputy county administrator, the excess of revenue over expenditures is retained by the Board of Education to go to its fund balance.
The commissioners approved the amended budget.
EMPLOYEE ADVISORY BOARDNext up was the Employee Advisory Board, an authority that overlooks the corrections, emergency services, planning and codes, public works, recreation and parks, and administration departments. There is also a non-voting member department, the Department of Human Resources.
Todd Lord, chairman of the Advisory Board for Caroline County, thanked the commissioners for improving pensions for retirees and achieving competitive pay increases to help with recruitment and retention.
The board also wants cost of living adjustments due to the inflation following the pandemic.
Lord proposed an initiative to go forward as he hears from staff about pay and salaries.
"We recommend merit pay increases annually for step based off of employee evaluations. We want to get away from the bunching of salaries. Health care plans for retirees, that is another one of our initiatives being discussed heavily in departments," Lord said.
He said the goal was to increase retention and have attraction for the employees under the board's care.
"Right now we want to provide a health care plan that employees can take into retirement," Lord said. "Having their pension in retirement would be a huge benefit in retention for our staff."
Commissioner Frank Bartz responded, "Health care for retirees, that is a hard undertaking for the county."
Another commissioner said the same.
Porter said, "I don't foresee that we are going to be able to do health care benefits for people who are retiring at 55. The same inflation figures that you are using, we are facing as well."
President Travis Breeding said, "We have to find that balance — taking care of our employees and taking care of our tax payers and the constituents of the county."
PUBLIC WORKS REORGANIZATIONRobin Eaton, director of the Department of Public Works, asked the commissioners for the authority to reorganize the department to create a project manager position. He spoke of maintaining the 80 miles of dirt roads in the county.
"Our original structure had three crew leaders, so doing away with one of those crew leader positions and creating a project inspector slash utility locator," Eaton said.
"It is actually three crews. Two under crew leaders and one dirt road crew with four employees under the road superintendent," Kathleen Freeman, county administrator, said.
The commissioners approved the reorganization.

title: Talbot County Proposes Hotel Tax Increase to Local Delegation
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County proposes hotel tax increase to local delegation

 October 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 589
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County leaders met with the local delegation Tuesday afternoon to discuss creating legislation during the upcoming General Assembly to raise the county's hotel taxes.Talbot County's current public accommodations tax rate, or hotel tax rate, is 4%, the lowest of any county in the state. The tax is levied on those staying in hotels or short-term rentals in the county, collected by the business and then paid to either the county or one of three towns.
Easton, Oxford and St. Michaels collect revenues from such properties within one mile outside town limits. The county collects revenue from all other properties not within those boundaries.
A potential increase to 6%, which would increase total revenue collected by around $1 million in fiscal year 2024, requires approval from lawmakers in Annapolis.
Cassandra Vanhooser, the county's director of tourism and economic development, along with Talbot County Council members briefed Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), Del. Christopher T. Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) on the proposed increase.
"I'm anticipating that this is going to be our principal legislation request for the delegation this year," council Vice President Pete Lesher said.
Adams and Mautz explained that state lawmakers will be tasked with addressing significant budget problems in the upcoming session. Adams said it's likely lawmakers will try to pass the budget by voting for state tax increases that were not passed last year.
He said it's probably the first year he will vote against the budget. Any tax bill will require his careful consideration, Adams noted, saying he'd like to hear the council's opinions on potential hotel tax legislation.
Council Member Keasha Haythe said the spike would help "level the playing field" for the county, as well as increase funding for the tourism and economic development department. Revenue the county collects from the accommodations tax goes to that department.
"This particular tax I do believe is necessary for Talbot County and tourism and (the) hospitality industry," Haythe said.
Mautz agreed with Haythe's points but brought up the benefits of Talbot County's low accommodations tax rate.
"I also agree with the perspective that would say, if your accommodation tax is lower than the neighboring county, then you have an advantage as far as attracting (people)," Mautz said. He added that the council should take into consideration that it may make the area more attractive for investors.
Jessica Bellis, CFO at the Avalon Foundation and a member of the Talbot County Tourism Board, expressed her support for the increase. She said the taxes benefit her organization since they are cycled back into Talbot County's and Easton's respective economic development and tourism departments.
"We can't market in the big world, as tiny little Avalon Foundation or as a small Airbnb in Talbot County," Bellis said. "We really rely on that tourism office for its marketing power."
Hutchinson said the county should ensure business owners are on board and lay out to the delegation how the taxes collected cycle back into the local economy.
Council President Chuck Callahan said it's important for the county to do its "due diligence" and gather feedback from businesses before voting on the topic as a council. While the bill could be pre-filed by the local delegates in November, January was agreed upon as a deadline for the county to have a draft bill ready for the legislators.
"This is a really important issue," Mautz said. "We definitely don't want to be in a situation where we go up to Annapolis and are not prepared."
"It's a different discussion when you go across the bridge," he said.

title: Caroline County Commissioners Discuss FY 2025 Budget, Years Ahead
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline County commissioners discuss FY 2025 budget, years ahead

 May 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 878
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On May 7 the Caroline County Commissioners convened to present the fiscal year 2025 budget, but the budget discussion looked at what's to come in years ahead.Discussions featured two prominent, long-term issues — the county's revenue-generating landfill and the state-mandated Blueprint for Education program.
The budget overview also covered the operating budget, capital budgets, proposed tax rates and municipal real property tax differential rates.
Looking forward, Commissioner Larry Porter said The Mid-Shore II Regional Landfill will generate $420,000 a year in revenue if it stays in Caroline County.
In the late 1980s, due to new federal regulations, the counties had to close their landfills and replace them with new landfills. In response to this new regulation, Talbot, Caroline and Queen Anne's counties engaged with MES to form a partnership where each county would take turns hosting a landfill for a 20-year term. Kent County later joined that partnership.
Caroline County is hosting the current landfill and, under the original arrangement, would be off the hook at the end of 2030 when Queen Anne's County would take over the responsibility of host. However, the partnering counties have agreed to allow the landfill to stay in Caroline County for 12 years longer than initially planned.
Dan Fox, deputy administrator, said the county will receive a revenue increase of around $12.3 million over the duration of the extended agreement at a meeting held earlier on May 7. The counties agreed on a $3 per ton post fee until 2030. In 2031 it will rise to $6.
"Landfill is a revenue benefit to the county. Down the road, we will need this money," Porter said.
The other topic discussed by commissioners was the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a massive educational program that includes salary increases for teachers and more funding for early education.
The commissioners are concerned about its expense to the county.
While dramatically boosting state funding for public education over a decade, the Blueprint also asks local school districts — and taxpayers — to do their part.
In a letter to Gov. Wes Moore, the Maryland Association of Counties last November listed a litany of concerns. They said the Blueprint's cost estimates don't take into account the bottom-line local impact of several major spending items, including construction costs for additional classrooms needed under the plan's expansion of pre-K and the new minimum $60,000 teacher salary starting in 2026.
"It is a bad program and we have to figure out a way to pay for this," Porter said.
Education-related expenses made up the top expenditure for Caroline County in FY 2025. The Board of Education will receive about $17.1 million if the proposed budget is approved, about $2.3 million more than last year.
Rounding out the top four expenditures are the sheriff ($5,534,994), corrections ($5,889,769) and emergency medical services ($5,563,069).
The top three revenue generators for fiscal year 2025 are property taxes ($28,704,000), income taxes ($20,200,000) and a disparity grant from the state ($4,686,791).
Though commissioners voted to maintain the same tax rates as last year, the county will bring in more revenue from property taxes in FY 2025 due to an increase in the assessed value of properties in Caroline County.
Because of this increase, the state will provide less funding to the county in its annual disparity grant.
According to the Maryland Department of Legislative Services, the disparity grant is "where the local income tax is below 75% of the statewide average. Under the program each eligible jurisdiction receives a grant that enables the per capita local income tax revenues to reach 75% of the statewide average."
Deputy Administrator Dan Fox said that our state disparity grant is being funded at $615,525 less than last year.
"That is a state-driven formula that is based off of wealth. We changed in percentage there, which means we receive less money this year," Fox said.
The tax differential rate was discussed for various municipalities.
Porter described the tax differential as "revenue that the county does not collect. It is not money being taken from the towns or given to the towns. It does not affect town budgets in any way. It is money that the town does not collect."
Fox said, "The county is looking to maintain the property tax rate at 98 cents per 100 of all unincorporated areas as well as the towns that do not receive a differential," he said.
"This year we are looking provide Denton with the same tax rate as the prior year with 92 cents- a six cents differential to get you to 92 cent county tax rate. Federalsburg will have a county tax rate of 90 cents. Greensboro will remain at 92 cents. Preston would receive and remain at 97 cents and Ridgely would be at 93 cents," said Fox.
Commissioner Frank Bartz said they go through the budget line by line. And although there were some conversations, by and large they agreed on each item.
Two people Sue Simmons, interim director of Caroline County Arts Council and Dr. Cliff Coppersmith, President of Chesapeake College, both came up and stated how grateful they were for the county's support.
They had scheduled an hour and a half for this meeting, but it only took around 45 minutes. One commissioner, Travis Breeding, was "under the weather" and did not attend live.
The FY 2025 budget is scheduled for potential adoption during the Commissioners of Caroline County meeting on May 28.

title: Caroline Commissioners Vote to Keep Proposed Tax Rates the Same
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Caroline Commissioners vote to keep proposed tax rates the same

 April 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 347
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners unanimously voted to leave the county's proposed property tax rate unchanged for fiscal year 2025 at a meeting on Tuesday.The current tax rate, which would remain the same for the next fiscal year, is 98 cents per $100 of assessed valuation.
In an interview, County Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox said that rate hasn't changed since 2015.
The vote included the tax differential rates for towns in the county. Tax differentials are lower county property tax rates for properties within municipalities. At the meeting, Commission Vice President Larry Porter asked about Ridgely's tax differential.
"I would say that the logical question would be Ridgely," he said.
On March 13, the Commissioners of Ridgely suspended the entire Ridgely Police Department with pay, effective immediately, pending an investigation by the Office of the Maryland State Prosecutor, according to a press release from the town.
At a County Commission meeting March 19, the commission said that the Caroline County Sheriff's Office and the Maryland State Police would divide responsibilities for providing law enforcement to the town.
At the meeting Tuesday, Fox said his current understanding is that Ridgely is discussing the possibility of continuing its contracted service with the the Caroline County Sheriff's Office at 140 hours per week.
"So if that holds true, I think they, by formula, would be entitled to the same differential," he said.
Fox said the hard part of this is that the town still has the opportunity to back out until a contract is signed and endorsed. He said Ridgely's differential is about a $60,000 reduction in property taxes.
"So that would be the number if the board chose not to do a differential," Fox said. "We would receive an additional property tax revenue."
Before making a motion to keep the tax rates the same, Commission President Travis Breeding said he was ok with keeping the rate the same.
"I'm ok with keeping it the same for the year and seeing where they end up," he said about Ridgely.
Caroline County will be holding a public budget hearing on May 7 at 6 p.m.
Reporter Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado contributed to this article.

title: Caroline County Organizations Make Their Cases for FY2025 Funds
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline County organizations make their cases for FY2025 funds

 March 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 761
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On March 12, several locals stood before the Commissioners of Caroline County to make their cases for funding from the county's fiscal year 2025 budget.At the hearing, which was designed for commissioners to hear testimonies on operating and capital requests, documents were distributed, giving a picture of the county's revenues and expenditures going into the annual budgeting process.
The requested expenditures for fiscal year 2025 come to $72,095,934, and the revenue estimates for 2025 are $71,459,230. That leaves a projected shortfall of $636,704.
The commissioners will have to pass a balanced budget before the new fiscal year begins on July 1. This will require addressing the more than $600,000 deficit.
Commissioners Larry Porter and Frank Bartz presided over the March 12 hearing. Commission President Travis Breeding was not present.
There were four groups who pleaded their cases to either retain current funding from the county or get an increase.
Phil Starkey, president of the Queen Anne-Hillsboro Fire Department, spoke on behalf of all the firefighting companies in Caroline County.
"The initial request was a 10% increase on the operating side," he said. "Fire companies struggle with fundraising efforts. Materials to do fundraisers have gone up along with everything else that we do. Equipment has gone up. Trucks are up to a million dollars, equipment. You guys know, 10% (increase) is a fair ask in my opinion, considering most of our stuff is going on 20% (more than) last year."
Starkey asked that the commissioner prioritize retaining programs that aid local fire departments with volunteer retention.
"The other thing is the $2,500 real estate property tax reduction program. It is a good retention tool," he said. "You guys supply us with the LOSAP program (Length of Service Awards Program). You get someone who comes in at 20, they have to wait until they are 62 before they get any benefits. This tax program is a good program to retain people that have to meet their 50 (annual) points. To retain the $33,000 to meet the needs of the (fire reporting) program is a needed thing. It is a big cost on the fire departments clear across the board."
He also highlighted the 508 money that comes from the state of Maryland and pays $330,000 a year across all of the fire companies in Caroline County. Mostly it helps to buy equipment and trucks, Starkey said.
Porter expressed support for Starkey's requests, saying local fire departments "have to fundraise just to be volunteers."
Three other residents advocated for the county's support at the hearing. These were Debby Bennett, executive director of the Caroline County Library; Sue Simmons, interim manager for the Caroline County Council of the Arts; and Susan Reynolds of the Human Service Council.
"What the commissioner's budget allows us to do is have two additional staff," Reynolds said. "Without that budget, we either have to cut a full time person, of which there is only two of us, or I would have to cut programs. I request $25,000. We got about $57,000 less from the state. We have had to cut Men for Change, the YMCA program and the mentoring program."
Bennett was next in front of the commissioners.
"We are asking for an increase in the operating budget," she said. "It is always about the staffing and trying to recruit and retain good staff. On the capital side, I want to thank you for your funding. The local match for the last part of the renovation at the central library, which was the pitched roof in the back of the library and the elevator, that is 85% done. We are requesting $30,000 capital funding for the central library parking lot."
Porter responded to her statements.
"Bottom line, we have got to have places that we can keep warm, and keep cool and keep the doors open," he said.
Towards the end of the meeting, Simmons said, "I want to bring to your attention to not only the Arts Council's request, which is $6,500. It is a relatively small fraction of the budget. The majority comes from a non competitive grant through the Department of Commerce through the Maryland State Arts Council. I want to say thank you and please write that same level of check."
The next public meeting concerning the county's budget is scheduled for May 7 at 6 p.m. at the Caroline County Courthouse. At it, the commissioners are expected to continue receiving testimony on operating and capital budget requests. They will also hear testimony on the constant yield tax rate and municipal property tax differential rate, which are expected to be set in a proposed budget by the commissioners on April 9.

Caroline Commissioners OK reallocation bill

 September 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 DENTON - The Caroline County Commissioners passed legislation Tuesday, Sept. 12, to use funds originally intended for renovating the county detention center for additional county renovation projects.The commissioners reallocated a portion of the proceeds of the $34.2 million consolidated public improvement and refunding bonds of 2019 to pay for roof replacements for Federalsburg and Preston elementary schools and North Caroline High School, as well as HVAC in the Fretterd Center in Denton.The first reading of Bill 2023-002 took place Aug. 15. No public comments were offered at each of the three readings of the bill."Earlier this year it was identified that we have not used the proceeds of the 2019 bond issuance for renovation of the detention center. And as a result, the commissioners have directed us to reallocate the funding of the project," County Attorney Stewart Barroll said.In other business, the commissioners heard a proposal about a potential Hobbs Solar Project to be built on the capped landfill.Jack Martell, manager of business development, and Greg Werner, manager of Massachusetts-based Nexamp Solar, Inc. presented a slide show and answered questions from the commissioners about the proposed 5,000-panel solar project.The company proposed to "finance, build, own and maintain" solar facilities on 15 acres at the landfill at 26375 Hobbs Road and "extend the financial benefits of the generated electricity, land lease and tax revenue" to the county government and public schools.Nexamp Solar projected a total benefit of $121,152 at the end of the first year, and a total benefit at the end of its 20-year lifespan of nearly $2 million.The commissioners took no action on the proposal at this meeting.Also on the agenda was Susan Runnels, director of the Caroline Human Services Council, who discussed transportation needs and how they're currently being to serve two towns in the county."In my opinion, mobility on demand doesn't work in Caroline County," Runnels said.Few people used the service, which serves Greensboro and Federalsburg residents for in-county rides. Those towns qualify for state grant funding for transportation in lower income areas.For example, Runnels said the service, which uses Delmarva Community Transit, supplied 48 rides from Greensboro and 15 from Federalsburg from March through June. Many of those rides were called by the same persons, she said."I don't think this is feasible for us," she said. "But we need some kind of transportation in the county we'd be better off going back to taxi service." Runnels said she would prefer to take almost $27,000 in state grants that she has to return to the state and use those funds to help to pay for driver's education classes for teen drivers or vehicle repairs in the target communities."We can't have our dollars just sitting in a parking lot waiting for a call," she said.

title: Shore Projects Slated to Receive Federal Funding
content:
Shore projects slated to receive federal funding

 August 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)
