 WASHINGTON - U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen and Sen. Ben Cardin announced the inclusion of over $34 million in key Senate Committee legislation for community-led projects in Maryland, including four on the Eastern Shore.These funds, included at the senators' request, support a wide array of projects to improve public transit, trail networks, roads, bridges, affordable housing, and community and economic development.These projects are part of the Senate Appropriations THUD Subcommittee's proposed funding legislation for fiscal year 2024, which was released as part of the annual Congressional Appropriations process and passed on a bipartisan basis by the full Senate Appropriations Committee."One of our top priorities is securing federal investments to support vital initiatives in our communities. That's why, working together, Federal Team Maryland fought for these funds that will help reconnect communities, modernize our infrastructure and link more Marylanders to public transit, affordable housing, job opportunities, and more," Van Hollen said in a news release. "This federal funding makes a real impact, and we're committed to working to get these investments over the finish line." The bill will proceed to consideration before the full Senate - funding is not finalized until the Appropriations bills are passed by the full Senate, reconciled with the House of Representatives, and signed into law by the President."One of our top priorities is securing federal investments to support vital initiatives in our communities.That's why, working together, Federal Team Maryland fought for these funds that will help reconnect communities, modernize our infrastructure and link more Marylanders to public transit, affordable housing, job opportunities, and more," Van Hollen said. "This federal funding makes a real impact, and we're committed to working to get these investments over the finish line." There are four Eastern Shore projects included in the funding legislation.The Benedictine School in Caroline County is slated to receive $1.8 million to renovate the residential facility's outdated living areas and health facilities to better suit the needs of students and their families.Habitat for Humanity Choptank is slated to receive $450,000 to prepare sites in Ward 3 in Cambridge for the construction of safe, affordable and energy-efficient homes to help low-income families achieve sustainable homeownership.Mace's Lane Community Center is slated to receive $1 million to be used for the final phase of renovation of the historic Mace's Lane School into a museum and community center that will house a Boys & Girls Club, youth sports, education and cultural programs, community meeting space and senior services.Kent Attainable Housing Inc. is slated to receive $810,000 in funding to support the construction of affordable homes for families in Chestertown and Butler town. In addition to constructing housing units for first time buyers, the program provides financial literacy and support services to help residents budget and establish good credit."Creating and maintaining livable and functional communities are at the heart of THUD appropriations.It's critical that we provide federal support for locally driven Maryland projects, both through Congressionally Directed Spending and through competitive grant programs that support our roads, bridges, trails, ports, and transit systems, as well as affordable housing," Cardin said. "These projects advance many of our top priorities, including new funding for the Franklin-Mulberry Corridor in Baltimore and continued capital funding for WMATA. In the coming weeks I will be urging my colleagues in Congress to enact these investments in final appropriations legislation for FY2024.

title: Federalsburg Elects First Two Black Council Members in Historic Election
author: Natalie Jones And Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com, njones@chespub.com
content:
Federalsburg elects first two Black council members in historic election

 September 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones And Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com, njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 814
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG - Just under 300 voters braved a gray and drizzly Tuesday to cast their ballots in Federalsburg's bicentennial election, making history in electing two Black women to the town council.While the election falling during the bicentennial year is special on its own, the day was historic for a different reason - it was the first election held under the town's recently passed election plan, and it was the first time a Black resident had been elected to the town council in the town's 200-year history.According to Kristy Marshall, Federalsburg's interim town manager, 283 residents voted in Tuesday's election, accounting for 17% of the town's registered voters.The mayoral seat and all four council seats - two council members for each newly created district - were up for election.Incumbent Mayor Kimberly Abner held her position at the helm of the town, earning 191 votes and a five-year term as mayor. Jeffrey Stevenson, Jr., a first-time candidate, received 83 votes.In the newly created District 1, which has a majority Black population, representation was achieved for Black residents with the election of two Black women to the council seats.Darlene Hammond received the highest number of ballots, earning 70 votes and a five-year term on the town council.Brandy James received 52 votes, earning a three-year term on the council.James held a narrow lead over incumbent councilman Scott Phillips, who received 49 votes.In District 2, only two candidates - Debra Sewell and H. Torbert "Toby" Williamson - ran for the two open council spots, locking in their seats on the council even before the election.Sewell received 135 votes, earning a five-year term. Williamson received 90 votes and a three-year council term.The new election plan, passed in June, changed the town's former at-large, staggered term election system to a two-district system that ensured more representation of Federalsburg's Black residents.No Black resident had ever been elected as a mayor or council member in the town's 200-year history until Tuesday's election.The change was spurred by a federal lawsuit filed earlier this year, which contended that the former election system discriminated against Black voters by keeping them from being able to elect their chosen representatives.Abner, who has served as Federalsburg's mayor since 2019, faced a challenge from Stevenson, a lifelong town resident who hoped to bring change, leadership and caring for the future of the community.To Abner, time already served as an elected official mattered."People look at experience and pay attention," she said.Paying the town's debt, fixing pump stations and paving roads are also among Abner's priorities.When asked why he was running, Stevenson gave a simple answer: "If not me, then who?" "Man, I always felt like I was a leader, and I was always willing to take the chances that everybody else won't take," he said."I'm getting older now, so I've had interest in politics because it matters to me now - I pay taxes, I'm invested in the city - so it's like the things that I wasn't concerned about as a child, as a man coming of age."For James, a 25-year Federalsburg resident and first-time candidate, choosing to step up and run for one of the District 1 council seats came from a simple question she asked herself, "Why not?" "It was more so like, 'Will I be here for another 25 years and just continue to complain and nag about things that need to be done, or will I be that person that tries to be a part of the change - you know, be the change you want to see," she said.To James, changing the town's level of transparency with residents is a major factor, especially when it comes to ensuring that the community knows what the town is doing, whether it's a municipal election or roadwork."I want to make sure that the information that is conveyed is information that is understood by anybody on any education level, like you shouldn't have to have a master's or doctorate degree to understand what they're talking about," she said. "I just want to make sure that it's plain and simple and understood."On a similar note, James said the town should publish relevant information in both Spanish and Creole to serve Federalsburg's Hispanic and Haitian populations.For Federalsburg's Black residents, the first election under the new plan is one they've long been waiting for."I appreciate everybody that (would) listen to me, that listened to my cry, and took interest in doing what they've done to get this," said Roberta Butler."It took a while, it took awhile - can you imagine, 200 years? That's a long time." 
 
 Caption: Federalsburg Mayor Kim Abner, left, poses for a photo with incumbent Councilwoman Debra Sewell, who ran in District 2 to preserve her seat.
 
Federalsburg resident Roberta Butler spoke of the election in biblical terms. She said finally, someone had heard her cry after 200 years.

title: Dels. Arentz, Jacobs and Ghrist announce reelection filings for District 36
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Dels. Arentz, Jacobs and Ghrist announce reelection filings for District 36

 September 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Headlines 
 
 501
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — The three Republican delegates representing Maryland's District 36 — Steve Arentz of Queen Anne's County, Jay Jacobs of Kent County and Jeff Ghrist of Caroline County — formally filed for reelection Wednesday."The District 36 team, which also includes Senate Minority Leader Steve Hershey, has long worked together to advance fiscal responsibility, economic growth, local infrastructure investment and policies that protect the values and livelihoods of the Shore's families and businesses," the incumbents said in a joint press release Wednesday. "Their record reflects years of collaboration and dedication to Caroline, Cecil, Kent and Queen Anne's counties."
Arentz, who has served as a District 36 representative since 2013, when he was appointed to fill the seat vacated by now Sen. Steve Hershey, underscored his focus on economic development and local business growth in the press release.
"The Eastern Shore deserves a team that knows how to deliver results," Arentz said. "From championing small business growth to securing investments in local infrastructure, I've been proud to stand shoulder to shoulder with my colleagues in serving this district. I am running for reelection because there is more work to do to strengthen our economy and preserve our way of life."
Jacobs was mayor of Rock Hall before being sworn in as a District 36 representative in 2010. In the press release, he emphasized his "commitment to protecting the Shore's values."
"Representing the people of District 36 is the honor of a lifetime," Jacobs said. "Our constituents expect us to fight for common sense, to push back against Annapolis overreach, and to ensure that rural Maryland is never forgotten. I am proud to run for reelection with my colleagues so we can continue to give the Upper Shore a strong and respected voice in the General Assembly."
Ghrist, who was elected to his seat in 2014, highlighted the importance of working families and education.
"As a lifelong resident of the Shore, I know the challenges and opportunities facing our families, schools and communities," Ghrist said. "I am committed to making sure our children have a quality education, our communities remain safe, and our families can thrive without being crushed by taxes and regulations. Running as part of this team ensures we will continue delivering results for the people who sent us to Annapolis."
Hershey, who serves alongside the three delegates, praised their record and offered his support for their reelection.
Earlier this month, Hershey, a Republican, announced that he had launched an exploratory committee to look into the viability for a gubernatorial campaign.
"Delegates Arentz, Jacobs and Ghrist have proven themselves to be tireless advocates for the Eastern Shore. Their leadership, experience and dedication are exactly what the Shore needs in Annapolis, and I wholeheartedly support their reelection," Hershey said. "As for my own future, I remain in the process of working through an exploratory committee to assess the viability of a run for governor in 2026. I will make a final decision by the end of the year whether to pursue that path or to seek reelection to my Senate seat."

title: Residents Want Federalsburg to Keep Promises of Transparency
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Residents want Federalsburg to keep promises of transparency

 July 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 599
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — After a 50-minute explanation from town officials about mounting issues in Federalsburg, the community spent over an hour and a half voicing concerns.The town addressed issues like misappropriation of town funds, employee resignations, $5 million of debt, water and wastewater treatment issues and police department cost, offering transparency that residents have said was lacking.
Federalsburg Mayor Kim Abner hopes this community forum is a step in the right direction for the town.
"I think that it went well," Abner said about the meeting. "I mean, it went as good as it can be expected. The problem is that a lot of stuff gets posted on Facebook that isn't true. We were trying to set the record straight about some other things that have happened. We're trying to be more transparent about what is going on down at Town Hall, and we want the public to be engaged."
During Monday's meeting, residents voiced multiple times that the town needed to maintain more open communication with the public.
Eric Padgett, business owner and owner of multiple properties in Federalsburg, spoke passionately about the town's issues and about the good in the town.
"I've been walking around town. I watch everything that's going on. Nobody is held accountable for nothing," Padgett said. "Count the town managers, every ... one of them have never walked around, drove around, asked anybody any questions about nothing. … The town needs to open up at 7 a.m. and close at 5 p.m. so these people who have a problem can go in there and do something about it."
A proposal to have the Caroline County Sheriff's Office take over policing duties for the town garnered a lot of back-and-forth among residents.
Former Police Chief Donald Nagel spoke on the topic by asking how important police protection was to the residents by show of hands. All residents raised their hand indicating it was important.
"I worked in this town 24 years or whatever, and it was rough, and we had to bring it back, and we brought it back," Nagel said. "I'm not here for any accolades or anything. I just know this town by word. You're not going to get the same service by having the sheriff's department in here that you have now. People know you're police officers, so please, don't do away with the police."
Multiple residents thought differently about the police department. Some indicated the Sheriff's Office could offer better coverage to the town.
Residents who spoke agreed on that property tax prices, wastewater problems and lack of transparency from the town government were pressing issues.
Resident Danielle Brodka acknowledged the town's efforts to be transparent, but without work, she doesn't believe the town residents' anger will change.
"Is it a wonder that everyone in this building is angry because there is so much that has been addressed?" Brodka said.
"I don't want you to think that I'm saying it's each one of you individuals," she said to town officials. "You all have different tenure, you all have different goals. But is it any wonder that everybody in this building is upset because there is a lot going on."
Brodka and many other residents in the room expressed their support of the town's plan to hold quarterly meetings like the one Monday.
"I am glad that you are going to have quarterly meetings because they are absolutely necessary," she said. "I am glad that you are telling me that there is going to be more follow through. But until we see it, I don't think anyone's going to believe it. I think this town is going to continue to be angry until we have results."

 DENTON — Two Candidates Have Qualified to Run in Denton's Upcoming Town Council Election. They Are Lester L. Branson and Angel L. Perez.Branson Is 82 and Perez Is 38. Perez Went on to List Leadership Positions He Has Held with 19 Boards and Organizations on the Eastern Shore in the Past 10 Years.

Another Big Thing Is That We Are Looking with the County, They Are Going to Have to Build Another Middle School. There Is a Possibility That Where Caroline County High School Is That There Is Land to Do That Out There. in the Future, Are They Going to Keep the Middle School There or Put It Somewhere Else in Denton or Are They Going to Go Out to North Caroline and Put It There? ... Another Thing Is to Build Water and Sewer Out in West Denton. There Are a Lot of Houses Where Their Septic Systems Are Going Out."

title: Ridgely to Hold Commissioner Election on Monday
author: Tom McCall
content:
Ridgely to hold commissioner election on Monday

 April 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 859
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — There are three people up for one commissioner's seat in Ridgely. Incumbent John Hurley and two others, Chad Leister and Lakia Harris-Pierce, will face off in a town-wide election Monday.Candidates spoke to issues currently impacting the town as reasons they decided to run.
All of the candidates are aware of an ongoing investigation by the Office of the State's Attorney into the Ridgley Police Department, which resulted in the entire department being suspended in March. The Sheriff's Office has taken over the duties of policing the town while the investigation takes place. Details of the investigation have not yet been made available to the public.
Other big issues raised by candidates include giving the next generation a reason to stay in Ridgely and keeping the small-town character alive despite the town's growth.
LAKIA HARRIS-PIERCE"I am running because I have a vision of a vibrant and strong community moving forward for the next generation," said Harris-Pierce. "That is a community that engages with each other. They are part of the decision making process with the leadership. They would also volunteer their time to upkeep the community."
Harris-Pierce is a veteran and has a background in social work. She is the only Black candidate for the commissioner seat, which she said gives her perspective into the needs of Ridgely's Black community.
"When I am out in the world, I see that we are behind in education, infrastructure and technology," she said. "These kids are going to grow up and leave here one day. The only (way) to bring them back is to keep it growing. There is nothing here for the next generation to come back to and build on."
Harris-Pierce has a masters degree in cannabis studies. As a cannabis policy expert, she said she would work to change the town moratorium on cannabis businesses to attract these businesses to the town. "It will bring in revenue, and it will bring in jobs," she said.
Focusing on the suspension of the Ridgely Police Department, she said, "Right now there is no solution because we would just have to wait for the investigation to be over."
"We haven't had any crime go up. The residents are all getting along. I think it comes down to trust and authenticity. The community is at a loss about what happened with our police department. Not just the police chief but the commissioners too, they hired those people," Harris-Pierce said.
JOHN HURLEYHurley has been a Ridgely commissioner since 2012. He has lived on the Eastern Shore his entire life and has lived in Ridgely since 1987.
In an email to the Star Democrat, Hurley wrote, "I love my small town and try to make our town better. In my 12 years as a Commissioner, the town has gone from a deficit to a surplus without raising taxes."
He touted his record of fiscal discipline.
"(It is) A small town with only so much money to go around- without raising taxes. Taxes have not been raised in the 12 years. I have been in office and I don't plan on raising them," Hurley wrote.
Hurley has a long history as a firefighter, having worked on the BWI Airport Fire Department for upwards of three decades. He is also a member of the Ridgely Volunteer Fire Department.
He wrote about the Ridgely Police department, "It may be a year until the outcome of the investigation comes to a finish. Until that happens, there really can't be a solution."
CHAD LEISTERLeister, an electrician, said he hopes, if elected, to provide fresh perspective to the Town Commissioners.
"A lot of people in town positions, they have been there for a decade or more and always run uncontested," he said. "I don't think someone should be running uncontested for an office position like that."
He also had some fiscal concerns about the suspension of the Ridgely Police Department.
"We are paying our police department, which I understand because we don't know if they are guilty or innocent. It is innocent until proven guilty," Leister said. "And then we are also paying to rent police officers from the Sheriff's Department. We have to know a solution soon. We can't be doing both. I think the State's Attorney that is in charge of this needs to come forth with a little more than they are giving us."
He spoke to what he thinks the voters are concerned about.
"Safety overall. We have lots of concerns about traffic," he said. "There is an influx of people moving to Caroline County — a lot of people want to make it more, and a lot of people like how life is, or was."
"... A challenge is to figure out the right way to expand Ridgely. How to contain the influx of people coming over but still keeping the small-town values. Ridgely is a great town to live in. Being in the Lions Club and organizing the town flea market, I have met a lot of amazing people. I have put a lot of volunteer work into the town," Leister said.
The winner of Monday's election will serve a three-year term as the town's commissioner.
The polls will be open from 1 to 7 p.m. April 22 at 2 Central Avenue — the town hall.

title: Aaron’s Place Presents Potential New Location to Caroline County Commissioners
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Aaron’s Place presents potential new location to Caroline County Commissioners

 October 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 433
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Cheryl Beulah, executive director of Aaron's Place, discussed the food pantry's potential new location with the Caroline County Commissioners on Tuesday.The proposed location on Meeting House Road will allow Aaron's Place to work in partnership with His Hope Ministries and the Chesapeake Culinary Center to provide a year-round homeless shelter and multiple different classes, additions and food storage locations, Beulah said.
Plans for the location have been in the works for the past two years while volunteers from Aaron's Place and His Hope Ministries have resolved issues with the Environmental Protection Agency resulting from a covenant on the property.
The EPA covenant came after the property was contaminated with volatile organic compounds in the 1980s, Beulah said at the meeting Tuesday. Extensive testing has been conducted over the years, with the contamination shrinking due to a large pumping and air system installed by the previous owner, Russel Metals.
The EPA covenant is restrictive, primarily concerning water usage, but the EPA has indicated that as long as the project does not break the wellhead and uses water according to county instructions, it can proceed. The EPA also said that if three negative VOC tests are obtained after the project is on the property, it would consider removing the covenant.
Beulah told the commissioners how great the location will be for the community after all renovations were completed.
"To take that big piece of building, that building and that property, clean it all up, fix it all up and have it as a resource center to serve the people in the community. All the agencies that can come together will come together under one roof, joining forces together, joining resources together, and providing us a significant services in our community," she said.
The commissioners asked Beulah and the group questions about what services will be included at the new location. The group responded with a full analysis of the building.
"So, it's three main components, three main partners. Aaron's Place, His Hope Ministry and the Food Aggregation, those are the three main ones," Beulah said.
The group said the project requires significant funding. They are forming a capital campaign committee and exploring various funding opportunities around the state, Beulah said, and wanted to make sure they had the commissioners' support for the project before proceeding.
While the commissioners did not suggest a certain amount of money to support the project, the commissioners all said they will support the project and provide any help they can offer.
"I think it's a very worthwhile project," Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said. "I think if nothing else, it'll make that entrance to this town beautiful."

title: Caroline Commissioners Hoping to Nail Down Site for New YMCA
author: Konner Metz
content:
Caroline commissioners hoping to nail down site for new YMCA

 July 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Caroline 
 
 602
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County and YMCA leaders are restarting efforts to build a new YMCA facility after discussions fizzled out in recent years.At a county meeting Tuesday, YMCA of the Chesapeake CEO Robbie Gill told county commissioners that the organization has always wanted to build a full facility in Caroline County. The biggest step to moving forward is choosing a location, he said.
"The goal is still to build a YMCA that can be a hub for community," Gill said. "We just haven't solved the first piece of the puzzle, which is the right site and getting everybody on board."
During Tuesday's talks, stakeholders didn't land on one location in particular, though commissioners indicated three potential considerations: land on Double Hills Road off of Route 404, the old Southern States property at Gay and Market streets in Denton, or near Denton Elementary School.
"It's probably time for us to, as you said, pick a site and start telling a story," Commission Vice President Larry Porter told Gill.
Gill briefed the commissioners on the YMCA's recent expansions on the Eastern Shore, including in St. Michaels and Centreville. A new facility serving Caroline County residents would need to be around 60,000 square feet or more, Gill said. The project could fall in the $20 million range.
The YMCA of the Chesapeake currently operates an 11,000-square-foot facility nestled in the Denton Plaza shopping center off of Route 404. Gill said it serves around 3,000 people. A full-fledged building could more than double that mark.
PAST ROADBLOCKS
Past efforts to expand the YMCA's presence in Caroline County have been met with roadblocks. Porter, a commissioner since 2010, said it's time to get the ball rolling.
"The thing that's frustrating for me is it seems like we've had this conversation several times, and we are still in the same spot we were," Porter said.
In 2018, the county and YMCA signed an agreement in which the county would donate 15 acres of land on Double Hills Road to the YMCA. It was conditioned on the project beginning by July 1, 2023.
Talks stalled, and the project didn't begin before the deadline.
Gill said on Tuesday that there "wasn't support from a (county) administrative standpoint" at the time. Other concerns, such as the fact that the Town of Denton didn't own the land, parking meters and, eventually, the pandemic, hindered efforts, he noted.
In 2022, the YMCA of the Chesapeake returned a $2.5 million donation from a New Jersey donor that was meant to go toward the Caroline County endeavor.
"We really didn't see a pathway forward," Gill said.
But now, as talks resurface, there's renewed interest in delivering a new YMCA.
Commission President Travis Breeding said it may be challenging to locate the YMCA next to a school, though he said near Denton Elementary on the south end of town could be a consideration.
When commissioners raised the idea of considering the current and soon-to-be moved Lockerman Middle School on the north end of town, Gill expressed some reservation.
"With the school going away there, and if you demo'd that and built (a YMCA) there, it's kind of tucked away," he said.
County Administrator Katheleen Freeman said the county will look at some potential sites and put together a list. Gill said the nonprofit organization can conduct market assessments on potential sites to determine viability.
The CEO said it "hurts my heart that we still haven't solved this one," but expressed confidence that pursuing a larger YMCA facility in Caroline County is a benefit to residents and local businesses.
"There's an economic engine behind the Y as well because it gives you kind of that third place in your community to connect to people," Gill said.

 Denton — The Caroline County Commissioners are moving to discuss building a new YMCA in Caroline County."I just make a comment, the YMCA, there's been a lot of discussion about the YMCA building a facility in Caroline County, and I think we need to start having a serious discussion with them about why they haven't," commission Vice President Larry Porter said. "I mean, they've built them all around us, and I think it's time to have have that discussion with Robbie Gill."
County Administrator Kathleen Freeman responded saying that she had talked to Gill, the CEO of the YMCA of the Chesapeake, the day before the meeting.
Freeman said that she and Gill discussed restarting conversations about bringing a new YMCA to Caroline County and they will continue to have discussions to make sure that it happens.

We just haven't quite been able to put the pieces to the puzzle together, and so I'm excited that Kathleen and the commissioners have an interest in beginning those conversations again."
The current YMCA facility is an 11,000-square-foot storefront facility that is in Denton just off of state Route 404 in a shopping center. title: Housing Secretary Visits His Hope Ministries
author: Tom McCall
content:
Housing secretary visits His Hope Ministries

 April 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 668
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Maryland Secretary of Housing and Community Development Jake Day, came to His Hope Ministries in Denton Tuesday to learn about the nonprofit's vision for the future.The organization, which provides services and shelter to those experiencing homelessness, wants to develop a new building and move to Market Street.
They toured bunk rooms at 409 Aldersgate Drive, where neat piles of clothes, toothbrushes, laundry detergent and ear buds lie. The shelter welcomes guests from September through the end of April, with accommodations for families, single men and women, and youths.
"They are seeking to grow because the demand is high," Day said. "Part of that is that there just are not enough housing units, particularly affordable housing units in the Mid-Shore. We have underbuilt for the last 15 years. The consequence is that people are unhoused."
Executive Director Stefanie Johnson showed Day some architectural plans for a new facility she would like to build to expand His Hope's services.
"I did show him our design so far. We have an idea in mind for land, but so far, it is not available from the town yet. We have our Senior Haven, which is a three bedroom one bath home. It has three seniors in it. Seniors or disabled — it is transitional so they can stay there for up to three years," said Johnson.
There is a vacant lot next to this senior home where His Hope hopes to build their expanded facility.
One of the barriers to completing the project is its cost. Some of the visit was talking about money.
Day said he believes the best fiscal options for His Hope to complete the project is through the Community Development Block Grant from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. The state has $7.5 million to fund CDBG annually, he said.
"Probably for the Eastern Shore it is CDBG money. It gets to the end user when it is ready to be executed and spent for construction and design. This federal money has to serve the low income population," Day said.
The other option Day mentioned is Sowing Empowerment and Economic Development Inc., a nonprofit organization providing food, education, and training while promoting self-sufficiency and empowerment directly to low-to-moderate-income families.
"I believe both predevelopment and development costs are eligible. SEED is the institutional version of this. For the town, all it has to be is a community development goal that they're interested in. Helping unsheltered homeless be sheltered has positive health outcomes. A hospital and a shelter would go hand and glove," Day said.
Andrew Breeding, treasurer for His Hope Ministries, called their hoped-for property the Market Street Property. The land is owned by the Town of Denton and used to be a Southern States facility.
"The challenge is putting a homeless shelter literally anywhere," said Breeding.
Johnson said some local politicians are hesitant about the idea of building a shelter in town. Day said that representatives from his office, including him, could come and testify to the town council on behalf of His Hope's story.
Day asked some pressing questions about how His Hope Ministries and the community interact.
"What's that look like between you and other organizations in the community?" he asked.
Johnson responded, "It is impeccable. When we closed (for the warmer months), we called and said, 'Hey, do you have room for our families? Talbot Interfaith in Easton, and in Cambridge the Salvation Army, we are all on speed dial. Even the Christian Shelter in Salisbury. This community is so giving."
Day also toured the office and youth drop-in center of His Hope Ministries on 105 Gay Street, housed in a spacious Victorian house with a broad porch. The inside is inviting and colorful. There is room for classes on financial literacy, and there are many positive affirmations on the walls.
Amidst a big black board filled with affirmations, Day was invited to grab some chalk and add his. He wrote, "A mistake will not define you. Get back up and keep going."
This report has been updated from earlier versions to correct the name of His Hope's treasurer.

 DENTON — On Tuesday, The Caroline County Commissioners enacted a legislative bill on establishing a fund to receive payments of compensatory preservation contributions to Caroline County when solar energy systems are developed on a parcel of land identified as Class 1 or 2 soils.The county has discussed this bill in workshops since September. After many adjustments to logistical wording of the bill, the county passed the legislation.
"It is earmarked for an additional contribution to the Maryland Ag Land Preservation Fund, which is used to purchase Ag Land Preservation easements on existing farmland," Breeding said. The county is happy to have the bill done, during the commissioners meeting Breeding thanked all working parties of Caroline County for their contributions to the bill.
"It's been a long process. It's been a lot of nuance details that we had to work through, and it feels good that we've been able to to get this accomplished, and we look forward to preserving the agricultural heritage of Caroline County," Breeding said.

title: Talbot County Passes DAF Restrictions
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County passes DAF restrictions

 July 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council passed new regulations on food processing residuals Tuesday.County leaders said the approved legislation helps Talbot fall in line with neighboring counties on restricting the residuals, also referred to as dissolved air flotation, or DAF, materials.
The materials often come in the form of animal waste from food processing, which then can be spread as fertilizer. State rules took effect last summer cracking down on DAF residuals, but some counties have since enacted local legislation to quell further resident concerns.
Jurisdictions like Caroline County saw tense debate over the matter. Many Caroline County residents complained of noxious odors from operations storing food processing residuals in open-top storage containers. Last year, Caroline County banned the open-top method.
Similarly, Talbot's legislation requires closed-top storage of food processing residuals. In addition to the open-top storage ban, Talbot's regulations require the storage applicant to:
Receive site plan approval from the county.Obtain an approved nutrient management plan from the state.Remain at least 500 feet from any residential property lines. If all affected property owners consent to a setback reduction, it can be decreased as far as 200 feet.
"We certainly don't want to be the only jurisdiction on the Shore that neglects to regulate this material," County Council Vice President Pete Lesher said.
Lesher, Council President Chuck Callahan and council members Lynn Mielke and Dave Stepp voted in favor of the legislation. Keasha Haythe, who was absent from Tuesday's meeting, did not vote.
Talbot's Planning Commission and planning officers Brennan Tarleton and Bryce Yelton ironed out the specifics of the regulations since it was drafted last year. Lesher thanked them for their efforts.
"This is one of the more technical issues that we've dealt with," Lesher said, "and I just want to express my appreciation for the staff and for the Planning Commission in working out the details of this."

title: Eastern Shore Legislators Push for Gov. Moore to Veto Solar Bill
author: Konner Metz
content:
Eastern Shore legislators push for Gov. Moore to veto solar bill

 May 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 626
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Eastern Shore legislators, House Republicans and agricultural advocacy groups in Maryland are making one last effort to nix controversial solar energy legislation by asking for a veto from Gov. Wes Moore.Senate Bill 931, the Renewable Energy Certainty Act, was passed by the General Assembly in April. It aims to increase the state's solar generation by streamlining the regulatory process for solar projects. Fencing, setback and vegetation requirements would be standardized.
House Republicans and the Eastern Shore Delegation both wrote letters to the governor urging him to veto the bill. While Moore (D) hasn't publicly signaled whether or not he's considering a veto, some believe it could be in play given he hasn't yet signed the legislation.
"I've heard it is possible," said Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) in an interview Wednesday. "I'm hopeful that he would see the opportunity and the wisdom and just say, 'No, not yet.'"
Qualms with the solar legislation largely relate to a reduction in the control local governments would have over solar project approvals, and the increase in Public Service Commission authority.
The legislation outlines a cap on how much land the Maryland Public Service Commission can grant to solar projects in each county — 5% of land designated for agriculture and forests.
Republicans attempted but failed during session to lower that cap.
Del. Chris Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said Thursday that Eastern Shore counties could have thousands of acres up for solar development even with the 5% cap.
At a legislative wrap-up discussion in Easton Wednesday, Mautz said solar interests came into Annapolis and "cleared the decks."
"They wanted to set up their own regulatory system, they wanted to set up their own siting system," he said. "And they wanted to run this through the Public Service Commission."
"It puts an X on the Eastern Shore," Mautz added. "We are the prime target for solar investment."
The Chesapeake Climate Action Network, an environmental nonprofit that's one of the bill's many advocate groups, encouraged supporters to contact Moore's office and lobby for no veto. Brittany Baker, the organization's Maryland director, said rumors of a veto were floating.
"The rumor mill was churning, and no one had a concrete answer here or there," Baker said.
Baker said in addition to streamlining processes that otherwise vary greatly across the state, the bill is set to codify best practices. And it could help local farmers who are looking to remain economically viable, she said.
"It provides another way for people to be able to stay on their farms and make revenue," Baker said.
PUSH TO VETO
The governor's office didn't comment specifically on whether Moore is considering a veto, but did provide a statement.
"As Governor Moore reviews the hundreds of bills put forward this session, he will continue to work with the State Legislature, local leaders, and all partners involved to ensure that we are signing legislation that will make Maryland safer, more affordable, more competitive, and the state that serves," the statement read.
Baker said despite rumors, the Chesapeake Climate Action Network believes Senate Bill 931 will become law.
"We're pretty sure at this point that the governor will not be vetoing this bill," she said.
Mautz acknowledged a veto is a tricky, party-line situation. He said it would be messy, but "less messy" than what happens down the line if the bill becomes law.
"For the governor to veto it, he's going to cross his own party," Mautz said. "He's going to cross some of his own advocates. It's going to be extremely controversial."
Adams acknowledged that vetoes are rare. But he said the bill not yet being signed may signal "at the minimum, that the governor's paying attention."
If Moore doesn't sign the Renewable Energy Certainty Act by May 27, it automatically becomes law. The governor's next slate of bill signings is scheduled for May 20.

title: Talbot Planning Commission Sends DAF Legislation to County Council
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot Planning Commission sends DAF legislation to County Council

 April 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 380
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council will soon be considering new restrictions on the storage of food processing residuals.Wednesday, the Talbot County Planning Commission unanimously voted to send a piece of legislation up to the council, deeming it consistent with the county's comprehensive plan.
The legislation aims to help Talbot County fall in line with neighboring counties on restricting the residuals, which are animal waste from food processing that are often applied to farmland as fertilizer.
Under state law, the residuals cannot be applied to land between Dec. 15 and March 1, requiring them to be stored during the winter months.
Last year, Caroline County restricted storage of food processing residuals, often referred to as dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals. It came amid significant resident complaints of the noxious odors and bugs that stemmed from farming operations keeping the product in open storage tanks.
Talbot's legislation would ban open-top storage of DAF or food processing residuals. Closed-top storage would be permitted provided it follows the following conditions, among others:
The storage applicant receives site plan approval from the county.The applicant has an approved nutrient management plan from the state.The applicant has at least a 500-foot setback from residential properties, or at least a 200-foot setback if all affected property owners consent.The applicant applies the materials on the same property where they are being stored.The applicant stores and applies the materials in a permitted zoning district.
The legislation would not ban storage of food processing residuals in a temporary storage unit — such as a "mobile, closed container" — near where they are being applied. Such temporary storage would be capped at 90 days.
Before the commission approved the legislation, the body set forth a few minor conditions to be amended.
"The one thing that we do want to make sure is that we exempt food processing residuals that are used for livestock feed," commission member Chip Councell said.
Bryce Yelton, assistant planning officer, said that would be an easy amendment to make, simply by adjusting the definition for food processing residuals in the legislation.
Councell added that the county discussed the DAF legislation with the Talbot County Farm Bureau last August. The farm bureau was supportive, he said.
While the commission is recommending approval to the County Council, the bill will still require a council vote to be enacted.

title: Caroline County Worried Solar Concerns Will Grow Bigger if Proposed Bills Are Passed
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County worried solar concerns will grow bigger if proposed bills are passed

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 544
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Denton — Proposed House Bill 1036 and Senate Bill 931 have been a discussion for Caroline County Commissioners since the state's legislative session began in January.According to Maryland General Assembly website, the proposed bills state, "Altering the factors the Public Service Commission must consider before taking final action on a certificate of public convenience and necessity; establishing certain requirements for the construction of a certain solar energy generating station or energy storage device."
While at legislative sessions last week, Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding and Vice President Larry Porter spoke to oppose the proposed bills, stating they did not provide enough authority over solar development to local jurisdictions.
"I think there were some valuable testimonies on both sides," Porter said. "Since some that time, we have received proposed amendments to the bill. My guess is we will receive some relief in some taxation and commissioning area, but I'm not sure they are going to give up siting authority."
The state has been pushing renewable energy in all counties in the state. To maintain some local autonomy over the effort, counties have created acre moratoriums and location ordinances for solar development.
Caroline County currently has a 2,000-acre moratorium in place.
The commissioners' concern about the proposed bill is the lack of control in the siting of solar in the county.
"I'm gonna break some news here, I think they drafted this bill with a total give away to the solar companies," Breeding said. "To shift the starting point completely in the favor of the solar companies, that's just speculation on my part."
"I think we going to get hosed, and we are getting hosed actively right now with the amendments," he said. "We're gonna walk away thinking we've gotten something out of the deal, but we still are gonna get preempted by the state as far as siting."
Caroline County has personally experienced an issue with siting regulations for a solar company wanting to set up a solar facility in an area in the county where solar is not allowed.
Chaberton Solar requested to put solar panels down in a residentially zoned area, where such developments are prohibited by the county.
The applicant was informed by the county prior to submitting its application that it did not have a complete site plan and had omitted some necessary details from the application in addition to the zoning violation, Barroll said.
The county filed an intervention with a public utility law judge in December stating the application was not complete as a result of these factors, but other entities attested that Chaberton met all the requirements to construct the planned solar facility.
The Power Plant Research Program of the state's Department of Natural Resources filed a paper that said it had reviewed the application and the application was complete. In December, the public utility judge pushed the application through to the next stage.
The county has since taken this solar case to court to block the planting of solar in the restricted area.
The county is concerned if proposed house bill 1036 and senate bill 931 are filed, they will face similar issues with siting as they face with Chaberton Solar.
"Everyone that was in that hearing room testifying against that bill was saying 'Do not stripe the counties of local zoning authority' and that message fell on deaf ears."

title: Caroline County Commissioners Discuss Multiple Solar Issues
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County Commissioners discuss multiple solar issues

 February 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 486
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Denton — At their meeting Tuesday, The Caroline County Commissioners discussed a solar application issue that led to the county intervening.An application for a 3.0 milliwatt solar facility near Federalsburg, filed by Chaberton Solar Pahar LLC, does not meet requirements laid out by the county, County Attorney Stewart Barroll said at the meeting. The company has requested to put solar panels down in a residentially zoned area where such developments are prohibited by the county, the commissioners said.
Barroll said the applicant had been informed by the county prior to submitting the application that it did not have a complete site plan and had omitted some necessary details from the application in addition to the zoning violation.
The county filed an intervention with a public utility law judge stating the application was not complete as a result of these factors, Barroll said.
But other entities attested that Chaberton met all the requirements to construct the planned solar facility.
Barroll said the Power Plant Research Program of the state's Department of Natural Resources filed a paper that said it had reviewed the application and the application was complete. In December, the public utility judge pushed the application through to the next stage.
"So the department of natural resources came in and over said a project that we said wasn't complete was complete," Caroline County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said.
"We're getting steam rolled by the state," Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding added.
Next steps in the application process will include public hearings, which the commissioners have been invited to, Barroll said.
The Caroline County commissioners are concerned about the precedent this case may set for future solar applications, the commissioners said Tuesday.
"We have to draw the line somewhere," Porter said.
At the meeting, the commissioners also discussed another solar application in which they will be intervening.
An approximately 40-acre solar facility to be constructed on a farm near Greensboro does not meet a new setback regulation the county implemented, requiring a 200-foot setback from adjoining properties. The commissioners said they would not oppose the project, which meets all other county requirements, should that issue be remedied.
Along with the state's role in solar applications, the commissioner voiced anxieties about legislation making its way through the General Assembly.
The county also has concern about proposed Senate Bill 931, which would prohibit a county from enacting zoning laws or adopting regulations restricting or prohibiting the construction or operation of ground-mounted solar systems or facilities.
The county currently has a 2,000 acre moratorium in place for solar development, which is being neared but has not yet been met.
This proposed bill would put the county in another situation where legislation the county has enacted, including an acreage moratorium on solar development, could be overruled by state agencies, the commissioners said.
"We're gonna have to fight every application. We're gonna spend time and money fighting every application, and we're probably gonna get steam rolled every time, that's the way its looking," Breeding said.

title: As Pressures to Increase Solar Mount, Caroline County Examines Options to Hold Its Ground
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
As pressures to increase solar mount, Caroline County examines options to hold its ground

 December 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 770
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — During a discussion of solar policy Tuesday morning, the Caroline County commissioners concluded that legal action might be necessary to get the state and the county to see eye-to-eye."I don't know if there's going to be any other avenue that we're going to go except to go to court," Caroline County Commissioner Vice President Larry Porter said. "I think that's probably where we're going to end up."
These comments were made during a discussion on the Hobbs Road solar project, a 15-acre project proposed by Nexamp Solar LLC to put solar panels on a field that is no longer usable for farming. The commissioners approved a measure Tuesday that gives Nexamp the option to lease the land, which was formerly used as a landfill.
But the commissioners were clear that despite the approval of this project, their general stance on solar development in the area had not changed.
"We know there's been a lot of concern and conversation in the community about solar projects, and we want to make it clear that the Commissioners hear you," The Caroline County government stated in a Facebook post prior to the meeting.
"They do not want to see our county overrun with solar farms. However, they also have to follow state regulations that require a certain amount of land to be used for renewable energy production," the post said. "By allowing this solar project on the Hobbs Road site, the Commissioners have actually preserved 15 acres of prime agricultural land that could have been used for this project instead."
After the commissioner's vote, Porter addressed concerns voiced by residents in the comment section of the county's post.
"There's been a good amount of discussion on Facebook about our participation in this," Porter said. "We've been called sell-outs and everything else because people for some reason think that we're in favor of this. I don't think there's just been any county that's fought harder against covering farmland with solar panels than Carolina County."
THE COUNTY'S STANCEThe county has a 2,000-acre moratorium for solar development in place, which is facing pressure as the state looks to expand solar energy use in the coming years to meet 100% clean energy goals by 2040.
In the past, the commissioners have voiced concerns that solar development threatens the area's rural nature and takes available land away from agricultural practices.
Porter mentioned throughout the Tuesday meeting that farmers receive offers from solar companies in their mail weekly offering large sums of money to use their land to place solar panels.
"I think the dilemma that we find ourselves in, I know everyone has the right of the farmer to do with his land what he wants," Porter said. "When someone comes in and says, 'we're going to make you this offer, and you have an opportunity to make money on your own land.' It's very difficult for us to sit up here and say, 'No, you can't.'"
Steve Kline, president and CEO of Eastern Shore Land Conservancy, attended the meeting on Tuesday and spoke with the commissioners on a plan that Talbot and Queen Anne's counties follow that he said could be beneficial to Caroline County.
"What ESLC encourages Caroline County to adopt is a per-acre mitigation fee," Kline said. "... In Talbot, the mitigation fee is based on Maryland ag land preservation foundation fair market appraisal averages. In Queen Anne's County, the system assesses a half percent transfer tax on projects converting farmland to solar, and all of those funds are allocated for land preservation projects.
"... While both counties have adopted a different approach, both counties use substantially all of their fees on land conservation. The ESLC strongly believes the best way to protect agricultural land against all the threats it faces is permanent conservations like the ones we write," Kline said.
Del. Jeff Ghrist (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) made a suggestion that all nine Eastern Shore counties fight together instead of separately to get communities on board with their plans to limit solar development. This, he said, will lend itself to a better outcome when it's time for legal action.
"Talbot County is going to host a meeting with all nine counties to talk about, and I think ahead of this meeting, we need to make sure that all nine counties are sharing whatever zoning laws that you all have already passed, and hopefully intend on enforcing. If there's some consistency with a lot of our zoning, as consistent we can possibly be, it's gonna be a lot easier to enforce it. It's gotta be a lot easier to message it to the public. And if you guys do it, it'll be easier to defend in court."

title: Dorchester County Council passes solar legislation, says more may be coming
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County Council passes solar legislation, says more may be coming

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 680
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In a 3-2 vote, the Dorchester County Council passed a bill that addresses setbacks and buffers, ownership, and decommissioning plans for accessory, small scale and utility scale solar energy systems.After the bill was passed at a meeting on Nov. 4, Council President Lenny Pfeffer said this is a start for solar legislation in the county.
"Laws can be amended and modified," he said. "But if we don't do something now, before the start of the General Assembly, we could be facing much worse without any safeguards in place."
Council members Rob Kramer and William Nichols voted against the bill. Council member Ricky Travers, Council Vice President Mike Detmer and Pfeffer voted in favor of it.
Under the new bill, solar developments located off scenic byways will need to be set back 100 feet from all property lines, and developments that are not located off of scenic byways will need to be set back 75 feet. Requirements regarding vegetative buffers, perimeter fencing, topsoil and site plans are also in the legislation.
The bill defines who the owners of a solar site are. Pfeffer said in an interview with the Star Democrat in September that the owners of the property and the operator of the solar development would both be considered the owner.
The bill was reintroduced in September after getting tabled in March. In the reintroduced bill, a section was added regarding decommissioning solar projects. Per the legislation, a decommissioning plan will need to be submitted and approved by the county prior to the building permit application.
In the September interview, Pfeffer said the bill was tabled so the council could wait for state solar legislation to go into affect and make sure the county was in line with it.
At the meeting Nov. 4, residents thanked the council for their efforts and shared concerns that the county bill doesn't do enough to restrict solar development.
The reintroduced bill left out a section in the original proposed bill that put a cap on how many aggregate acres of the county can house utility-scale solar energy systems.
Beth Hill said although she feels the bill is a step in the right direction, she thinks there needs to be a cap on the number of acres in the county that can be used for solar development.
"Other counties around us do have caps," she said, mentioning Caroline County, which has a 2,000-acre cap on total rural land available for solar development.
Tracy Whitby-Fairall, who attended a town hall on the subject that Detmer hosted the previous week, said she recognized the county's efforts. She called the bill a "good foundation for a strong framework" for the county.
"I think there are some things that could be improved," she said, later adding, "I hope this isn't the end of the legislation. I hope this is the beginning."
Erick Windsor, who asked the council to vote against the bill, talked about the county's history of thriving tomato, dairy and lumber industries, which are now gone. He said that large solar operations take land away from grain farming.
"And this is going to affect all the other industries in this county that work around grain farming, like chicken farming," he said. "So you hurt the chicken farmers and you're going to hurt the industry in Hurlock that processes all this stuff."
Windsor said more restrictions need to be put on solar so it doesn't "decimate" the north part of the county.
Detmer said the bill — especially the decommissioning component — is "crucial" to have at the county level before the Maryland General Assembly session begins in January. He talked about the possibility of additional legislation coming down from the state.
"The Wild West of solar that we are in right now, I'm very bothered by it," he said. "I think we have to plant our flag here in this place that we're ready to go right now. If we don't act tonight, the law's not going to be in place when the session starts."
Detmer said this isn't the end of creating legislation around solar, but action needs to be taken now.
"We've got to put the seatbelt on," he said.

title: Talbot County Looks into Restrictions on Food Processing Residuals
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County looks into restrictions on food processing residuals

 September 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 370
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Restrictions on the storage of food processing residuals are in the works for Talbot County.The county's Planning Commission and County Council held a preliminary work session Tuesday to discuss regulations for the residuals, which are animal waste from the food processing process.
Earlier this month, Caroline County passed a bill to restrict the storage of the residuals, which are often referred to as dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals. It came amid significant resident complaints of the noxious odors and bugs that stemmed from farming operations keeping the product in storage tanks.
Talbot County is looking to the neighboring county and hoping to be proactive.
"We think we need to get ahead of it," Planning Commission Vice Chairman Chip Councell said. He noted that Caroline and Wicomico counties were "behind the eight ball" in enacting legislation.
Councell said he met with the Talbot County Farm Bureau regarding potential restrictions.
"I think they would like to see some restrictions put on it, one being that any type of food residuals storage would have to be enclosed, so it couldn't be open-air," Councell said. "The storage of it would have to be used in that agricultural operation. A farmer couldn't store it for everybody in the neighborhood. He could store it for his operation only, so there wouldn't be commercial storage."
Councell clarified the county would focus on the storage of the residuals, not the land application. State legislation that went into effect July 1 created a formal permitting process for the usage of food processing residuals.
"There's a few bad actors out there that, frankly, I think see profit potential with handling the material," said Alan Girard, advocacy director at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, during Tuesday's meeting.
While Wicomico County banned the storage of residuals, temporary storage for 45 days is allowed. In Caroline County, storage is allowed once a permit is acquired, as long as the storage tank has a closed top.
Councell said the 45-day allowance may be adjusted once the legislation begins to be drafted.
"I think 45 days might be a little bit tight," Councell said.
At the end of the work session, Planning and Zoning Director Brennan Tarleton said discussion of potential DAF legislation will be added to the Planning Commission's agenda in November.

title: Residual Bill Passed by Caroline County Commissioners
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Residual bill passed by Caroline County Commissioners

 September 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News

 DENTON — On Tuesday morning, the Caroline County Commissioners voted to approve the long-discussed bill that would establish county regulations for storing food processing residuals, animal waste from the food processing process.These residuals, particularly dissolved air floatation, or DAF, residuals have been the topic of several heated discussions in the county since residents began raising health complaints and environmental concerns over how the material was being stored by some in the county late last year.
The county came up with a permitting system. There will be a universal permit requirement in order to store food processing residuals. It creates limitations on how residuals can be stored and permits the county to fine violators.
It would require that those storing the material use closed-top containers, going a step further than recently passed state legislation.
Attorney Stewart Barroll said commissioners and Caroline County staff had heard "voluminous" public comments that have been taken into account.
Prior to voting, two amendments were approved by commissioners involving distances from the storage containers.
Commissioner Franklin Bartz said he would prefer the storage distance and an occupied dwelling be increased to 2,000 feet measured horizontally rather than the 1,250-foot distance that was in the bill.
After discussion, the commissioners unanimously voted to approve the change.
Commissioner J. Travis Breeding requested a second amendment that would require the storage not to be within 500 feet of a well. This way, it would allow property owners to move wells somewhere else on their property to be 500 feet away from stored residuals to not contaminate water sources.
Commissioner Larry Porter brought up the discussion of postponing voting on the act until the Maryland Department of Agriculture shares their regulations. The vote had been postponed at the prior two meetings so the commissioners could review the proposed amendments to the legislation.
Breeding said there would not be a need to postpone for regulation changes because commissioners are acting well within the parameters of Maryland statue.
"There's only so much that the Department of Agriculture can do," Breeding said. "Everything that we have done inside of this legislature is not in conflict with the statue that the state has."
The bill was unanimously approved by the commissioners and has been enacted into the county law.

title: Solar Energy Discussed at MACo Summer Conference
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Solar energy discussed at MACo Summer Conference

 August 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 543
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OCEAN CITY — Solar energy was one topic of discussion that captured the attention of multiple Mid-Shore counties at the Maryland Association of Counties Summer Conference.Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding said solar energy came up a lot at the four-day conference, which went from Aug. 14 to Aug. 17 in Ocean City. Breeding said there are elected officials from different Maryland counties who feel that solar lobbyists are pushing the state to take away local authority when it comes to where solar energy system sites can go and how close those sites can be from roads and neighboring structures.
Caroline County currently has a 2,000-acre cap on solar projects. Once that limit is reached, the county will stop permitting new solar energy system projects on county land, Breeding said.
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said his fellow council member Ricky Travers asked about solar site acreage caps in a MACo session with the Maryland Public Service Commission. Specifically, Travers asked about how the commission feels about these caps.
Pfeffer said that after the session, the Dorchester County Council members had a conversation with Public Service Commissioner Kumar Barve, and the council was able to explain its concerns about increasing solar sites in the county. Pfeffer said the only part of the county that can host these sites is the north part of the county, and that is where the council hopes to grow the county's tax base.
"They were very interested and didn't realize some of the demographics and logistics of Dorchester County," Pfeffer said about the Public Service Commission. "So I'm hoping that is successful for us, they'll take a look at it and they won't establish any legislation that's one-size-fits-all."
Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher called the conference one of the best he's been to. He said it ran smoothly and was well put together.
Breeding said that MACo's summer and winter conferences give Maryland counties an opportunity to get together, discuss and "try to come up with a unified message."
"It was a good conference," Breeding said. "We got to talk to all of our partners in other counties, bounce ideas off of them, discuss problems and issues that we're all facing and kind of brainstorm on how to resolve those issues."
Pfeffer, who is the secretary of MACo this year, said that all counties have problems.
Pfeffer said the opportunity to discuss these common problems, no matter how many zeros come after them, can benefit each county.
Breeding said he is taking some ideas on solar power back home to Caroline County this year. He talked about the systems that Talbot and Queen Anne's counties have in place, including Talbot County's point system that is used to help preserve prime farmland for farming and determine where solar sites can go.
Lesher said he didn't attend the solar session at MACo, but said the Talbot County Council tackled legislation dealing with solar energy sites last year when it put the point system in place.
"Which I think is model legislation for other rural jurisdictions," he said. "Right now we're in the testing period for this. Will this hold up? Will this have the desired impact of preserving farmland and channeling solar toward areas where we have more marginal soils that are not the highest priority for cropland?"

title: Public Weighs in on Emergency Food Processing Residual Bill
author: Tom McCall
content:
Public weighs in on emergency food processing residual bill

 August 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 561

 Read News Document

 An earlier version of this story contained incorrect information about the status of the bill. The commissioners did not vote on the bill Tuesday.DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners held a public hearing on a controversial bill concerning the permitting of food processing residuals Aug. 6.
If the bill is passed after the commissioners' third hearing on Aug. 20, storing these residuals in Caroline County would require a permit. The bill also allows for inspection and civil or criminal penalties if a storage site is found to be in violation.
"This is not banning storage of food processing residuals," Commissioner Larry Porter said. "If someone feels strongly about using it as a soil amendment and wants to store it, they can come in and apply once these regulations are set."
The bill requires the use of closed-top storage tanks for food processing residuals, going a step further than state regulations passed during this year's General Assembly. House Bill 991, which took effect July 1, created a state permitting process under the Maryland Department of Agriculture for the use, storing and hauling of the residuals.
Caroline County's bill is the latest development in what has been months of packed public hearings and extended moratoriums on residual storage tanks. For county commissioners, the main hurdle has been cracking down on a few "bad actors" that store the residuals irresponsibly.
The bill garnered mixed reviews from Caroline County residents, environmental experts and representatives of the poultry industry at prior public hearings. Several took to the podium Aug. 6 to voice their opposition or support of the legislation.
Mike Woodward, the owner of a Ridgely farm right next to an open-top residual storage facility, voiced support for the bill.
"I am 400 yards from the tank itself... We have a lot of issues with flies. The odor is atrocious at times," Woodward said. "We had a vet come out. We were having trouble with our horses. Their eyes were watering and runny and nasty. We couldn't figure out what was going on with them. The vet checked them out and the flies were laying larvae inside their eyes."
Brad Sears, a Ridgely commissioner, said, "I come before you on behalf of the Town of Ridgely in support of the emergency legislative bill. I offer this testimony to advocate for the men, women and children, who live, work and attend school and play within the town limits. We have concern because of improper storage of FPR (food processing residuals) poses well documented threats to human life, health and wellbeing."
He said open-top containers do nothing to limit "odors, the exposure to vectors, the airborne bacteria and viruses."
Holly Porter, executive director of the Delmarva Chicken Association, has been a vocal opponent of the county's bill in prior public hearings. She spoke again in opposition of the legislation on Tuesday.
"I really and truly would like the commissioners to consider some way of grandfathering in the farmers who are utilizing and storing food processing residuals for years without the complaints we have had in the past," she said. "If we do not do that, we are impacting other farmers who are becoming collateral damage because of one unfortunately bad actor."
Responding to Holly Porter's comments, Larry Porter said, "Grandfathering in, unfortunately would have to include grandfathering in what Miss. Porter referred to as the 'bad actor.' ... you can't enforce laws on some people and not all people."
