title: Food Processing Residuals Bill Set for Public Hearing
author: Konner Metz
content:
Food processing residuals bill set for public hearing

 July 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 671
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — New Caroline County legislation that aims to mitigate irresponsible storage of food processing residuals is set for a public hearing in early August.On July 9, the Caroline County Commissioners introduced an emergency bill that will create a permit process in order to store food processing residuals. It creates limitations on how residuals can be stored and permits the county to fine violators.
If passed, it would require closed-top storage tanks, going a step further than state regulations passed during this year's General Assembly. House Bill 991, which took effect July 1, created a state permitting process under the Maryland Department of Agriculture for the use, storing and hauling of the residuals.
"You should also bear in mind, MDA is not renowned for its enforcement," County Attorney Stewart Barroll, who drafted the bill, said at a July 10 Planning Commission meeting. "And this is a county. We can't enforce MDA regulations. We can enforce county ordinances. And so having it in here is belt and suspenders."
The Planning Commission, made up of five members including County Commissioner Travis Breeding, narrowly passed a favorable recommendation for the legislation on July 10. Breeding and Chair Jeff Jackson voted yes, Vice Chair Hannah Cawley voted no, and commission member Keith Bilbrough abstained. Member Roger McKnight was not present.
"In my personal opinion, the state has done an excellent job putting something together," Cawley said. "And if it were up to me … I'd like to see how far the state gets with theirs and then make amendments on the county level."
Bilbrough asked for more time and information, adding he wasn't "necessarily opposed."
After the favorable vote, the bill is set for a public hearing on Aug. 6 at 9:15 a.m. in the Denton Health & Public Services Building.
In that same building in January, the county commissioners heard from a record crowd of more than 150 people on the storage of dissolved air floatation residuals, a type of food processing residual. That and subsequent meetings led the county to place and later extend moratoriums on the storage of residuals. The moratoriums last until this fall but may be replaced by the permit bill at hand.
Three new amendments to the legislation were added during the July 10 Planning Commission meeting: food processing residuals cannot be mixed with other substances in storage containers, the county will no longer request an applicant's nutrient management plan, and language concerning temporary storage is adjusted to "mirror" state regulations.
The Planning Commission heard opposing views from local industry and environmental leaders.
Holly Porter, executive director of the Delmarva Chicken Association, asked the planning commission to not vote favorably. She believes the county bill is "25 pages of confusion" and will negatively impact farmers and businesses who responsibly store food processing residuals.
"I have repeatedly been told that Caroline County does not have the resources to enforce the bad actor that's out there, and yet now we have the resources to create a permitting scheme, that again, repeats and is more onerous than the state's," Porter said. "Caroline County has the ability to make text amendments right here with the zoning table of use regulations."
Matt Pluta, Choptank riverkeeper for ShoreRivers, and Alan Girard, Eastern Shore director of the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, each spoke in support of the bill.
"I don't think the size of the bill really matters," Pluta said. "I think it's how effective the bill is … I do think this bill does a really good job of making sure the county is taking control of what they are responsible for."
Girard questioned if the fines outlined in the legislation — $500 for a first offense and $1,000 for a subsequent one — were too relaxed.
While the planning commission was split on whether to recommend the amended bill, Breeding said the commissioners agree on the need to crack down on open-top storage tanks.
"The sentiment of the commissioners is it needs to be closed-top storage," Breeding said. "Because there's nowhere in this county that you're not going to store this stuff and have an adverse effect on a neighbor."

title: Caroline Commissioners Discuss Landfill, Solar Batteries
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline commissioners discuss landfill, solar batteries

 May 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Life 
 
 568
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At their May 7 meeting, the Caroline County Commissioners extended a moratorium on solar array batteries and finalized an agreement to retain the regional landfill for another 18 years.Caroline County has agreed to 2042 being the end of life for its landfill. Mid-shore II Regional Landfill is governed by a four-county agreement between Queen Anne's, Kent, Talbot and Caroline counties.
In the late 1980s, due to new federal regulations, the counties had to close their landfills and replace them with new landfills. In response to this new regulation, Talbot, Caroline and Queen Anne's counties engaged with MES to form a partnership where each county would take turns hosting a landfill for a 20-year term. Kent County later joined that partnership.
Caroline County is hosting the current landfill and, under the original arrangement, would be off the hook at the end of 2030 when Queen Anne's County would take over the responsibility of host. However, the partnering counties have agreed to allow the landfill to stay in Caroline County for 12 years longer than initially planned.
Dan Fox, deputy administrator, said the county will receive a revenue increase of around $12.3 million over the duration of the extended agreement. The counties agreed on a $3 per ton post fee until 2030. In 2031 it will rise to $6.
"That is a big number as far as our budget," Fox said.
Commissioner Larry Porter said the increased revenue will be helpful as he looks to the future of Caroline County's finances.
"The tipping point is knowing what is coming down the road to the county from a financial standpoint. The Blueprint numbers for education, the numbers for the budget projections that will start this fiscal year from the state," Porter said. "It has been our goal to have maintained property tax rates. We have done this for eight years and are going to do it again this year. Beyond that we cannot control the additional things that will be mandated by the state of Maryland. To turn away the opportunity to generate revenue without raising property tax rate is something we have to consider."
The next action agenda item was solar energy batteries and the commissioners' belief that they are dangerous.
The commissioners extended a moratorium on the batteries until March 31, 2025. Explaining this decision, they said that the local fire departments and first responders are not equipped and staffed to safely deal with these energy storage systems were they to catch on fire.
"When the electric is generated from the solar panels, if it is not distributed to the grid, it is stored in batteries that are then stored in, like, large storage containers," Porter said. "How would it be addressed if those storage facilities were malfunctioning and caught on fire?"
He said the moratorium will remain in place until these batteries can safely be put in place.
During public comments, James Baker brought up the issue of what to do with a solar energy battery at the end of its 20 year life cycle. He said he thought it would cost taxpayers.
At the May 7 meeting, the commissioners also made two proclamations. The first was to Ken Eaton and Mark Kerzener, who represented the Mid-Shore chapter of A Brotherhood Against Totalitarian Enactments of Maryland. The commissioners proclaimed May a month for motorcycle safety and awareness.
The other proclamation went to Derek Simmons, superintendent of Caroline County Public Schools. It was a proclamation for teacher appreciation month.

title: Caroline Commissioners Hear Options for Landfill After 2030
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Caroline commissioners hear options for landfill after 2030

 April 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 785
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County could remain the host of the regional landfill for 12 years longer than originally planned.At a Caroline County Commissioners meeting Tuesday morning, Queen Anne's County Administrator Todd Mohn, CPA and Queen Anne's County Consultant Joe Zimmerman and Queen Anne's County Commissioner James Moran came to speak about the possibility of using the Mid-Shore II Regional Landfill in Ridgely through 2042 rather than building a new landfill in Queen Anne's County for 2031.
During their presentation, Mohn said Maryland Environmental Service has been working with county administrators to evaluate the future of Mid-Shore II, and it has concluded that the landfill could "easily provide service" to the citizens of the region through approximately 2042.
The Mid-Shore II landfill, which was opened in 2011, provides services to Talbot, Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties.
Mohn explained that in the late 1980s, due to new federal regulations, the counties had to close their landfills and and replace them with new landfills. In response to this new regulation, Talbot, Caroline and Queen Anne's counties engaged with MES to form a partnership where each county would take turns hosting a landfill for a 20-year term. Kent County later joined that partnership.
Caroline County is hosting the current landfill and, under the original arrangement, would be off the hook at the end of 2030 when Queen Anne's County would take over the responsibility of host. However, if the partnering counties agreed, they could instead extend the lifetime of Caroline County's landfill.
During the presentation, Mohn listed reasons why Queen Anne's County feels this option makes sense. For Caroline County, he said that this option would provide economic stability for Ridgely businesses and that the county would get a host fee for the extension of service.
He said the option would also maximize the value of public infrastructure, defer liability for debt to construct a new landfill, maintain shorter haul routes for Talbot County and avoid the cost of a transfer operation.
Moran said landfills are at a premium.
"We want to maximize that," he said about the space in each landfill. "And if this (provides) us with an extra 30 years of life that we didn't have coming into this 80-year deal, then that's a good thing for the environment, it's a good thing for the Eastern Shore."
If this proposal moves forward, all of the partnering counties would need to come to an agreement on a modified arrangement, including the host fee for Caroline County.
At the meeting, Zimmerman presented three options for host fees and annual tipping fee increases for the Mid-Shore II landfill:
A host fee of $2 per ton of waste growing to $4 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.15% in tipping fees.A host fee of $3 per ton of waste growing to $5 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.35% in tipping fees.A host fee of $4 per ton of waste growing to $6 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.5% in tipping fees.
"We think these are achievable options," Zimmerman said about the three options. "It's really the question of how much risk the counties want to take on in terms of their competitive posture."
He said that historically, tipping fees have, on average, annually increased by 1.42%.
Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding said he has made it clear to MES that he agrees with keeping the landfill operating in Caroline County for environmental and economic reasons, but he would like to make sure the county retains "any of the savings associated with the extension of the landfill."
He said the county's residents are the ones burdened with the affects of the landfill operations, including truck traffic and bad smells from time to time.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter spoke about the impact of MES operations on the county.
He said that although this proposal is an opportunity to generate more revenue without raising property taxes, having the landfill in the county has affected the condition of the roads where trash is being driven, including trash left on those roads. He said the extension of the landfill's services would be a hard sell to the public.
"For me, anything that we do is going to have to involve MES stepping up to the plate and fulfilling what I think the obligations and responsibilities are," he said, adding that roads would be part of that obligation, in his mind.
Porter asked the presenters if it appears that the other partnering counties are on board with keeping the landfill in Caroline County and paying a host fee. Mohn said everyone seems to be in agreement.
"The question is, what is that host fee going to be?" Mohn said.
Porter said the county will have a public hearing on this in the future. He did not give a date.

title: Caroline Commissioners hear from record crowd on DAF storage
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Commissioners hear from record crowd on DAF storage

 January 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 1976
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — "Are we the Green Garden County?" Tolbert Rowe asked rhetorically, alluding to Caroline County's longtime nickname.The Caroline County native, businessman and well-known leader wrapped up an hour and a half of public comments to cheers and applause: "At some point, we're going to have to sue somebody, and I say do it, because we're tired of people coming and pooping in our yard and not cleaning up after themselves."
The Caroline County Commissioners heard from Rowe and some two dozen of the more than 150 county residents and visitors who attended a public hearing on DAF residual storage from 6 to 8 p.m. Tuesday, Jan. 23, in the conference room of the Health and Public Services Building in Denton.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter said it was the largest attendance for a public hearing he had seen during his 14-year tenure.
{p class="p1"}The DAF storage issue and how to deal with it began when the commissioners, at their Dec. 12 meeting, heard from property owners who complained about odor and flies believed to be emanating from a DAF residuals storage pit on River Road near Greensboro.
As a result, the commissioners adopted Resolution 2023-025 as a "temporary moratorium on certain use of land or structures for storage of food processing residual and/or DAF residuals in Caroline County" for 60 days, starting Dec. 19.
The moratorium doesn't apply to structures or land used for storage of those residuals prior to Jan. 1, 2023.
Many at the hearing fear the same type of operation is gearing up on the outskirts of Ridgely.
While the standing room only crowd at the public hearing was concerned, upset and seeking answers, they were civil and appreciative of those who testified and the commissioners' efforts to study the issue and decide how to regulate it.
Since that time, the commissioners enacted a 60-day moratorium on new DAF residual storage while they research the issue and decide how to regulate it.
A diverse crowd of farmers and environmentalists, outdoor enthusiasts and parents, business owners and civic leaders, as well as officials from the Maryland Departments and Agriculture and Environment attended the hearing, many of whom filled the hallway outside the conference room.
Deputy County Administrator Daniel Fox narrated a slide show describing the purpose and scope of the hearing and defining the terms.
DAF RESIDUALS DEFINEDDAF, or dissolved air flotation, "is a method used to process wastewater that comes from any food processing plant in which dissolved air is injected into the wastewater. These air bubbles attach to particles, causing them to float to the surface where they can then be removed by a skimming device," Fox read.
However, "DAF Residuals is the semi-solid slurry of small particles of fats, proteins and other fibrous materials that were removed from the skimming process." Much of this material is generated from poultry processing plants on Delmarva, and some comes from industrial and wastewater treatment sludge.
It is DAF residuals and the responsible handling of the byproduct, which comes from outside the county, that prompted many to share their concerns, knowledge and experiences.
Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding opened the hearing.
"I want to be clear: The county has received no formal applications for the storage of DAF," he said. "All storage that has been occurring in the county so far has been undisclosed to us, and it has largely been in repurposed facilities around the county — either former dairy cattle manure bins or other structures that have been repurposed. … It's just been done without our knowledge."
Breeding said the commissioners' intention is "to have a workshop with Maryland Department of Agriculture, Maryland Department of Environment and industry representatives to generate some type of regulations to control the storage, so it doesn't have a negative impact on the county.
"Once those regulations are generated, it will go through the legislative process, which does include public hearings again, so there will be another opportunity for the residents of the county to comment on whatever final decision or final proposal the commissioners come up with."
The commissioners stated public comments will be accepted during the legislative process.
CONCERNS AIREDWhile not naming anyone in particular, several referred to a "bad actor" they wanted held accountable, and they appealed to the commissioners to extend the 60-day moratorium.
Nearly 50 people signed up to testify, but about half said their concerns had been addressed by others who were asked to limit their remarks to three minutes.
Most speaking were concerned with their health — breathing the "stench" emitted from stored DAF residuals, pathogens possibly leeching into well water and waterways, and the increase of flying insects and the possibility of their carrying diseases.
Jean Meyer of Greensboro said she lives adjacent to one of the several farms owned by the "individual that we're talking about tonight" who "got a permit for nothing that he's done."
"We all have shallow wells; (DAF residuals) could contaminate the water," Meyer said. "Who's gonna put in a new well, who's gonna pay for my medical bills, if I should become sick from the runoff?"
An electrician and a former worker in the nuclear field both said they would be cited for noncompliance.
"I work in the nuclear field and … if you blatantly disregard rules and regulations, you get the hammer dropped on you," said Dan Marron of Greensboro.
A case was made by Ridgely Town Commissioner Anthony Casey, who focused primarily on the former Hanover Foods property and "a proposed DAF site a half-mile away from the town limits (that) will affect the entire population of the town, currently at 1,870."
Casey listed how DAF residual storage near the town would have a "crippling effect on the town's culture and economy," including the possible relocation of the Cow Barn Athletic Complex. Also adversely affected would be "every business," Ridgely Elementary School, Ridgely Memorial Park, the Rails to Trails path, Martin Sutton Park and the Caroline Humane Society, among others.
Events such as Ridgely's Winter Festival, the Lions Club's annual Strawberry Festival and the annual district Little League All-Star tournaments would be marred by the odor and increased number of flies, Casey said.
"The town of Ridgely is 100% against DAF storage of any kind," he said, speaking on behalf of the town commissioners, town staff and residents. He urged the county commissioners to "not only approve resolution 2023-025" but to "shut this operation down entirely."
Debbie Bostic, who lives on Peaviner Road across from "the pit where the sludge is supposed to be dumped" on the former Hanover Foods property, said she was worried about the increased heavy truck traffic and pollution of nearby waterways. "We will no longer be able to enjoy the great outdoors," she said.
The 400-member Tuckahoe Equestrian Club was represented by several members, and two running groups who use Tuckahoe State Park for events expressed their concerns.
STATE VS. COUNTY ROLESThe county commissioners and staff distinguished the county's role in regulating DAF residual storage from the state of Maryland's authority.
"Caroline County has no authority to prohibit the application of DAF to farmland," Fox told the audience. However, "MDA and MDE do not regulate the storage of DAF residuals; therefore, Caroline County is not preempted by the State regarding the storage of DAF residuals."
While both Delaware and Virginia require permits for DAF residual storage, Maryland does not, prompting its being trucked into Eastern Shore counties.
"It's a dumping ground, and it's got to stop," Alan Girard said following the meeting. The Eastern Shore director of the Chesapeake Bay Foundation said, "The state needs to step up. The General Assembly has the power to charge (MDE and MDA) to safely regulate this material. And that's what they should do."
Girard and Matt Pluta, Choptank Riverkeeper with ShoreRivers drew attention to the environmental impacts, their remarks eliciting applause and cheers from the audience, composed mostly of rural residents and farmers.
Girard cited examples of DAF residual storage complaints CBF has fielded from other Maryland counties, as well as steps the foundation has taken to get answers from state agencies.
He referred to a University of Maryland report issued in September in which "they say there's no comprehensive public database to track DAF generation, shipment and composition."
Girard said once a year state chemists test "material …. generated from these industrial rendering facilities — I know people have concern with that term; I don't use it lightly."
"So, when it gets in the storage facilities and comingles, and farmers are trying to abide by their nutrient management regs and receive a load of this stuff, what's in it? Nobody knows," he said. "And there's good farmers in the room behind me that are trying to do the right thing. … They try to apply it safely."
Pluta said DAF residuals are "an industrial waste product. … It is generated by facilities that hold discharge permits, but the loophole in the state is that once it's turned over to a hauler or somebody to use on their farm it becomes a soil amendment."
Citing pathogens researchers have found in DAF material, Pluta questioned why DAF isn't regulated by the state. "They have regulations for poultry manure. They even make you register your beehives. Why can't we register DAF?" he said. "Why is the state pushing this on to the counties to manage, when they certainly have the tools to manage it at a state level?"
Girard made a distinction between responsible farmers and those who skirt permitting requirements and regulations.
"We need to make sure that we're backing our farming community, making sure that the bad actors are held accountable, and we can allow agriculture to continue on the Delmarva Peninsula," Girard said.
CALLS FOR CAUTIONDenton resident Holly Porter is executive director of the Delmarva Chicken Association, a trade organization representing the $5 billion industry. She pointed out the "three-legged stool" of the chicken companies, and the chicken growers and grain farmers, many of whom in Caroline County, who use soil amendments.
She said it appeared the county was dealing with a "bad actor."
"We've heard that (DAF residuals) are a registered soil amendment by the Maryland Department of Agriculture and by the state chemists. These are ag products," she said.
Disputing the representation of DAF residuals as "industrial" products, she asked, "What other industrial item is stored? That would be called commercial fertilizer, which is also made in an industrial site, is an ag product and is used on farm fields as well."
Cow Barn Events owner Marty Collison is also a poultry farmer.
"This DAF operation would put me out of business," he said. His venue hosts indoor and outdoor events, including weddings. However, he suggested to the commissioners that science equals solutions.
Collison advised against "knee jerk reactions. Do your homework. Get the data. Know what is out there, what they're spreading. Is it really dangerous? And then make an informed decision, and it may have to be some compromise between the ag community and the events venue community."
Girard advised the commissioners to "pass the moratorium and wait for the state to act, and if they don't act … keep the moratorium in place. We need a statewide solution."
The commissioners stated, "Any property that the County is aware of that is in violation of the moratorium has been issued a cease-and-desist order."
"We are we are working through the court system," Breeding said. "We don't have the ability to just go out and put somebody in handcuffs. It's got to go through the court system, so we're working through that."
The loudest round of applause and cheering followed a brief statement by Steve Fleegle, who can see the Hartland Holdings River Road operation from his home. "I have not heard one positive thing out of this whole hearing tonight, and we've been here for almost an hour."
"All we're doing is enriching people from out of state with these chicken plants," Fleegle said. "I implore you guys to shut this thing down as soon as you can, because it's not fair to us. We were here first. We didn't ask for this, and we don't deserve this."

title: Coffee with the County Brings Representatives and Businesses Together
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Coffee with the County brings representatives and businesses together

 April 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 354
 Words 

 Read News Document

 PRESTON — Tuesday, the Caroline County Chamber of Commerce hosted Coffee with the County, bringing county agencies and business together to discuss different resources.Tracey Snyder, executive director of the Caroline Chamber of Commerce, highlighted the event as one of many planned to allow government representatives and business to meet each other and make connections. About 30 people attended.
"We love doing this. The main reason why we do it is to build communication," Snyder said. "Everybody's doing all their great things in their towns, but we don't always reach over to the next town, and I don't know why that is. So as chamber director that serves the whole county, my goal is to try to build that communication."
The chamber and county representatives participated in a speed-dating-like event Tuesday. For 10 to 15 minutes, a group of representatives would sit with chamber members and discuss their positions and what they offer to their town or to the county.
After hearing from all sitting at the table, representatives would ask different questions to each other on what they could improve and how to help each other.
Multiple business cards were passed around, and connections were made.
"It's giving those businesses more resources," Snyder said. "It's also giving the businesses more resources within our county that they may not know exist. So that's really what it's all about.
"I feel like the chamber is a conduit. That's really our role. We connect others together through networking, marketing and things like this."
Multiple county representatives attended the event and enjoyed the conversation and feedback that was given about the work in the county.
"I mean it's good to interact with the community and the towns to get feedback from them," said county Commissioner Frank Bartz. "The department head directors communicating what they do on a day-to-day basis, which they might not know, and they get to put a face with somebody they haven't met yet. So, that gives them a little bit of a one-on-one to where they can feel free to contact them. They don't feel like, 'Oh, I don't want to bother anybody.' So, that's good on that end of that."

title: Caroline County Towns Forge Connections at Chamber Event
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline County towns forge connections at Chamber event

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 479
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — Around 70 members of the Caroline Chamber of Commerce met at the Greater Impact Church to have a dialogue of connection between six towns in the county.On Oct. 9 representatives from Preston, Denton, Greensboro, Goldsboro, Federalsburg and Ridgely were given 10 minutes to talk about their municipality. There were six tables, one for each municipality, and attendees rotated between them.
Everybody in the room was a stakeholder for Caroline County. A lot of business cards and handshakes were exchanged.
Tracey Snyder, executive director of the Caroline County Chamber of Commerce, coached the town leaders to "Share what is happening in your fabulous, wonderful town. Share who you are and let them share who they are."
She said, "The power is the municipalities. If they don't communicate with each other, how are we going to grow? We need each other. We are a small but mighty county. Not competing, supporting."
Although this was Snyder's idea, she had a think tank to help her.
The audience contained economic development departments, commissioners, CASA, Caroline GOP, Chesapeake College, Channel Marker, Compass Regional Hospice, Choptank Community Health and more.
Not only the town representatives showed up. There were also county, state liaisons in attendance.
Carl Anderton Jr., director of rural economic strategy from the Maryland Department of Commerce and Gov. Wes Moore's office, said, "The whole point is there is strength in numbers.
"There may be something that Federalsburg is doing well that Denton is trying to do. Then Denton uses it from Federalsburg ,and there is no need to recreate the wheel," Anderton said.
He said there are 16 rural counties in Maryland, and his goal was to be available to help counties and municipalities, especially if they are have trouble with agencies.
Amber Korell, town manager of Preston, went from table to table.
"I met so many folks that I need to invite to our Preston Connects Program. I have gotten over twenty business cards. Preston Connects is a program we offer to partners and other organizations to come out to our town and utilize our office space," she said.
Another town representative, Stephanie Berkey, clerk treasurer for the town of Ridgely, shared information about the town's upcoming events.
"We have a website www.christmasinridgely.com It is all things we do throughout the holiday season. Starting at Thanksgiving through New Year's Day. We have a lights display. They are already putting the lights up," she said.
She was very animated in her presentations.
"As a townsperson this was fun. I made some good contacts. I gave a lot of ideas about our holiday Christmas in Ridgely to people," Berkey said.
After attendees rotated to all six tables, Snyder called time and everyone clapped. All the town representatives were called up to the stage for a group photo.
Blue tote bags were given out to everyone so they could carry out all the swag and business cards. People kept talking all the way out to the parking lot.

title: Federalsburg Police Chief Resigns; Sheriff's Office Takes Over Leadership
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Federalsburg police chief resigns; sheriff's office takes over leadership

 July 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline 
 
 375
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — At the July 7 town meeting, Federalsburg Mayor Kim Abner announced Police Chief Joseph Gasser resigned from his position on June 25."The mayor and council would like to announce the resignation of Chief Gasser from the Federalsburg Police Department effective June 25," Abner said. "We want to thank Chief Gasser for his service to the town and wish him well on his future endeavors."
Within the announcement, Abner said that the Caroline County Sheriff's Office would take over leadership of the Federalsburg Police Department to give the mayor and council time to figure out police department leadership.
"I was contacted by the mayor and council and asked to take over day-to-day operations and management oversight of the department," Sheriff Donald Baker said to the Star Democrat in an interview Tuesday. "I agree to do that on an interim basis for 30 to 60 days until the mayor and council decide what they are going to do moving forward and what that looks like for the Federalsburg Police Department."
The mayor also announced a public forum meeting for July 21 at 6 p.m. at the Federalsburg Town Hall to discuss their options moving forward with the police department, public safety and policing.
While the sheriff's office and the town of Federalsburg are in the early stages of conversation, Baker believes all options are on the table for the Federalsburg Police Department, including an memorandum of understanding with the sheriff's office that could discontinue the police department.
"I believe that everything is on the table to include signing an MOU somewhat like Ridgley's, directly with the sheriff's office of the county," Baker said. "Again, everything is on the table. and we are really early in this stage, but we absolutely could absorb any officers that were left."
Gasser was appointed to police chief position in January. He came into the position with a military background, and he had been serving the Town of Federalsburg for almost 30 years.
Ridgley has maintained a contract with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to have assigned officers covering the town since last year. In March 2024, the town suspended its police department amid a state investigation.
More recently, Ridgley has agreed to continue the memorandum of understanding with the sheriff's office for the next fiscal year.

title: Ridgely Commissioners, Residents Weigh in on Potential of Reinstating Police Department
author: Konner Metz
content:
Ridgely commissioners, residents weigh in on potential of reinstating police department

 March 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 769
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Over a year after suspending the now-defunct Ridgely Police Department, town commissioners say reestablishing the force will cost the town nearly double its projected payment to the county sheriff for police coverage.At a workshop Wednesday, Commissioner Brad Sears told residents that restoring the department would cost an estimated $852,000. Ridgely currently receives dedicated coverage from the Caroline County Sheriff's Office based on a memorandum of understanding. Renewing that MOU for fiscal year 2026 would cost $493,000, per estimates.
A number of residents questioned the Town Council's openness to consider reinstating the department. Concerns raised stem back to the town's controversial decision to suspend and subsequently lay off the department last year amid a criminal investigation into the police chief that came up empty.
Residents were only permitted to testify in front of the commissioners Wednesday if they had signed up around a day in advance.
Heather Amador said the workshop felt like the town was "checking a box."
"I feel solid that your minds are made up," Amador told commissioners. "Some of you openly expressed that at the last town meeting. It feels pretty certain that my words and efforts will be for nothing."
"We're not going to make any decisions tonight," Sears said. "We're not really going to take questions, because we want to focus on what you, the public, have to say. And we want to take some time to properly consider what you have to say."
The commissioners suspended former Police Chief Jeff Eckrich and the entire department March 12, 2024, amid a state criminal investigation into Eckrich due to "suspected" perjury and misconduct in office.
On July 25, 2024, an investigation report by the Office of the State Prosecutor found no "sufficient evidence of criminal activity warranting further investigation or prosecution."
But by that time, the Ridgely officers had already been laid off with the start of the new fiscal year July 1. The town began selling and transferring its police vehicles and equipment in the weeks before the state prosecutor's report was released.
Since then, Ridgely has maintained a contract with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to have assigned officers covering the town. Last week, the Sheriff's Office announced a third officer was assigned to the Ridgely patrol group.
At Wednesday's meeting, Sears explained why Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker and Chief Deputy Rodney Helmer weren't in attendance.
"They wanted to attend, but they were advised by their attorney not to attend because there is potential litigation outstanding," Sears said. Lt. George Paugh attended in their place.
While two residents submitted written testimony in support of maintaining Caroline County Sheriff's Office coverage, residents who spoke at the meeting largely asked for two other options: reinstating the town's force or ending the Sheriff's Office contract and operating like towns such as Goldsboro and Preston, which receive general county and state police patrol.
"Since the sheriff has taken over, we've had no community policing like before," said Christine Eckrich, wife of the former Ridgely chief. "And a lot of the hours have not been covered. So now my question is, what are we paying for? Why are we double paying for the Sheriff's Office to come to Ridgely."
Resident Anna Mansfield questioned if the budget estimates for a reestablished town force and the county coverage are comparable.
"Was the Ridgely Police Department afforded the ability to reduce their hours to meet the amount of hours expected for the desired budget?" Mansfield asked commissioners.
Sears, who assumed his seat in July 2024 after the department's suspension earlier that year, prepared the cost estimates by reviewing past police budgets, meeting with a consultant and comparing projections to other local departments.
He said it's key to have "rationale and cost effective reasons" when considering creating a police department.
Resident Jennifer Nesselroad stood up to express her displeasure.
"We had a police department, and we don't need to start a new one because you illegally took ours away," she said, leaving the room.
President John Buckle said in an opening statement that "the commissioners will listen carefully to what everyone has to say." Commissioner John Hurley provided no comment at the workshop.
As the meeting closed, Sears emphasized that reinstating the police department would require infrastructure and safety improvements to the department's office within the town hall building.
"But the police department existed how many years without those features," resident Robin Martin said.
"Things have changed a lot over the last five to 10 years," Sears responded. "The racial incidents, the general degradation of respect for authority, COVID and so on has changed our cultural landscape. Violence is on the upswing."
"It's very difficult to be a police officer," he later added. "It's very difficult to attract and retain police officers."

title: Down to One Officer, Greensboro Considers Closing Police Department
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Down to one officer, Greensboro considers closing police department

 September 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 592
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — The future of the Greensboro Police Department is up in the air.Mayor David Spencer announced at Thursday evening's Greensboro Town Council meeting that the town will consider closing its police department, which is now down to one officer, Chief Lenox Trams.
Four options were provided to the mayor and commissioners by Town Manager Tammy Kelledes:
Continuing running its own police department.Working "in conjunction with" the Caroline County Sheriff's Office "to fill the spots (it doesn't) have now for (its) own officers."Entering into a "contractual agreement" with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office.Closing the police department, not entering into an agreement and turning "the town over to the sheriff's department and the Maryland State Police."
"The current public safety demands are too much for a one-person police department to handle," Spencer said. "In addition, the mayor and council must consider the increasing costs of retaining a police department and the struggles caused by a shortage of police officers and police applicants throughout the state."
"We will listen to all comments and suggestions and take all of those into consideration," he added. "We will not be making a decision tonight."
The mayor emphasized Thursday was just the beginning of a "fluid" and long-term process.
Greensboro has been receiving assistance from county police in recent weeks to reduce the burden on the town's only officer. Spencer said Greensboro has been paying a $75-per-hour rate for county deputies to cover the town, which will continue "in the meantime."
"When they come in here, they're staying here," Spencer said. "They're not patrolling the county, they're only patrolling the town."
A person recently hired by the town did not complete police academy training, Spencer said in response to a resident question.
Spencer said the town has asked Trams to continue going through officer applications on file in hopes that an applicant who is already certified can be brought on board. Otherwise, certification and training can take up to a full year.
"If you put somebody through the academy, it takes about a year," Trams said. "When you hire them after you do the background, for the nine months that they really aren't much good to you, you are paying their salary and their health insurance."
During his department update, Trams urged those with non-emergencies to call the county at 410-479-2515 since the Greensboro department is limited. "If (we're) working, they will certainly send us. If we're not working, then they will send the next agency that is in rotation," he said.
PUBLIC FEEDBACKAfter Spencer read the four options aloud, resident Paula Turner pushed for more details and asked for the town to host a special meeting.
"Of those options, where is the breakdown of cost, of savings?" Turner asked "If No. 4 is voted in, if that's what the town wants, show us how … (the) money that's budgeted will be allocated back into our town. I want numbers."
Kevin Parks spoke in support of the police department remaining. He referenced the struggle to attract police officers due to Maryland's repeal of the Law Enforcement Officers' Bill of Rights back in 2021.
"I don't want to see the police department closed up," Parks said. "The chief's doing the best he can. If you want to fuss about the police department, call your legislators and your senators for the state of Maryland and tell them to give them their bill of rights back."
Spencer said the town's budget has room for three officers. Public Works Supervisor Brandon Cunningham asked if the town would continue paying for county assistance if it hired a second officer only.
"Those decisions have not yet been made," Spencer said.

title: Ridgely Residents Call for Police Department to be Reinstated
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Ridgely residents call for police department to be reinstated

 August 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 665
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Following tense public comment at Monday's Ridgely Town Meeting, residents are calling for the Ridgely Police Department and its officers to be reinstated after nearly five months of suspension.The Commissioners of Ridgely suspended the department in March, with pay, pending an investigation by the Maryland Office of the State Prosecutor. At Monday's meeting, residents raised that the department and its officers had been exonerated by investigators surfaced.
Multiple people asked for the department to be reinstated. Resident James Romph questioned the commissioners and town employees on the investigation.
"What is the update on the Ridgely Police Department investigation?" Romph asked.
"Sir, I'd love to answer that but I was told to keep my mouth shut," David Crist, the town's director of public works, responded.
"I'm going to answer it for you, for the public," Romph said. "The entire police department has been exonerated. The state has concluded their investigation and found no fault with the police department or the police chief, criminally or administratively. They're exonerated."
As of Tuesday, town employees and the Office of the State Prosecutor did not immediately respond to requests regarding the report and whether or not it cleared the department and its officers.
Romph claimed the commissioners had "known for over two weeks and didn't share that with you," speaking to the standing-room-only crowd, which included members of the police department.
"No we have not, we have not been notified," Commissioner John Hurley said. Crist backed the commissioners up, saying they hadn't been notified but confirming that he had been. Romph questioned why Crist did not inform the commissioners or the public.
"From my counsel, I was told this is a personnel matter, you cannot speak," Crist said. "I'm not a lawyer, I don't know law. But if the town attorney tells me to zip it, I'm zipping it."
Since the initial suspension, the town has not provided clear reasoning for the investigation. Nor has the Office of the State Prosecutor.
The town came to a temporary memorandum of understanding with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, agreeing that the Sheriff's Office and Maryland State Police would split duties to cover the suspended department.
In May, the town agreed to a new memorandum of understanding with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, this one providing a "long-term partnership" for fiscal year 2025. It included "a provision for maintaining 480 hours of coverage per month," per a town release, and took effect on July 1.
Caroline County Chief Deputy Rodney Helmer told The Star Democrat on Tuesday that the updated MOU is still in effect. As of Tuesday, the county had not heard from the town requesting to cease the MOU. Such a request would require 30 days of notice, Helmer said.
Residents have brought concerns about the county's law enforcement coverage compared to what town police provided. Resident and business owner Holly Justice says it hasn't been the same.
"When you deal with a big giant, you lose a lot of those small-town things," Justice said in an interview. "The county, they have a lot of area to cover, and although we have officers that they did dedicate to this territory, it's just not the same."
Justice created a petition Tuesday, asking the town to reinstate the officers. As of Tuesday evening, it had over 30 signatures.
"People's lives were jeopardized with this," Justice said. " … These people have families. My heart goes out to them. But I also understand the town's side, being told by their counsel that they can not speak about this matter.
"Instead of joining in with the brigade and yelling and fussing, I said, 'What's a better way to come at this? What's a better way to be heard and be seen?'"
Resident Lakia Harris-Pierce said she believes residents should be informed on the investigation's results. "They need to make the investigation public, we have the right to know," she said.
Town commissioners are meeting in closed session Wednesday afternoon to discuss personnel matters, according to an agenda posted to the town's website.
Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado and Tom McCall contributed reporting to this story.

title: Serving, Protecting for 250 Years - The Caroline County Sheriff's Office Celebrates Its Sesquicentennial
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Serving, protecting for 250 years - The Caroline County Sheriff's Office celebrates its sesquicentennial

 November 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 979
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - To mark the 250th anniversary of the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, a new badge has been struck, containing symbols of its history dating to colonial Maryland.But the badge itself is a symbol of the long line of sheriffs who have held the office since 1773, when Thomas Hughlett of Greensboro was appointed by the British governor after the county was formed from parts of Dorchester and Queen Anne's counties.Bookending the long blue line is Sheriff Donnie Baker, who, like Hughlett, is also a Greensboro native. He's the county's 77th sheriff.Caroline County Deputy Lt. Jacob Andrew is the unofficial historian of the sheriff's office. And because he's the fifth generation of the Andrew family to serve the office during the past century, he's well-qualified for the job."Jake was just teaching me something," Baker said. "I didn't know that the first sheriff was buried up there (in Greensboro)." According to Andrew's research, Hughlett was a plantation owner appointed to a one-year term by the governor to be in charge of weights and scales because he was deemed trustworthy.Ironically, the next year he became captain of the Caroline County Militia Fifth Company, which encompassed Greensboro, Goldsboro and Bridgetown during the American Revolution.Hughlett later became a judge. He is buried in a crypt in a tiny, privately-owned graveyard in a Greensboro subdivision, the site of the Hughlett family farm.During the Civil War, John Wilson Saulsbury served a two-year term from 1861 to 1863 and was required to swear allegiance to the Union.Andrew said Sheriff James Temple, who served from 1923 to 1926 "was actually a pretty cool guy." A veteran of the Spanish-American War, Temple was known as the walking sheriff."He had the first Buick in Caroline County. He always told everybody that," Andrew said. However, "he hated driving it.So, if he had to go serve a warrant on somebody, he'd walk from Denton to Ridgely, lock them up and walk them back." "The original sheriff's office was pretty much a shed on the courthouse green, and it was very easy to break out of," Andrew said. The lynching on the green of Federalsburg blacksmith Marshall Price following accusations of murder in 1895 prompted the government to build a new jail across Gay Street on the Choptank River, where it stands today.In 1921, William Curtis Andrew, Jacob Andrew's great-great grandfather, became sheriff and served a two-year term. His son, William E. Andrew served from 1938 to 1946 and, following a four-year term by Saulsbury Sparks, served again from 1950 to 1961, dying of a heart attack in his office.William's son Louis C. Andrew served from 1961 to 1994, retiring when he was 70. His son, then-Deputy Charles Andrew, served as acting sheriff until Phil Brown was elected sheriff the following year.Back then, the sheriff and his family lived in the center section of what is now the Caroline County jail. Two wings were added to the large brick structure, but Charles Andrew remembers when the original section was home."I got to know a lot of inmates," he said.He recalls the night his "mother had a fit" when a naked woman was brought in by the state police."They had to come in the front door and walk down the hall which separated the living room and dining room directly back to that one-room office" at the back of the house, he said."I would have been seven or eight" years old, Charles Andrew said. "So, she made my father go to the commissioners, and that's when they put stairs on the side of the building to come in the outside door." "Back then, when my father started, he was only making $2,600 a year," he said. "They had to supply their own vehicle. The only thing the county gave them was a radio that went into their own private car." That center section of the current jail is called the Andrew Building today.Until 1994, both the sheriff's office and jail were under the jurisdiction of the sheriff, according to Charles Andrew. When Brown became sheriff, the county Department of Corrections was formed as a separate agency, and Charles Andrew served as the superintendent for 13 years, after serving in the sheriff's office for 20 years.Charles's son Jacob, now the fifth generation to serve in the sheriff's office, serves the county with almost 50 fellow deputies. After serving in the Air Force, Jacob Andrew joined the sheriff's office and has been on the job for 19 years. "I love it. I love my job," he said.The commemorative badge symbolizes not only his family's history of serving county citizens in the sheriff's office, but a long legacy of the office's commitment to public safety stretching back to the nation's founding.At the five points of the badge's star are a Revolutionary War soldier, the Caroline County Circuit Court building, the original courthouse before the renovations, the original sheriff's office on Gay Street, and the current office, completed in 2021 on Double Hills Road."One of the things that former Sheriff Randy Bounds wanted to do was have a wall of sheriff's (pictures)," Baker said."So I told him that Jake is going to fulfill that dream of his." The sheriff's office is seeking memorabilia from the public for a future museum or showcase. If you have any artifacts, photos or clippings you'd like to share, contact Lt. Jacob Andrew at 410-479-4124 or jandrew@carolinemd.org. 
 
 Caption: CONNIE CONNOLLY/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Sheriff Donnie Baker commissioned this commemorative badge for the 250th anniversary of the Caroline County Sheriff's Office
 
COURTESY OF CCSO
 
Joining current Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker, center, are former Sheriff Phil Brown, left, and Sheriff Randy Bounds.
 
COURTESY OF CCSO
 
H. Saulsbury Sparks served as Caroline County Sheriff from 1934 to 1938, and again from 1942 to 1946. Note the handcuffs on his desktop.
 
COURTESY OF CCSO
 
Charles Andrew, left, served as acting sheriff and was a deputy for 20 years with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office.

title: Ridgely Not Planning to Reinstate Police Department
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Ridgely not planning to reinstate police department

 September 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 735
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Despite a state criminal investigation against Ridgely's police chief coming up empty, Ridgely commissioners announced on Monday that they have no plans to reinstate the town's police force, which has been suspended since March.A report from the Maryland Office of the State Prosecutor stated an investigation was opened into Ridgely Police Department Chief Jeff Eckrich due to "suspected" perjury and misconduct in office. The investigation found no "sufficient evidence of criminal activity warranting further investigation or prosecution," the July 25 report said.
The commissioners suspended Eckrich and the entire department on March 12, providing minimal explanation to residents. Since, the town has entered into an agreement with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to provide police coverage in place of the suspended officers. With the start of the new fiscal year July 1, the Ridgely officers were laid off.
Chip MacLeod, an attorney representing the town, read aloud a statement at the beginning of Monday's town meeting.
"The commissioners recognize the pain this unfortunate situation has caused their friends and neighbors in the town," MacLeod stated. "At the same time, the commissioners are pleased that most of the former Ridgely Police Department employees have secured employment elsewhere. Thus, the commissioners realize that those employees would be unlikely to return to their former positions even if those positions were available."
"The commissioners recognize that reestablishing the Ridgely Police Department would be a complex and expensive undertaking," MacLeod later said. "Such an effort would require a high level of citizen support, not just political support, for operating the Ridgely Police Department, and a commitment to funding and seeing the process through. Accordingly, the commissioners believe that it is in the best interest of the town to continue the present arrangement with the sheriff and the county through at least fiscal year 2025 and to reevaluate the sheriff's engagement when preparing the fiscal 2026 budget."
MacLeod said commissioners and town staff will provide no additional comment regarding the police department.
Many residents reacted negatively after the statement was read. Some asked why there wasn't an apology provided to the officers, and others pointed out the town didn't acknowledge the police chief was cleared of wrongdoing.
One resident asked the Caroline County Sheriff's Office sergeant in attendance which three officers are currently assigned to the town for coverage.
"We're not answering no questions. I'm in charge," Commissioner John Buckle said.
Resident Jennifer Nesselroad spoke during public comment, asking the commissioners for an itemized list of police and town vehicles. She also expressed frustration with the commissioners' statement.
"You never apologized for disbanding our police department, not even issuing an apology for everybody being exonerated," Nesselroad said. "That was very, very rude and inconsiderate to us and those police officers that gave every day around this town, even for you all, everybody sitting up here. That was very cowardly."
Heather Amador asked commissioners why the town did not follow its charter, which states the commissioners must hold a vote to remove an officer or town employee.
"A criminal investigation's going to trump anything in the town charter," MacLeod said.
"Absolutely, against one, against the chief," Amador said. "The others were never under investigation."
"You heard the statement I read," MacLeod said. Amador responded, "I did, but it doesn't answer my question."
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Ridgely resident Robin Martin expressed concern over the fact that the commissioners have not clearly stated who directed them to suspend the police department back in March.
Monday's statement from the commissioners noted that on March 12, the Caroline County Sheriff's Office executed a search and seizure warrant issued by the county's circuit court. It stated that "commissioners were directed to order all RPD officers to surrender" firearms, vehicles and other equipment to the town, but did not clarify who provided that direction.
The decision to suspend the department came "without guidance" from the state prosecutor, according to the state prosecutor's report.
"I think we have a distrust for the commissioners of the town," Martin said. "We've been way more involved in things that are happening in the town, because we don't trust that they have our best interests at heart anymore."
During public comment, Martin asked commissioners for "less closed-door activity and more community involvement" in town decisions. After the meeting, Martin said her heart breaks for the officers.
"They participate in everything around town, and I think that's kind of what Ridgely should be about, community policing," Martin said. "This has been something so shameful for the town."

title: Caroline Commissioners Weigh Potential Locations for New Lockerman Middle
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline commissioners weigh potential locations for new Lockerman Middle

 June 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 666
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — During the Caroline County Commissioners' open comment report Tuesday morning, Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter brought up the discussion on Lockerman Middle School's proposed locations.Porter said he preferred that the new middle school go on the North Caroline High School property, one of two locations being considered during the design processes for the building begin. The other location, near the county sheriff's office on Double Hills Road, presents several challenges, Porter said.
"I think at this point I would like to say that I am in favor of the North Carolina location as opposed to being built in town," Porter said.
Commissioners Frank Bartz agreed with Porter and cited traffic and safety concerns on Route 404.
The commissioners also had discussions about the school's location at their meeting two weeks ago.
At that meeting, County Administrator Kathleen Freeman presented the two location options. Commissioners President Travis Breeding sparked a conversation about how much sway the commissioners have over the school's location.
"How much influence do the commissioners actually have over where the school gets constructed?" Breeding asked two weeks ago. "As part of the funding of this, other than a survey, we haven't really been consulted."
Breeding then explained the issues they would run into with each potential location.
"From what I gather, it seemed like a lot of people really preferred the Double Hills location. But, with Double Hills, we've got to work out a ton of details with the Town of Denton as far as sewer, water allocation for that to work, potentially pump station upgrades," Breeding said.
He then mentioned traffic issues on Route 404 with beach traffic towards the end of the school year and students from northern county towns like Marydale, who would have to take the bus a long distance to the potential Double Hills location.
Porter, said he didn't recall that "the county did not have a lot of input" on the design of new county buildings in the past.
Freeman assured Breeding that the county will be involved with the full feasibility study for both sites to determine which site makes the most sense.
Breeding also brought forward discussion of how much influence the commissioners will have for the design of the school.
"Then also, how much input do we have over the the design?" Breeding asked. "I mean, we don't want a situation where we're building something that's way more expensive than it needs to be or making it as functional as we can and keeping the cost as low as we can."
Bartz raised an issue where if the county has to build a new detention center, a school on the Double Hills Road site would cause a problem. The Caroline County Sheriff's Office is located near that Double Hills Road site, making the location logical for a detention center, he said.
The county is in talks with Queen Anne's County about a new 388-bed regional detention center that would house all Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent county prisoners. After conversations about control and cost of the center, discussions between the three counties have slowed down.
Lockerman name
Porter pointed out conversation that are being had about the Lockerman's name staying at the location of the current building instead of being attached to the new school.
Though the existing building will no longer be used as a school when the new school is built, Porter said he was in favor of keeping the Lockerman name attached to the facility in the interest of honoring its history.
"I think it's going to be important that the history of the school and the name of Lockerman be retained," he said. "I don't know what the future use is going to be for that building, but it's important, I think, from the alumni standpoint, from the community standpoint, that the history be be kept there for whatever use is going to be done in the future."
Breeding suggested drafting a letter of intent to the Caroline County Board of Education stating that it would be the commissioners' intention to retain the name of the building.
